teile.einleitung: A hybrid regime is a mixture of democracy and dictatorship. There are elections, but they are not truly free and fair. The opposition, the media and the courts are obstructed or controlled.
wichtigste: A hybrid regime mixes democratic and authoritarian features.
In “The Economist” Democracy Index, hybrid regimes score more than 4 and at most 6 out of 10 points.
The V-Dem institute speaks of electoral autocracies.
Levitsky and Way coined the term “competitive authoritarianism”.
In 2014 Viktor Orbán spoke of an “illiberal democracy”.

abschnitte.text: Not every country is either a democracy or a dictatorship. Many states lie somewhere in between. In a **hybrid regime** elections take place, and there are often opposition parties too. But the government makes sure it can hardly lose. For example, it controls important **media**, obstructs critics or influences the **courts**. That is why a change of power through elections is very difficult.

The magazine “**The Economist**” publishes a **Democracy Index** in which every state gets 0 to 10 points. More than 4 and at most 6 points means a hybrid regime; below that, authoritarian regimes begin. The research institute **V-Dem** in Gothenburg distinguishes between closed autocracies, **electoral autocracies**, electoral democracies and liberal democracies. In electoral autocracies there are elections with several parties, but no real competition. Switzerland counts as a democracy in both classifications.

The researchers **Steven Levitsky** and **Lucan Way** speak of **competitive authoritarianism**. The opposition is allowed to stand, but because of unfair conditions it has hardly any chance of winning. In 2014 the Hungarian Prime Minister **Viktor Orbán** said in a speech that he wanted to build an “**illiberal democracy**”. What he meant was a state with elections, but with weakened civil liberties. Whether a particular country is a hybrid regime is often judged differently.

gewusst: The word “hybrid” means “mixed” or “made up of different things”.

teile.einleitung: In Poland, Józef Piłsudski is regarded as the founding father of the independent state after the First World War. From 1926, however, he ruled in an authoritarian way and severely restricted democracy.
wichtigste: Piłsudski was head of state of independent Poland from 1918 to 1922.
In 1920 Poland stopped the Red Army in the “Miracle on the Vistula”.
With the May Coup of 1926 he took power.
His regime was called Sanacja, which means “healing”.
Opponents were convicted in the Brest trial or held in the Bereza Kartuska camp.
In 1934 Poland signed a non-aggression pact with the German Reich.

abschnitte.text: In the First World War Piłsudski led Polish **Legions**. He refused to have them swear an oath to the Central Powers and was arrested. In 1917 and 1918 the Germans held him prisoner in **Magdeburg Fortress**. In November 1918 he was released and returned to Warsaw. He became provisional head of state, in Polish **Naczelnik Państwa**.

In the **Polish-Soviet War** the Red Army advanced as far as Warsaw in 1920. In the Battle of Warsaw in August 1920 Poland stopped the advance. This victory is called the **“Miracle on the Vistula”**. It secured the independence of the young state.

In **May 1926** troops loyal to Piłsudski marched on Warsaw. After fighting, the government resigned. Piłsudski then dominated Poland until his death in 1935. His regime called itself **Sanacja**, meaning “healing”. Political life was to be “healed” of corruption and quarrels between parties.

In 1930 the regime had members of parliament from the centre-left opposition imprisoned in **Brest Fortress**. In the **Brest trial** they were sentenced to prison terms. From 1934 there was the **Bereza Kartuska** camp, where opponents were held without a court ruling. The **April Constitution** of 1935 greatly strengthened the president at the expense of parliament.

Piłsudski wanted to make Poland safe between Germany and the Soviet Union. A non-aggression treaty with the Soviet Union had existed since 1932. In January 1934 Poland also signed a non-aggression pact with the **German Reich**. Hitler cancelled it in 1939.

gewusst: Piłsudski's body lies in Wawel Cathedral in Kraków, but his heart is in his mother's grave in Vilnius.
His imprisonment in Magdeburg made Piłsudski a national hero.

teile.einleitung: In a state of emergency a government is given special powers because of a serious crisis. Fundamental rights can be restricted for a time. Because this is dangerous, clear rules and limits are needed.
wichtigste: In a state of emergency the government receives special powers.
It is only meant to last as long as the crisis lasts.
Dictators like to exploit it to suspend fundamental rights.
The ban on torture always applies, even in an emergency.
In Switzerland Article 185 of the Federal Constitution allows emergency ordinances for a limited time.

abschnitte.titel: What is a state of emergency?
abschnitte.text: A **state of emergency** is declared when a state is in great danger, for example through war, terrorism, uprisings or natural disasters. The government may then act more quickly, often without asking parliament. **Fundamental rights**, such as freedom of assembly, can be restricted. A particularly strict form is **martial law**, under which the army takes over police tasks.

Dictators like to exploit a state of emergency, because it lets them suspend fundamental rights and persecute opponents. In Egypt it was in force for about 30 years after the assassination of President **Anwar Sadat** in 1981, until 2012. In Poland General Wojciech Jaruzelski declared martial law on 13 December 1981 and banned the trade union **Solidarność**. In 1922 the constitutional lawyer **Carl Schmitt** wrote: “Sovereign is he who decides on the exception.”

After the terrorist attacks in **Paris** on 13 November 2015, a state of emergency was in force in France for about two years. After the failed **coup attempt** in July 2016, Turkey declared a state of emergency. During this time tens of thousands of people were arrested or dismissed. In **South Korea** President Yoon Suk-yeol declared martial law on 3 December 2024, but parliament lifted it that same night.

Article 15 of the **European Convention on Human Rights** allows departures from some rights in an emergency. But some rights always apply, for example the **ban on torture**. Courts and parliaments are also meant to make sure that special powers do not last longer than necessary.

Under **Article 185** paragraph 3 of the Federal Constitution, the Federal Council can issue ordinances in the event of serious disturbances to public order or security. These **emergency ordinances** must be limited in time. During the coronavirus pandemic in 2020 the Federal Council declared an “extraordinary situation” and issued emergency law. After that parliament had to decide on further measures.

gewusst: In the Second World War the Federal Council governed with special powers that parliament had given it.
The state of emergency in Egypt lasted longer than many people there had been alive.

teile.einleitung: The Islamic Revolution changed Iran fundamentally in 1979. The Shah was overthrown, and the monarchy became an Islamic Republic under Ayatollah Khomeini.
wichtigste: The revolution overthrew Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.
The Shah left Iran on 16 January 1979.
His secret police, SAVAK, was feared.
On 1 April 1979 Khomeini proclaimed the Islamic Republic of Iran.
The hostage-taking at the US embassy lasted 444 days.
Since 1980 Switzerland has been the protecting power for the USA in Iran.

abschnitte.text: Before 1979 Iran was ruled by **Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi**. His secret police, **SAVAK**, spied on opposition members, arrested them and tortured them. This made the regime hated by many people. Very different groups stood against the Shah: clergy, students, left-wingers and liberals.

In 1978 the protests grew bigger and bigger. On 8 September 1978, **“Black Friday”**, the military fired on a rally in Jaleh Square in Tehran. After that, reconciliation was hardly possible any more. On 16 January 1979 the Shah left the country. His last Prime Minister, **Shapour Bakhtiar**, stayed in office for only about five weeks and fled to France.

After a **referendum** at the end of March 1979, **Ayatollah Khomeini** proclaimed the Islamic Republic of Iran on 1 April 1979. An overwhelming majority had voted in favour. Since then religious leaders in Iran have had great political power. The Shah died in exile in Egypt in 1980.

On 4 November 1979 students occupied the **US embassy** in Tehran and held 52 Americans captive. The hostages were only released in January 1981, after **444 days**. The USA broke off relations with Iran. Since 1980 **Switzerland**, as the **protecting power**, has represented the interests of the USA in Iran. It also passes on messages between the two states.
In September 1980 Iraq attacked the weakened Iran. This began the **First Gulf War**. It lasted eight years and ended in 1988 with a ceasefire. Hundreds of thousands of people were killed.

gewusst: For decades the Swiss embassy in Tehran has represented the USA, even though the two countries have no direct relations.
The Tehran hostage crisis lasted 444 days.

teile.einleitung: Liu Xiaobo was a Chinese literary critic and human rights activist. For his non-violent struggle for freedom, he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2010 while he was in prison.
wichtigste: Liu Xiaobo came from China.
In 1989 he supported the student protests in Beijing with a hunger strike.
In 2008 he co-wrote Charter 08.
In 2009 he was sentenced to 11 years in prison.
In 2010 he received the Nobel Peace Prize, and in Oslo an empty chair stood in his place.
He died in July 2017 as a prisoner.

abschnitte.text: In 1989, students protested for more freedom in **Tiananmen Square** in Beijing. Liu Xiaobo supported them and went on **hunger strike**. When the military crushed the protests, he helped during the night so that many students could leave the square.

In 2008, Liu Xiaobo co-wrote **Charter 08**. Among other things, the manifesto called for the **separation of powers**, free elections and **freedom of expression**. Separation of powers means that the government, parliament and the courts are kept apart. The name is modelled on **Charter 77**, a civil rights movement in Czechoslovakia.

In 2009, a Beijing court sentenced Liu to **11 years** in prison for “inciting subversion of state power”. In 2010 he received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. Neither he nor his family were allowed to travel to **Oslo**. At the ceremony, an **empty chair** stood in his place. It became a symbol of him.

Liu Xiaobo died of liver cancer in **July 2017** without ever being free again. His wife **Liu Xia** was punished too, even though she was never charged. She was kept under **house arrest** for years. Only in 2018 was she allowed to leave for Germany.

gewusst: Liu Xiaobo received the Nobel Peace Prize while he was in prison.
The empty chair in Oslo became a worldwide sign for imprisoned critics of regimes.

teile.einleitung: Carl Lutz was a Swiss diplomat. During the Second World War he saved tens of thousands of Jews in Budapest from deportation. He is regarded as one of the greatest rescuers of that time.
wichtigste: Carl Lutz came from Walzenhausen in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden.
From 1935 to 1940 he worked in Jaffa in Palestine.
In Budapest he issued letters of protection.
The Glass House became a place of refuge for thousands.
He is credited with saving about 62,000 people.
Only in 1995 was he rehabilitated by the Federal Council.

abschnitte.text: Carl Lutz was born in 1895 in **Walzenhausen** in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden. As a young man he went to the USA and entered Swiss service there. From 1935 to 1940 he worked as a consular official in **Jaffa** in Palestine. There he got to know about Jewish immigration to Palestine. This experience helped him later.

From 1942 Lutz worked as vice-consul at the Swiss legation in **Budapest**. There he also represented the interests of other states. In 1944 the deportations of Hungarian Jews to extermination camps began. Lutz issued **letters of protection**, which placed their holders under Swiss protection. Originally they were meant for emigrants to Palestine, but he greatly extended them.

The **Glass House** was a former glass factory in Budapest. Lutz declared it an annexe of the Swiss legation. Thousands of people found protection there. He worked together with other diplomats, for example the Swede **Raoul Wallenberg**. In total Lutz is credited with saving **about 62,000** people.

After the war the Swiss authorities at first accused him of having **exceeded his powers**. An inquiry did find that his conduct had been correct, but the protective papers were regarded as going beyond his authority. The Yad Vashem memorial in Israel honoured him as **Righteous Among the Nations**. Only in 1995, twenty years after his death, was he rehabilitated by the **Federal Council**.

gewusst: The rescue carried out by Carl Lutz is regarded as one of the largest civilian rescue operations of the Second World War.
His wife, Gertrud Lutz, helped him with the rescue work.

teile.einleitung: Fascism is a political movement that came into being in Italy after the First World War. Benito Mussolini founded it and set up a dictatorship. The name goes back to an old Roman symbol.
wichtigste: The term comes from the Italian word “fascio”, meaning bundle or league.
In ancient Rome the fasces were bundles of rods with an axe.
The lictors carried the fasces in front of senior officials.
In 1919 Mussolini founded the “Fasci di combattimento” in Milan.
Fascism includes a cult of the leader and a ban on the opposition.
The coat of arms of the canton of St Gallen shows a bundle of rods with no connection to fascism.

abschnitte.text: **“Fascio”** means bundle or league in Italian. In ancient Rome there were the **fasces**: wooden rods tied together, often with an axe in the middle. They showed the power of the highest officials to punish. Attendants, the **lictors**, carried them in front of officials such as the consuls. That is why they are also called **lictors’ bundles**.

On 23 March 1919 **Benito Mussolini** founded the **“Fasci italiani di combattimento”**, meaning fighting leagues, in Milan. In 1921 this became the National Fascist Party. From 1922 Mussolini ruled Italy and built up a dictatorship. For the fascists the bundle meant **strength through unity**: a single rod breaks easily, but a whole bundle does not. The people were to be united under one leader.

A fascist state puts a **leader** above everything and promotes a **cult of the leader** around him. Other parties and any opposition are banned. The press and the courts are controlled. The fascists used the **Roman salute** with the right arm stretched out. They claimed it came from ancient Rome and in this way wanted to recall the greatness of the Roman Empire. National Socialism in Germany also took over many features of fascism.

abschnitte.titel: The coat of arms of St Gallen
abschnitte.text: Since the canton was founded in 1803, the coat of arms of the canton of **St Gallen** has shown a **bundle of rods** with an axe. It has nothing to do with fascism, because it is more than a hundred years older. It stands for the unity of the districts of that time. In the 1930s there were also fascist groups in Switzerland, the so-called **Fronts**. But they had little success in elections.

gewusst: The French Republic also used the fasces as a symbol for a long time, with no fascist meaning at all.
Mussolini had himself called “Duce”, which means leader.

teile.einleitung: A political prisoner is a person who is locked up because of their opinions, their political activity or their work on behalf of others. They have not committed a real crime but are inconvenient for those in power. There are many political prisoners especially in dictatorships.
wichtigste: Someone who is locked up because of their opinions is called a political prisoner.
Political prisoners have usually fought peacefully for freedom, rights or democracy.
They are often convicted without a fair trial or in a show trial.
The organisation Amnesty International has worked for such prisoners since 1961.
Amnesty calls people imprisoned for their beliefs “prisoners of conscience”.
Nelson Mandela was a political prisoner in South Africa for 27 years.
In a state under the rule of law, nobody may be locked up because of their opinions.

abschnitte.text: A **political prisoner** is in prison because they spoke out or became involved politically. This can be a newspaper article, taking part in a demonstration or founding a party. The government often claims that the person committed a different crime. In truth, it wants to **silence** critics.

Political prisoners often do not get a fair **trial**. Sometimes they are held without charge, and sometimes the verdict has been decided beforehand. Many have no free access to a lawyer or to their family. In some countries they are also mistreated or tortured in prison.

In 1961 the British lawyer **Peter Benenson** called on people to stand up for prisoners all over the world. This led to the human rights organisation **Amnesty International**, whose symbol is a candle in barbed wire. Its members write letters to governments and draw attention to prisoners. Amnesty also has a Swiss section based in Bern.

**Nelson Mandela** spent 27 years in prison in South Africa, many of them on the prison island of Robben Island. After his release in 1990, he became the first Black president of his country in 1994. The Chinese writer Liu Xiaobo received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2010 while he was in prison. Today too, in many countries there are journalists, students and politicians who are imprisoned because of their opinions.

abschnitte.titel: Protection under the rule of law
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, the Federal Constitution and the **European Convention on Human Rights** protect people from being punished for their opinions. Independent courts check whether an arrest is lawful. Everyone has the right to a lawyer and a fair trial. These rules are an important difference between a state under the rule of law and a dictatorship.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who is locked up only because of their beliefs and has not used violence.
A worldwide organisation that works for human rights and for prisoners.
A court case in which it is decided whether someone is guilty.
Rights that all people have, for example freedom and protection from torture.

gewusst: In 1936 the German journalist Carl von Ossietzky received the Nobel Peace Prize for 1935 while he was being held prisoner by the National Socialists.
A single letter can achieve little, but thousands of letters from Amnesty members have already helped prisoners gain their freedom.

teile.einleitung: In the autumn of 2022 Iran saw its largest protests for years. They were triggered by the death in police custody of the young Kurdish woman Jina Mahsa Amini. Above all, women and young people demanded more freedom.
wichtigste: Jina Mahsa Amini died on 16 September 2022 at the age of 22.
The morality police had arrested her for supposedly wearing the wrong clothes.
At the heart of it was the compulsory headscarf for women.
The slogan “Woman, Life, Freedom” became known worldwide.
The government responded with violence, arrests, executions and internet blocks.
In 2023 Amini and the movement received the Sakharov Prize.

abschnitte.text: **Jina Mahsa Amini** was a 22-year-old Kurdish woman from the town of Saqqez. In September 2022 she was arrested in Tehran by the **morality police**. This police force enforced the strict dress rules and accused her of breaking them. Shortly afterwards, on **16 September 2022**, Amini died in custody. Her death set off protests across the country.

Since the Islamic Revolution, women in Iran have had to wear a **headscarf** in public. Many feel this rule is a sign of oppression. During the protests, women took off their headscarves as a demonstration, waved them or burned them. Many also cut off their hair in public.

The slogan **“Woman, Life, Freedom”** comes from the Kurdish women's movement. It became the motto of the protests throughout the country. In many cities around the world, including in Switzerland, people took to the streets in solidarity. As well as women, many students, schoolgirls and workers took part.

The security forces took **violent** action against the demonstrators. Many people were killed, and thousands were **arrested**. Several protesters were even **executed** after trials. The authorities repeatedly blocked mobile **internet** and platforms such as Instagram and WhatsApp. This was meant to stop videos from reaching other countries.

In 2023 the European Parliament awarded Jina Mahsa Amini and the protest movement the **Sakharov Prize** for Freedom of Thought. In the same year, the Iranian women's rights activist **Narges Mohammadi** received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. She was in prison at the time and could not accept the prize herself.

gewusst: At the 2023 Nobel Peace Prize ceremony, Narges Mohammadi's two children accepted the prize on her behalf.
Jina is Amini's Kurdish name, and Mahsa her official Persian name.

teile.einleitung: On 20 July 1944 a group of officers tried to kill Adolf Hitler with a bomb. They wanted to end the war and the crimes of the Nazi state. The assassination attempt failed.
wichtigste: Colonel Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg planted the bomb.
The assassination attempt took place at the Wolf’s Lair in East Prussia.
The bomb was hidden in a briefcase.
A heavy map table protected Hitler from the full force of the blast.
With the “Valkyrie” plan the conspirators wanted to take power.
Stauffenberg was shot that night at the Bendlerblock in Berlin.

abschnitte.text: **Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg** was a **colonel** on the General Staff. He had been badly wounded in the war. As chief of staff of the Replacement Army he was allowed to attend briefings with Hitler. He belonged to a circle of officers and civilians who wanted to overthrow Hitler.

abschnitte.titel: The bomb at the Wolf’s Lair
abschnitte.text: The **Wolf’s Lair** near Rastenburg in East Prussia, in what is now Poland, was one of **Hitler’s headquarters**. Stauffenberg brought the bomb in a **briefcase** and placed it near Hitler. Then he left the room on a pretext. The briefing took place in a wooden hut, not in the bunker. The briefcase stood behind a massive wooden **map table**, which is why Hitler survived with slight injuries.

Stauffenberg flew to Berlin to lead the overthrow. The **“Valkyrie”** plan was actually intended for an emergency inside the country. The conspirators wanted to use it to take over the government with the Replacement Army. But soon it became known that Hitler was alive, and many orders were not carried out.

That same night Stauffenberg and some fellow conspirators were shot in the courtyard of the **Bendlerblock** in Berlin. After that the regime had many people arrested. The judge **Roland Freisler** held show trials at the People’s Court, in which he shouted at and humiliated the accused. Many were sentenced to death and executed.

Today the Bendlerblock houses the **German Resistance Memorial Centre**. In Germany 20 July is a day of remembrance for the resistance against National Socialism. The conspirators are seen as people who risked their lives to end an unjust regime.

gewusst: Four people in the room died in the explosion, while Hitler himself was only slightly injured.
Today the Bendlerblock is once again used by the German Ministry of Defence.

teile.einleitung: In the 1980s, Manuel Noriega was the most powerful man in Panama. As head of the army he controlled the country without officially being president. In 1989 he was overthrown by a US military invasion.
wichtigste: From 1983, Noriega ruled Panama as commander-in-chief of the armed forces.
His patron was the ruler Omar Torrijos, who died in a plane crash in 1981.
Noriega worked as an informant for the CIA for years.
In December 1989, the USA invaded Panama in Operation Just Cause.
In 1992 he was convicted in the USA of drug trafficking and money laundering.

abschnitte.text: Noriega made a career in Panama's army. His patron was **Omar Torrijos**, who led Panama as its ruler from 1968. Under him, Noriega ran the intelligence service. After Torrijos died in a **plane crash** in 1981, Noriega rose further. From 1983 he was **commander-in-chief of the armed forces** and thus the real ruler. This is called a **de facto ruler**: he held the power, even though others were officially president.

For years, Noriega worked as an **informant** for the **CIA**, the foreign intelligence service of the USA. At the same time, he helped drug traffickers and earned a lot of money. Opponents were persecuted. In 1985 the critic **Hugo Spadafora** was murdered, and Noriega was blamed for the crime. When his candidate lost the 1989 election, Noriega had it declared invalid.

In December 1989, the USA sent troops to Panama. The military operation was called **Operation Just Cause**. During the invasion, **Guillermo Endara**, the winner of the 1989 election, was sworn in as president. Noriega fled to the **Vatican embassy** in Panama City. At the beginning of January 1990 he surrendered to the US troops.

abschnitte.titel: Trial and the end of his life
abschnitte.text: Noriega was taken to the USA and put on trial. In 1992 he was sentenced to a long prison term for **drug trafficking and money laundering**. Later he was extradited to France and then to Panama, where he had also been convicted. He died in Panama in 2017.

gewusst: Outside the Vatican embassy, US soldiers played loud rock music for days to make Noriega give up.
Because of the scars on his face, Noriega had the nickname “Pineapple Face”.

teile.einleitung: The Ministry for State Security, “Stasi” for short, was the secret police and intelligence service of the GDR. It watched its own population, spied on people and persecuted critics of the government. The Stasi is regarded as one of the largest surveillance systems in history.
wichtigste: The Stasi was the secret police of the GDR and watched the population.
It was founded on 8 February 1950 and existed until 1990.
Its head from 1957 to 1989 was Erich Mielke.
The Stasi called itself the “shield and sword of the party”, meaning the state party, the SED.
In 1989 it had about 91,000 full-time staff and around 189,000 unofficial collaborators.
After the Peaceful Revolution, citizens occupied the Stasi buildings.
Today the people affected can look at their Stasi files.

abschnitte.text: The **GDR** (German Democratic Republic) was a state in the east of Germany from 1949 to 1990, governed by the **SED** party. The Ministry for State Security was its secret police and its intelligence service at the same time. Its headquarters were in Berlin-Lichtenberg on Normannenstrasse. From 1957 to 1989, **Erich Mielke** ran the Stasi.

The Stasi wanted to know everything that people thought and did. It tapped telephones, opened letters and hid bugs in flats. Particularly important were the **unofficial collaborators**, IM for short, who spied on friends, neighbours, colleagues or even family members. In 1989 there were about 189,000 such informers.

Anyone who criticised the government, wanted to flee to the West or worked for peace in the church came to the attention of the Stasi. Some were arrested and interrogated in the **Berlin-Hohenschönhausen** prison. Others were secretly “decomposed”: the Stasi deliberately destroyed their reputation, their work and their friendships. Many victims were still suffering the consequences years later.

In the autumn of 1989, hundreds of thousands of people in the GDR demonstrated for freedom; this is called the **Peaceful Revolution**. When the Stasi began destroying its files, citizens occupied its offices, and on 15 January 1990 also the headquarters in Berlin. In this way a large part of the files was saved. In 1990 the Stasi was dissolved, shortly before Germany was reunified.

If the saved documents were placed in a row, they would be more than 100 kilometres long. Since 1992, the people affected have been allowed to read what the Stasi collected about them. Some found out that good friends had betrayed them. Since 2021 the files have been managed by the **Federal Archives**, and experts are painstakingly piecing torn-up papers back together.

begriffe.erklaerung: A police force that works in secret and watches its own population.
A secret informer who spied on other people for the Stasi.
German Democratic Republic, a state in the east of Germany from 1949 to 1990.
The state party of the GDR, which governed the country alone.

gewusst: The Stasi even collected smell samples from people in jars so that sniffer dogs could track them down later.
The former Stasi prison in Berlin-Hohenschönhausen is now a memorial that you can visit.
The film “The Lives of Others” about the Stasi won an Oscar in 2007.

teile.einleitung: Muammar Gaddafi ruled Libya for over 40 years, from 1969 to 2011. He came to power through a coup and ruled as a dictator. He also had a fierce quarrel with Switzerland.
wichtigste: Gaddafi overthrew the King of Libya in a coup in 1969.
He wrote down his ideas in the “Green Book”.
From 1977 he called his system the Jamahiriya.
The Lockerbie aircraft bombing in 1988 was blamed on his regime.
In 2008 the arrest of his son Hannibal in Geneva caused a crisis with Switzerland.
In October 2011 he was killed by rebels.

abschnitte.text: Gaddafi was a young officer. On 1 September 1969, he and other officers overthrew King **Idris** in a bloodless **coup**. After that he led Libya with great power. The capital is **Tripoli**, where Gaddafi had his seat of government. Libya is rich in **oil**, which brought him a lot of money.

Gaddafi wrote down his political ideas in the **Green Book**. From 1977 he called his system the **Jamahiriya**, which means something like “rule of the masses”. Officially, the people were supposed to govern themselves in assemblies. In reality, power lay with Gaddafi and his trusted circle. Critics were persecuted, and there were no free elections.

On 21 December 1988, a passenger aircraft exploded over the Scottish town of **Lockerbie**. 270 people died. The attack was blamed on the Libyan regime. Libya was under **sanctions** for a long time. Only after many years did Libya pay compensation and move closer to the West again.

In July 2008, police in **Geneva** arrested Gaddafi's son **Hannibal** because employees had accused him. Gaddafi reacted furiously. In Libya, two Swiss business people were detained, one of them for almost two years. In 2009 Gaddafi even suggested dissolving Switzerland and **dividing it among its neighbouring countries**. Only in 2010 did the situation ease.

In 2011 there were protests in many Arab countries, the **Arab Spring**. In Libya too, people rose up against Gaddafi. He had the army fight them. NATO intervened with air strikes to protect the population. In October 2011, Gaddafi was captured and killed by rebels near his home town of Sirte.

gewusst: When travelling, Gaddafi often had a large Bedouin tent put up in which he received guests.
Libya's flag under Gaddafi was completely green, without any symbol.

teile.einleitung: Free elections are a hallmark of every democracy. The people decide who represents them in parliament or in government. In a dictatorship free elections are usually missing, or they are only for show.
wichtigste: In free elections you can choose between different parties and people.
In a secret ballot nobody can see whom you vote for.
In dictatorships there is often no real choice, or elections are rigged.
In Switzerland you may vote in federal elections from the age of 18.
The National Council is elected every four years.
Since 1971 women in Switzerland have been allowed to vote at national level.

abschnitte.text: An election is free when everyone can decide without being **forced**. Several parties and people are standing. The vote is **secret**: everyone fills in their ballot paper alone, and nobody sees whom they vote for. That way nobody can put pressure on anyone. The votes are counted honestly, and whoever loses accepts the result.

Dictatorships sometimes hold elections too. But often only one party or one candidate is standing, so there is **no real choice**. Sometimes elections are also **rigged**: votes are counted wrongly or invented. The result is then fixed in advance. Because the people cannot vote freely, they cannot replace the rulers either.

In Switzerland the **National Council** is elected anew every four years, most recently in the autumn of 2023. It has 200 members. To vote in federal elections you must be a Swiss citizen and at least **18 years** old. You put your ballot paper into a **ballot box**. Today, however, a great many people vote by post, in other words they send their ballot paper by mail.

For a long time only men were allowed to vote in Switzerland. Only in **1971** did Swiss men approve **votes for women** at federal level. Since then women have been allowed to vote in national elections and referendums. In the same year the first women were elected to the National Council. The canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden only introduced votes for women on cantonal matters in 1990, after a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court.

gewusst: In the canton of Glarus young people can already take part in cantonal and municipal elections and votes at the age of 16.
In Appenzell Innerrhoden women were only allowed to have a say on cantonal matters from 1990.

teile.einleitung: Democracy is a form of state in which the people can freely choose who governs. The word comes from Greek and means “rule by the people”. Democracy is the opposite of dictatorship, and Switzerland is one of the best-known examples of it.
wichtigste: In a democracy the people choose in free elections who governs.
Democracy is the opposite of dictatorship.
The idea comes from ancient Athens.
Regular, competitive elections make a peaceful change of power possible and limit terms of office.
Fundamental rights such as freedom of opinion and freedom of the press are important for every democracy.
Switzerland is a semi-direct democracy with many referendums.
The separation of powers prevents anyone from gaining too much power.

abschnitte.text: The word **democracy** is made up of the Greek words “demos”, meaning people, and “kratia”, meaning rule. In ancient **Athens**, about 2,500 years ago, the citizens met in the popular assembly and decided together. At that time, however, only free men were allowed to take part, not women, slaves or foreigners. Modern democracy developed mainly from the 18th century onwards.

In a democracy the people elect the government and parliament in **free elections**. Free means that everyone may vote in secret and that there is a real choice between several parties. After a certain time there is a new election. In this way a government that the people do not like can be voted out peacefully. Courts and the media keep a check on those in power.

In a **direct democracy** the people themselves vote on specific issues. In a **representative democracy** the people elect representatives, who then decide. Most countries, such as Germany or France, are mainly representative. Switzerland combines both and is therefore called a **semi-direct democracy**.

Swiss citizens aged 18 and over may vote in elections and referendums at federal level. There are referendums several times a year. With a **popular initiative** and 100,000 signatures you can demand a change to the Federal Constitution. With a referendum and 50,000 signatures you can have a vote held on a new law. In the cantons of Appenzell Innerrhoden and Glarus there is still the **Landsgemeinde**, an open-air assembly where people vote by raising their hands.

For a democracy to work it needs **fundamental rights** such as freedom of opinion, freedom of assembly and freedom of the press. Regular elections with real competition limit the time that those in power can stay in office. The separation of powers makes sure that parliament, government and the courts check one another. Minorities are also protected, even if the majority thinks differently.

Democracies were not always open to everyone either. In Switzerland women only got the right to vote and stand for election at federal level in 1971. Appenzell Innerrhoden had to introduce it in 1990 after a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court. Today many people around the world live in democracies, but by no means all.

begriffe.erklaerung: A proposal from the people that everyone votes on once enough signatures have been collected.
A vote by the people on a law that parliament has passed.
Rights that every person has in relation to the state, for example freedom of opinion.
The right to take part in referendums and elections.

gewusst: In Switzerland people vote on specific issues more often than in almost any other country in the world.
In ancient Athens some offices were not elected, but drawn by lot among the citizens.

teile.einleitung: Oligarchy comes from Greek and means “rule by the few”. It refers to a system in which a small group, often rich or noble families, holds power and governs mainly for its own benefit.
wichtigste: Oligarchy means rule by the few.
For Aristotle, oligarchy was the self-serving rule of the rich.
In ancient Athens there were short-lived oligarchic governments in 411 and 404 BC.
After 1297, Venice became an oligarchy of nobles.
In Swiss cities such as Bern, a few patrician families governed until 1798.
In Russia, very rich and influential business people are called oligarchs.

abschnitte.titel: Aristotle and the forms of government
abschnitte.text: The Greek thinker **Aristotle** sorted forms of government according to who rules and for whose benefit. If a few good people rule for the good of all, he spoke of **aristocracy**. If a few rule for their own advantage, he called this **oligarchy**. For him these were mainly the rich. This classification is still used today.

During the Peloponnesian War, oligarchs in Athens overthrew the popular assembly in 411 BC. The **Council of Four Hundred** lasted only a few months. After the defeat by Sparta, the **Thirty Tyrants** ruled by force in 404 BC, but democracy returned as early as 403 BC. In **Venice**, the **Serrata** of 1297 limited the Great Council to old noble families.

There were also oligarchies in the old Swiss Confederation. In **Bern**, **Lucerne**, **Fribourg** and **Solothurn**, only a few so-called families eligible for government could join the government. This system is called the **patriciate**. Other citizens and the rural population had hardly any say. This system ended with the French invasion in 1798.

The sociologist **Robert Michels** studied the German SPD. In 1911 he put forward the “iron law of oligarchy”. It says that large organisations such as parties or associations produce a small leadership group over time. Even democratic groups, he said, are not protected from this. This theory is still debated today.

After the end of the Soviet Union, state enterprises in Russia were privatised. In the **loans-for-shares auctions** of 1995, large companies went cheaply to a few bankers. In the mid-1990s these **oligarchs** had great political influence and supported Boris Yeltsin's re-election in 1996. People mockingly spoke of the “rule of the seven bankers”.

gewusst: The Thirty Tyrants ruled Athens for only about a year.
The patriciate of Bern ruled over the largest territory of all city states north of the Alps.

teile.einleitung: Myanmar in South-East Asia was ruled by the military for many decades. The army is called the Tatmadaw. Again and again the people protested against the generals, and most recently the military staged a coup on 1 February 2021.
wichtigste: Myanmar used to be called Burma; the military government changed the name in 1989.
The armed forces of Myanmar are called the Tatmadaw.
In 1988 there was the great 8888 Uprising.
In 2007 Buddhist monks led the Saffron Revolution.
The military government had the new capital Naypyidaw built.
In 2017, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled to Bangladesh.
On 1 February 2021, General Min Aung Hlaing staged a coup.

abschnitte.text: In 1962, General **Ne Win** overthrew the civilian government. After that, the military ruled the country for almost 50 years. The army is called the **Tatmadaw**. In 1989 the military government changed the name of the country from **Burma** to **Myanmar**. Many countries use the new name today, but some still say Burma.

On 8 August 1988, a large popular uprising began. Because of the date 8.8.88 it is called the **8888 Uprising**. The army crushed it with violence. During this time, **Aung San Suu Kyi** became the leader of the democracy movement. Her party won the election in 1990, but the military did not give up power. She was under house arrest for many years and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991.

In 2007, thousands of **Buddhist monks** protested against the military government. Because of the monks' saffron-coloured robes, the protests are called the **Saffron Revolution**. These protests were suppressed too. After that, the army promised slow reforms.

The military government had a new capital built in the middle of the country: **Naypyidaw**. It replaced the old capital Yangon. From 2011 there were more freedoms, but the army kept a lot of power. In 2017 the army took violent action against the Muslim minority of the **Rohingya**. Hundreds of thousands fled to neighbouring **Bangladesh**.

On 1 February 2021, the military staged another coup and removed the elected government. The coup was led by General **Min Aung Hlaing**. Aung San Suu Kyi was arrested. After that there were large protests and armed fighting between the army and resistance groups.

gewusst: Naypyidaw is one of the largest cities in the world by area, but it has very wide, often almost empty roads.
Aung San Suu Kyi's father, General Aung San, is regarded as the founder of independent Burma.

teile.einleitung: The International Criminal Court is a court that can convict those responsible for the most serious crimes in the world. These include genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. It is based in The Hague in the Netherlands and is meant to make sure that powerful people such as dictators do not go unpunished either.
wichtigste: The International Criminal Court convicts those responsible for crimes against humanity.
It is based in The Hague in the Netherlands.
It is founded on the Rome Statute of 1998.
The Rome Statute came into force on 1 July 2002, and the court has been working ever since.
It prosecutes individual people, not whole states.
Switzerland is a member, but some large states such as the USA, Russia and China are not.
It has no police force of its own and needs the help of member states.

abschnitte.text: The **International Criminal Court**, often called the ICC for short, is a permanent court for the whole world. It prosecutes individuals who are responsible for the very worst crimes. They may be presidents, generals or leaders of armed groups. However, it only steps in if a country itself is unwilling or unable to punish the perpetrators.

As early as after the Second World War, leading war criminals were put on trial in **Nuremberg** and Tokyo. In the 1990s there were special courts for the former Yugoslavia and for Rwanda. On 17 July 1998 many states agreed in Rome on the **Rome Statute**, the founding treaty of the court. It came into force on 1 July 2002.

The court is responsible for four kinds of crime. In **genocide** the aim is to destroy an entire ethnic group. **Crimes against humanity** are, for example, mass murder, torture or the enslavement of civilians. In addition there are war crimes and, since 2018, the crime of aggression, meaning a war of aggression.

More than 120 states have recognised the Rome Statute (as of 2025). **Switzerland** has been a member since 2001 and supports the court. However, some large and powerful countries are not members, including the USA, Russia, China and India. This makes the court's work harder, because it has no police force of its own. It depends on member states arresting suspects and handing them over.

The first verdict was given in 2012 against the Congolese militia leader **Thomas Lubanga**, because he had used children as soldiers. The court has also issued arrest warrants against sitting heads of state. In 2023, for example, it issued an arrest warrant against the Russian President Vladimir Putin over the deportation of Ukrainian children. Many proceedings take many years.

There is another important court in The Hague, the **International Court of Justice** of the United Nations. It settles disputes between states, for example about borders. The International Criminal Court, by contrast, charges individual people. Because of these courts, The Hague is often called the “City of Peace and Justice”.

begriffe.erklaerung: The crime of trying to destroy an entire ethnic group, in whole or in part.
The treaty of 1998 that founded the Criminal Court.
An order that a person is to be arrested.
A serious breach of the rules that apply even in war.

gewusst: The highest sentence at the International Criminal Court is life imprisonment; there is no death penalty there.
The rules for protecting people in war, the Geneva Conventions, are named after the Swiss city of Geneva.

teile.einleitung: Separation of powers means that power in the state is divided into three parts. No single person and no single authority should have all the power. This protects people's freedom.
wichtigste: State power is divided into three branches: making laws, governing and judging.
In Switzerland the parliament, the Federal Assembly, makes the laws.
The Federal Council is the government of Switzerland.
Courts judge independently; the Federal Supreme Court is in Lausanne.
Parliament meets in the Federal Palace in Bern.
In a dictatorship there is usually no separation of powers.

abschnitte.text: State power is divided into **three branches**. The **legislature** makes the laws. The **executive** governs and makes sure the laws are put into practice. The **judiciary**, meaning the courts, gives judgements when someone has broken a law. Each branch has its own people, and they keep a check on one another.

The idea is quite old. It was made famous by the French thinker **Montesquieu**. In his book “The Spirit of the Laws” from 1748 he wrote that power must be divided so that nobody becomes too powerful. This idea shaped the constitutions of many countries, including Switzerland's **Federal Constitution** of 1848.

In Switzerland the **parliament**, the **Federal Assembly**, makes the laws. It consists of the National Council with 200 members and the Council of States with 46 members. Both meet in the **Federal Palace** in Bern. The government is the **Federal Council** with seven members. The highest court is the **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne. For many laws the people can also have their say in a vote.

In a **dictatorship** there is usually no separation of powers. The ruler or a single party holds all three branches. He makes the laws, governs and also decides what the courts rule. That is why nobody keeps a check on him. Anyone who criticises him has hardly any chance of a fair trial.

gewusst: Montesquieu's book “The Spirit of the Laws” was first published in Geneva in 1748.
The Federal Council also has its offices in the Federal Palace, in the west wing.

teile.einleitung: No one should stay in power for ever. A change of power can happen peacefully through elections or through overthrows such as revolutions and coups. How power changes hands shows a lot about how free a country is.
wichtigste: In a democracy, the government changes through elections.
Whoever loses an election hands over power peacefully.
In a revolution, a large part of the people rises up.
In a coup, a small group seizes power.
In Switzerland, the Federal Assembly elects the Federal Council.
The presidency of the Confederation changes every year.

abschnitte.text: In a **democracy**, the people decide at the ballot box who governs. After a certain time, new **elections** take place. If a government loses, it hands over power without violence. This is called a **peaceful transfer of power**. It is seen as an important sign of a working democracy.

The seven members of the **Federal Council** are elected by the **Federal Assembly**. This is the National Council and the Council of States together. The election takes place every four years, after the parliamentary elections. Every year the Federal Assembly also elects a new **President of the Confederation** from among the members of the Federal Council. In this way, nobody gets too much power.

In a **revolution**, a large part of the people rises up against those in power. A famous example is the **French Revolution** of 1789, which was directed against the king and the privileges of the nobility. A revolution can also be peaceful. In 1989, many people in the GDR protested without violence. On 9 November 1989, the **Berlin Wall** fell.
In a **coup**, a small group seizes power, often army officers. The people are not asked. Another word for it is **coup d'état**. After a coup, a dictatorship or a military government often follows.

In a **monarchy**, power is often inherited. The person who will be the next king or queen is called the **heir to the throne**. Usually this is the eldest child. In many monarchies today, however, the king has little power, because an elected parliament makes the laws.

gewusst: France still celebrates its national holiday on the day of the storming of the Bastille, 14 July.
In Switzerland, the Federal Council cannot be voted out during its term of office. However, existing members are sometimes not re-elected.

t1cwcsbp.t: Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo

teile.einleitung: The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo are women from Argentina whose children disappeared during the military dictatorship. Since 1977 they have walked in a circle in the most important square in Buenos Aires, demanding truth and justice. They have become a symbol of brave, peaceful protest all over the world.
wichtigste: The Plaza de Mayo is in Buenos Aires, in front of the seat of government.
The mothers were searching for their missing children.
Their protests began in 1977.
Their symbol is a white headscarf.
Traditionally they walk round the square on Thursdays.
The Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo search for their stolen grandchildren.

abschnitte.text: From 1976 to 1983, a military junta ruled **Argentina**. It had many real or supposed opponents secretly abducted. Most of them were never seen again. They are called the **disappeared**, “Desaparecidos” in Spanish. Human rights groups estimate their number at up to 30,000. The families were given no information.

abschnitte.titel: In a circle round the square
abschnitte.text: In 1977, some mothers met in the **Plaza de Mayo** in **Buenos Aires**, right in front of the government palace. Gatherings were **forbidden** at that time. When the police told them to move on, they began to walk in pairs **in a circle** round the square. That way they were not a standing gathering. To this day they traditionally walk round the square every **Thursday**.

The symbol of the mothers is a **white headscarf**. Originally these were their children's **cloth nappies**, which they tied round their heads. Today the white headscarf is also painted on the ground of the square. It has become a symbol of remembering the disappeared.

The mothers lived dangerously. **Azucena Villaflor**, one of the founders, was herself abducted in December 1977 and never came back. Even so, the others carried on. For a long time **Hebe de Bonafini** led the “Asociación Madres de Plaza de Mayo”. Later the movement split into two groups.

The **Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo** search for their **stolen grandchildren**. During the dictatorship, small children were taken from prisoners and given to other families, often to military families. Many grew up without knowing their true origins. With the help of **genetic tests**, the grandmothers have already found well over a hundred grandchildren.

gewusst: After the end of the dictatorship in 1983, several leaders of the junta in Argentina were put on trial and convicted.
To help their search for their grandchildren, the grandmothers helped to set up a special genetic database in Argentina.

teile.einleitung: Fulgencio Batista was a Cuban officer and politician. He shaped Cuban politics for many years, first as head of the army, then as elected president and finally as a dictator. In 1959 he was overthrown by the revolution led by Fidel Castro.
wichtigste: In 1933 Batista rose to become a powerful army chief through the revolt of the sergeants.
In 1940 he was properly elected president and governed until 1944.
In March 1952 he returned to power through a military coup.
In 1953 Fidel Castro and his followers attacked the Moncada Barracks.
On New Year's Eve 1958/1959 Batista fled to the Dominican Republic.
He died in exile in Spain in 1973.

abschnitte.text: Batista was born in Cuba in 1901 and joined the army. In September 1933 the **sergeant** led a revolt of the non-commissioned officers. After that he was **army chief** and in practice controlled Cuban politics. In 1940 he won the **presidential election** and governed until 1944 under a new, progressive constitution. Afterwards he lived in the USA for a few years.

On **10 March 1952** Batista staged a coup shortly before planned elections in which he had little chance. He partly suspended the constitution of 1940 and ruled as a **dictator**. Opponents were persecuted, and **corruption** was widespread. In Havana the US gangster **Meyer Lansky**, working closely with Batista, expanded the business of casinos and hotels.

On **26 July 1953** Fidel Castro and his followers attacked the **Moncada Barracks** in Santiago de Cuba. The attack failed and Castro was put on trial. There he gave his speech “History will absolve me”. Later his **26th of July Movement** fought against Batista's army in the mountains. Because of the harsh repression, the USA imposed an **arms embargo** in March 1958, which weakened Batista's army.

On New Year's Eve 1958/1959 Batista gave up and fled. First he went to the dictator **Trujillo** in the **Dominican Republic**. Later he lived in Portugal and finally in **Spain**, where he died near Marbella in 1973. In Cuba, Fidel Castro took power and set up socialist one-party rule.

gewusst: Batista was first an elected president and only later became a dictator.
In Portugal Batista lived on the Atlantic island of Madeira.

teile.einleitung: A secret police force is a police force that works in hiding. In a dictatorship it secretly watches people who think differently and arrests them. Well-known examples are the Gestapo in National Socialist Germany and the Stasi in the GDR.
wichtigste: A secret police force secretly watches people who think differently.
It is an important tool of dictatorships.
It works without being checked by independent courts.
The Gestapo was the secret police of the National Socialists.
The Stasi spied on the people in the GDR.
In the Soviet Union the NKVD and the KGB were feared.
After the end of the GDR, people were able to read their Stasi files.

abschnitte.titel: What is a secret police force?
abschnitte.text: A **secret police force** is a state authority that works undercover. In a dictatorship its job is to find and get rid of opponents of the government. It taps telephones, opens letters and sends informers to meetings. It is often allowed to arrest people without a court ruling. Its name alone spreads fear, and that is exactly the intention.

The **Gestapo**, short for Secret State Police, was founded by the National Socialists in 1933. It persecuted political opponents, Jews and many other groups. People were interrogated, tortured and taken to concentration camps. Many were betrayed by neighbours who reported them to the Gestapo. After the Second World War the Gestapo was condemned as a criminal organisation.

In the GDR the secret police was officially called the **Ministry for State Security**, Stasi for short. It existed from 1950 to 1990. In 1989 it had around 90,000 full-time employees. On top of that there were almost 190,000 **unofficial collaborators**, who secretly spied on friends, colleagues or even family members. The Stasi kept files on millions of people.

abschnitte.titel: The Soviet Union and other countries
abschnitte.text: In the Soviet Union under Stalin, the **NKVD** was responsible for arrests, shootings and the prison camps of the Gulag. Later the secret police was called the **KGB**. Its headquarters was the Lubyanka in Moscow. Many other dictatorships in Europe, Asia, Africa and South America also had feared secret police forces.

abschnitte.titel: Files and coming to terms with the past
abschnitte.text: When the GDR collapsed in 1989, citizens occupied Stasi buildings to save the files from being destroyed. Since 1992 people affected have been allowed to read their own **Stasi files**. In this way many found out who had spied on them. The files fill more than 100 kilometres of shelves. The former Stasi headquarters in Berlin is now a museum.

abschnitte.titel: The Secret Files Scandal in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: Democracies have intelligence services too, but courts and parliament keep a check on them. In Switzerland it came out in 1989 that over decades the federal police had created around 900,000 index cards on people and organisations. This **Secret Files Scandal** (Fichenaffäre) caused great outrage. Afterwards the rules on surveillance were made stricter.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who secretly watches other people and betrays them.
The Secret State Police in National Socialist Germany.
The secret police of the GDR, officially the Ministry for State Security.
An index card on which information about a person is collected.

gewusst: The Stasi even kept smell samples from people in preserving jars so that sniffer dogs could find them.
For years experts have been piecing torn-up Stasi files back together from scraps of paper.

teile.einleitung: Lech Wałęsa is a Polish electrician who became a freedom fighter. He led the trade union Solidarność and helped to end the communist dictatorship in Poland.
wichtigste: Lech Wałęsa was born in Poland in 1943.
He was an electrician at the shipyard in Gdańsk.
In 1980, the workers in Gdańsk put pressure on the government with a strike.
Wałęsa led the trade union Solidarność.
In 1983 he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
From 1990 to 1995 he was President of Poland.

abschnitte.text: Lech Wałęsa was born in Poland in **1943**. He trained as an **electrician**. At the large **shipyard** in **Gdańsk**, where ships are built, he looked after cables and electricity. At that time Poland was ruled by a communist government. There were no free elections.

In 1980, the workers in Gdańsk stopped working. With this **strike**, they demanded more rights. The government had to negotiate with them. Wałęsa became their leader. A strike can put pressure on a government without violence.

In 1980, the trade union **Solidarność** was formed. The Polish word means “solidarity”. A **trade union** is an association of workers who stand up for their rights together. Solidarność soon had around ten million members. Wałęsa led it.

In 1983, Wałęsa received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. He did not collect it himself, because he feared he would not be allowed back into Poland afterwards. His wife accepted the prize in **Oslo**. After the end of communism, the Poles elected him **President**. He was in office from 1990 to 1995 and was the first President of Poland freely elected by the people.

gewusst: Lech Wałęsa went from electrician to president of his country.
The trade union Solidarność soon had around ten million members.

teile.einleitung: A putsch is a violent and usually surprise seizure of power, often by the military. The previous government is removed without the people being asked. By the way, the word “putsch” comes from Swiss German.
wichtigste: A putsch is a violent seizure of power, often by the military.
Another word for it is coup, or in French “coup d'état”.
The word “putsch” comes from Swiss German and originally meant a push or a blow.
It became well known through the Züriputsch of 1839.
After a successful coup, a military dictatorship often follows.
Many coups fail, for example the Beer Hall Putsch in Munich in 1923.
In recent years there have been several coups in Africa and in Myanmar.

abschnitte.text: In a **putsch**, a small group seizes power in the state, without an election and against the constitution. Usually it is army officers, sometimes also politicians or armed groups. A putsch often happens quickly and by surprise, sometimes within a few hours. It is also called a **coup d'état**.

The word “putsch” comes from **Swiss German**, where it meant “push” or “collision”. It became famous through the **Züriputsch** of 6 September 1839. At that time, conservative farmers from the Zurich Oberland overthrew the liberal cantonal government of Zurich. From there the word spread into the German language and later even into other languages.

The plotters usually first occupy important places such as the seat of government, airports and the **radio and television stations**. Then they announce that they now hold power. The previous members of the government are arrested or flee. Curfews often follow, and the constitution is suspended.

On 11 September 1973, the military in **Chile** under Augusto Pinochet staged a coup against President Salvador Allende. The **Beer Hall Putsch** in Munich on 8 and 9 November 1923 failed, and Hitler went to prison for a short time because of it. The coup attempt against Mikhail Gorbachev in Moscow in August 1991 also failed. In Turkey, a coup attempt by parts of the military failed in July 2016.

In **Myanmar**, the military took power on 1 February 2021. In Africa there have been several coups in recent years, for example in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger. The African Union and other states usually condemn such seizures of power. Afterwards people often suffer, because aid money is stopped and rights are lost.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for a putsch, meaning a violent seizure of power.
Someone who takes part in a coup.
The most important law of a state, which sets out who may govern and how.
A ban on going out on the street at certain times.

gewusst: The Swiss word “putsch” has even made it into English, where people also speak of a “putsch”.
A coup by a government that gives itself more power is sometimes called a “self-coup”.

teile.einleitung: Lustration means that people applying for public office are checked to see whether they were involved with a former regime. This became important above all after the end of the communist dictatorships in Central and Eastern Europe.
wichtigste: Lustration checks office holders for involvement with the former regime.
The word comes from the Latin “lustratio”, which means “purification”.
In 1991, Czechoslovakia had one of the first comprehensive lustration laws.
Lustration controls access to public office; it is not a punishment.
In Poland, the Institute of National Remembrance looks after the files.
In 2014, after the Euromaidan, Ukraine passed a lustration law.

abschnitte.text: After the end of communist regimes, people applying for public office were checked. People wanted to know whether they had, for example, worked with the **secret police**. Those who were implicated could be excluded from certain posts. The word comes from the Latin **“lustratio”**, which means **purification**. In ancient Rome, the lustratio was a purification sacrifice.

Lustration is not a **criminal trial**. It is an **administrative procedure** that checks whether someone is suitable for certain positions. Criminal guilt does not have to be established for this. People who are affected are not put in prison, but they may not hold certain offices.

In 1991, **Czechoslovakia** passed one of the first comprehensive lustration laws. It excluded former staff of the state security service and senior party officials from certain state offices and was considered particularly strict. In **Poland**, the **Institute of National Remembrance** (IPN) looks after the files of the former state security service. In 2014, after the **Euromaidan**, **Ukraine** passed a law against office holders from the time of President Yanukovych and former KGB staff.

Lustration is controversial. Secret service files can be incomplete, forged or one-sided. As a result, innocent people could be wrongly implicated. Critics therefore warn against **collective guilt** and the political misuse of offices and files. The Ukrainian law was partly criticised internationally as going too far.

gewusst: A term from ancient Rome is used today for checking officials.
The Polish Institute of National Remembrance also researches history and carries out criminal investigations.

teile.einleitung: In a military government, officers of the army rule a country. They usually come to power through a coup. In a democracy, on the other hand, the elected government is above the army.
wichtigste: In a military government, army officers rule.
A group of officers in power is called a junta.
The word “junta” comes from Spanish.
In 1973, General Pinochet took power in Chile.
Switzerland only elects a general in war or great danger.
In the Second World War, Henri Guisan was the Swiss general.

abschnitte.text: When officers rule a country, it is called a **military government**. Such a group of officers is called a **junta**. The word comes from **Spanish** and means “assembly” or “council”. The army often takes power with a **coup**. Parliament and elections are then often abolished or restricted.

Military governments often impose **martial law**. Then especially strict rules apply. There is often a **curfew**: nobody may go out on the street at night. Newspapers and radio are censored, and critics are arrested. Many military governments promise to hand over power soon but then stay for a long time.

On 11 September 1973, the military in **Chile** staged a coup against the elected president Salvador Allende. General **Augusto Pinochet** took power. His government persecuted thousands of opponents. Only in 1990 did Pinochet hand over power to an elected president. There were also military governments in Argentina, Brazil, Myanmar and Thailand.

In normal times Switzerland has no general. Only in war or great danger does the **Federal Assembly** elect a general. So far there have been four generals. The best known is **Henri Guisan**, who led the army in the **Second World War**. In 1940 he gathered the officers on the **Rütli** meadow and called for resistance.

In a democracy, the **elected government** is above the army. The army has to obey and may not make politics itself. Parliament decides on the army's money and on its deployments. This is meant to stop soldiers from seizing power.

gewusst: The first Swiss general, Guillaume-Henri Dufour, also had the first accurate map of Switzerland made.
Henri Guisan was greatly admired even during his lifetime, and many streets and squares are named after him.

teile.einleitung: Pol Pot was the leader of the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia and one of the cruellest dictators of the 20th century. From 1975 to 1979 he wanted to turn his country by force into a pure farming state. Under his rule an estimated 1.7 to 2 million people died, about a quarter of the population.
wichtigste: Pol Pot was the leader of the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia.
His real name was Saloth Sar, and he was born in 1925.
On 17 April 1975 the Khmer Rouge captured the capital, Phnom Penh.
The cities were emptied, and people had to do forced labour in the countryside.
Money, schools, religion and markets were abolished.
About 1.7 to 2 million people died from murder, hunger and disease.
At the beginning of 1979 the Vietnamese army drove the Khmer Rouge out of Phnom Penh.

abschnitte.text: Pol Pot's real name was **Saloth Sar**, and he was born in Cambodia in 1925. In the 1950s he studied in **Paris**, where he came across communist ideas. Back in Cambodia he became the leader of the communist movement known as the **Khmer Rouge**. Khmer is the name of the largest people in Cambodia.

Cambodia is in South-East Asia between Thailand, Laos and Vietnam. After a long civil war, the Khmer Rouge captured the capital **Phnom Penh** on **17 April 1975**. The country was renamed “Democratic Kampuchea”. The rulers declared 1975 “Year Zero”: everything was to start again from the beginning.

Pol Pot wanted a state of farmers without cities, money or property. Within a few days, millions of people had to leave the cities and work in rice fields. Schools, hospitals, markets, religion and even money were abolished. Families were torn apart, and many people died of **hunger**, exhaustion and disease.

The Khmer Rouge persecuted everyone they considered enemies: teachers, doctors, monks, officials and people from minorities. Sometimes it was enough to wear glasses or speak a foreign language. In the **Tuol Sleng** prison, also called S-21, thousands were tortured. The execution sites are now called the **“Killing Fields”**.

abschnitte.titel: End and coming to terms with the past
abschnitte.text: In January 1979, the army of **Vietnam** captured Phnom Penh and drove out the Khmer Rouge. Pol Pot hid in the jungle on the border with Thailand. He died in 1998 without ever having stood trial. A special court with the support of the UN later convicted several of his most important comrades.

begriffe.erklaerung: The communist movement that ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1979.
The deliberate murder of many people from a particular group.
Work that people are forced to do against their will.
Places where the Khmer Rouge murdered people.

gewusst: The former Tuol Sleng prison in Phnom Penh is now a museum that remembers the victims.
The Khmer Rouge scornfully called people from the cities “new people”.

teile.einleitung: Operation Condor was a secret cooperation between several military dictatorships in South America. In the 1970s and 1980s, their intelligence services persecuted political opponents, including across national borders.
wichtigste: Operation Condor was founded in Santiago de Chile in November 1975.
The driving force was the Chilean intelligence service DINA under Manuel Contreras.
The founding countries were Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia.
Later, Brazil and other countries joined as well.
Opponents were kidnapped and murdered, including abroad.
The “Archives of Terror” in Paraguay prove the cooperation.

abschnitte.text: In the 1970s, the military ruled in many countries of South America. Many opponents fled to neighbouring countries. So that they would not be safe there, the intelligence services joined forces. They exchanged information and helped each other to **persecute**, **kidnap** and **murder** people. The cooperation was top secret.

At the end of November 1975, **Manuel Contreras**, head of the Chilean **DINA**, invited people to a meeting in **Santiago de Chile**. The DINA was the intelligence service of Augusto Pinochet's dictatorship. Representatives from **Argentina**, **Uruguay**, **Paraguay** and **Bolivia** attended. At that time Bolivia was ruled by **Hugo Banzer**. Later **Brazil** joined, and other countries followed.

The operation is named after the **Andean condor**, a large vulture of the Andes. It is one of the largest flying birds in the world. The condor is the heraldic animal of Chile and several other Andean countries. Countries such as Mexico were not part of it; on the contrary, Mexico took in many refugees.

The persecution did not stop at the borders of South America. The best-known case is the murder of **Orlando Letelier**, a former minister under President Allende. DINA agents killed him with a car bomb in the middle of **Washington** in 1976. The attack caused great outrage in the USA.

For a long time, Operation Condor was denied. In 1992 the teacher **Martín Almada** found tonnes of files in a police building near Asunción in Paraguay. These **Archives of Terror** prove the cooperation of the dictatorships. Today they are part of the **UNESCO Memory of the World**. Later, people who had been involved were put on trial in several countries, and Manuel Contreras also received long prison sentences.

gewusst: Martín Almada had himself been imprisoned under the dictatorship in Paraguay before he found the files.
The Archives of Terror contain hundreds of thousands of pages.

teile.einleitung: The secret files scandal, known in Switzerland as the Fichenaffäre, was a big scandal in Switzerland. In 1989 it came out that the Federal Police had secretly been watching hundreds of thousands of people and organisations and keeping index cards on them. These cards were called fiches.
wichtigste: A fiche is an index card with information about a person.
In 1989 a Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry uncovered the fiches.
State security had created about 900,000 fiches.
In 1990 many people demonstrated in Bern against the “snooping state”.
Afterwards many of those affected were allowed to see their fiches.

abschnitte.text: The word **fiche** comes from French and means index card. The **Federal Police**, the state security service of that time, noted down information about people and organisations on them. In this way it wanted to identify possible dangers to the state, especially during the **Cold War**. Often quite harmless things were noted, such as attending a meeting or going on a journey.

At the end of the 1980s a **Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry** (PUK) investigated the Federal Department of Justice and Police. In 1989 it revealed that state security had kept about **900,000 fiches**. Many concerned left-wingers, trade unionists, peace campaigners and people from abroad. Most of them had done nothing wrong. Many people felt that their trust in the state had been betrayed.

In March 1990 there was a big **demonstration** in **Bern** against the “snooping state”. Many people demanded to see their own fiche. Hundreds of thousands applied for **access**. Often passages in the copies had been blacked out, in other words made unreadable.

After the scandal the rules for state security were rewritten. Parliament demanded more **control** over the intelligence services. Since then there has been repeated debate about how much surveillance is needed to protect the country, and where people’s **privacy** must come first. To this day the scandal is seen as an example of why the power of the state must be kept in check, even in a democracy.

gewusst: Among the people who had fiches were well-known figures from politics and culture.
A fiche is an index card of the kind that used to be used in libraries.

teile.einleitung: Nelson Mandela fought against apartheid in South Africa, the separation of people according to skin colour. For this he spent around 27 years in prison. In 1994 he became the first Black president of his country.
wichtigste: Mandela fought against apartheid in South Africa.
He spent around 27 years in prison, a long time of it on Robben Island.
There he was known by the prisoner number 46664.
He was released in 1990.
In 1993 he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
In 1994 he became President of South Africa.
His affectionate nickname is Madiba.

abschnitte.text: **Apartheid** means “separateness” in Afrikaans. From 1948 the government of South Africa strictly separated people according to **skin colour**. Black people were not allowed to vote, could not live everywhere and could not use the same schools, hospitals or beaches as white people. The Black majority was severely disadvantaged.

Nelson Mandela was born on 18 July 1918. He became a **lawyer** and joined the **ANC**, the African National Congress. At first he protested peacefully. When the government brutally crushed protests, he also supported sabotage against state facilities. In 1962 he was arrested, and in 1964 he was sentenced to life imprisonment.

Mandela spent around **27 years** in prison, 18 of them on the prison island of **Robben Island**. There he was known by the number **46664**. He had to do hard labour, for example in a quarry. All over the world, many people demanded his release. On 11 February **1990** he was finally freed.

After his release, Mandela negotiated with President **Frederik de Klerk** about ending apartheid. In 1993 the two of them received the **Nobel Peace Prize** together. In 1994 all South Africans were allowed to vote for the first time. Mandela became the first Black **President of South Africa**. He worked for **reconciliation** between Black and white people.

Many people affectionately called Mandela **Madiba**, after the name of his clan. After five years as president he stepped down voluntarily in 1999. He died on 5 December 2013. The UN declared his birthday, **18 July**, international **Nelson Mandela Day**.

gewusst: The prisoner number 46664 means: the 466th prisoner of the year 1964.
In 1995, wearing the shirt of the national rugby team, Mandela presented the World Cup trophy, a powerful sign of reconciliation.

teile.einleitung: On 11 September 1973, the military in Chile overthrew the elected government of President Salvador Allende. After that, a military dictatorship under General Augusto Pinochet ruled until 1990.
wichtigste: The coup took place on 11 September 1973.
Fighter jets bombed the La Moneda presidential palace.
Allende died in the palace the same day.
A junta of the army, navy, air force and Carabineros took power.
The National Stadium in Santiago became a prison camp.
The dictatorship lasted until 1990.

abschnitte.text: In 1970 the socialist **Salvador Allende** was elected president. His government nationalised companies and wanted to turn Chile into a socialist country. The country fell into a severe economic crisis, and society was deeply divided. During the **Cold War**, the **USA** did not want a socialist government in South America. The intelligence service, the **CIA**, therefore supported Allende's opponents.

On the morning of **11 September 1973**, the armed forces took power. Fighter jets **bombed** the presidential palace **La Moneda** in Santiago. Allende gave a last radio address and died in the palace. Only a few weeks earlier he himself had appointed **Augusto Pinochet** commander-in-chief of the army, because he thought he was loyal to the constitution.

A **junta**, meaning a government of military chiefs, took power. It was made up of the heads of the **army**, the **navy**, the **air force** and the **Carabineros** police. Pinochet quickly established himself as the leading figure. Parliament was dissolved, parties were banned and the press was censored.

After the coup, thousands of people were arrested. They were held prisoner in the **National Stadium** in Santiago, and many were interrogated and tortured.
