The well-known singer **Víctor Jara** was murdered a few days after the coup. During the dictatorship, more than 3000 people were killed or disappeared without a trace. Many fled abroad, including to Switzerland.

In 1980 the military government had a new **constitution** adopted that secured a lot of power for it. In 1988 a majority voted in a referendum against another term for Pinochet. In **March 1990**, an elected president took over the government again. The 1980 constitution, with many changes, still applies today; new drafts were rejected at the ballot box in 2022 and 2023.

gewusst: In Chile people speak of the “other 11 September”, because the coup falls on the same date as the attacks in the USA in 2001.
The National Stadium in Santiago is now a place of remembrance and is still used for football matches.

teile.einleitung: Denunciation means that someone reports another person to the authorities for base motives. Often envy, revenge or personal advantage lie behind it. In dictatorships a denunciation can mean prison or death for the person affected.
wichtigste: In a denunciation someone is informed on to the authorities.
In the Nazi state the Treachery Act of 1934 led to many reports.
The Blockwart (block warden) watched the neighbourhood for the Nazi Party.
In the GDR unofficial collaborators reported people to the Stasi.
In the Soviet Union Pavlik Morozov was celebrated as a hero.
In Switzerland false accusation is a criminal offence.

abschnitte.text: A **denunciation** is a report made for base motives. Not every report to the police is a denunciation. Anyone who reports a real crime is helping the rule of law. It becomes a problem when someone informs on another person out of **envy**, **revenge** or for their own advantage. In dictatorships, where even criticism is forbidden, denunciation becomes a great danger.

The **Treachery Act** of 1934 punished even jokes and disparaging remarks about the state and the party. Many cases began with reports from family, neighbours or work. The **block leader**, popularly called the **Blockwart**, was responsible for about 40 to 60 households and reported anything unusual. Using Gestapo files from Würzburg, the historian **Robert Gellately** showed that the Gestapo had few staff and relied heavily on tip-offs from the population.

abschnitte.titel: The Soviet Union and the GDR
abschnitte.text: After 1932 Soviet propaganda celebrated the boy **Pavlik Morozov** as a hero because he had supposedly reported his father. He was meant to show that the party was more important than the family. Today the story is regarded as heavily distorted. In the GDR **unofficial collaborators**, IM for short, secretly reported colleagues, friends or even family members to the **Stasi**. In 1989, according to estimates, there were about 189,000 of them.

abschnitte.titel: Protection under the rule of law
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland **Article 303** of the Criminal Code punishes **false accusation**. Anyone who accuses someone of a crime while knowing it to be untrue, in order to start criminal proceedings, can be punished with a prison sentence of up to five years or a fine. In this way the rule of law protects people against malicious reports. In addition, everyone is presumed innocent until a court decides otherwise.

gewusst: After the end of the GDR many people were able to read their Stasi files and found out in this way who had been spying on them.
The word “denunciation” comes from the Latin “denuntiare”, which means to announce or to report.

teile.einleitung: The Lateran Treaty of 1929 settled the relationship between Italy and the Pope. It created Vatican City as a separate, independent state.
wichtigste: The Lateran Treaty was signed on 11 February 1929.
Benito Mussolini signed for Italy and Cardinal Pietro Gasparri for the Holy See.
The Pope at the time was Pius XI.
The treaty created Vatican City.
It ended the Roman Question.
Catholicism became Italy's state religion until 1984.

abschnitte.text: In the past, the Pope ruled over a large Papal State in Italy. In 1870, Italy captured **Rome**. After that, the Pope did not recognise the Italian state. This dispute, which lasted for decades, is called the **Roman Question**. The Lateran Treaty resolved it.

The treaty was signed on **11 February 1929**. For Italy, the head of government **Benito Mussolini** signed, and for the Holy See, the Cardinal Secretary of State **Pietro Gasparri**. The Pope at the time was **Pius XI**, who held office from 1922 to 1939. It was signed in the **Lateran Palace** next to the Lateran Basilica in Rome. The treaty is named after it.

With the treaty, Italy recognised **Vatican City** as a separate, independent state. The Pope is its **head of state**. In addition, the Catholic religion became the only **state religion** of Italy. This rule was not abolished until 1984, with a new agreement.

To this day, the Pope is protected by the **Pontifical Swiss Guard**. It has existed since **1506**. Its guards must be Swiss citizens and Catholic. The guard's colourful uniforms are famous all over the world.

gewusst: The Swiss Guard has protected the Pope for over 500 years.
The treaty is named after the building in which it was signed.

teile.einleitung: The Nuremberg Laws were passed in National Socialist Germany in 1935. They made Jews second-class citizens. They were based on the false racial ideology of the National Socialists.
wichtigste: The Nuremberg Laws were passed in 1935.
Through the Reich Citizenship Law, Jews lost their full political rights.
The Blood Protection Law banned marriages between Jews and non-Jews.
The swastika flag became the only flag of the Reich.
The National Socialists decided who counted as a Jew according to their grandparents.
The laws were based on racial ideology.

abschnitte.text: The laws were passed in September **1935** at the NSDAP's Reich Party Rally in **Nuremberg**. That is why they are called the **Nuremberg Laws**. There were three laws: the **Reich Citizenship Law**, the so-called **Blood Protection Law** and the Reich Flag Law. Through the flag law, the **swastika flag** became the only flag of the Reich.

The **Reich Citizenship Law** distinguished between “Reich citizens” and mere nationals. As a result, Jews lost their **full political rights**, for example the right to vote. Because of the **First Decree** to the Reich Citizenship Law, the remaining Jewish civil servants were **forced into retirement**. As early as 1933, the **“Aryan paragraph”** had excluded civil servants of Jewish origin from state service.

The **Blood Protection Law** banned **marriages** between Jews and non-Jews. In addition, Jewish households were not allowed to employ non-Jewish women under 45 as domestic staff. Anyone who broke the law was punished. In this way Jews were to be pushed further and further out of society.

The laws were based on **racial ideology**. The National Socialists claimed that people belonged to different “races” of different value. This is scientifically wrong. To decide who counted as a Jew, they looked at the **grandparents**, and in fact at their religion. People with Jewish and non-Jewish ancestors were called **“Mischlinge”** (mixed race).

The Nuremberg Laws were an important step in the **persecution of the Jews**. They gave the exclusion a seemingly legal basis. After that came more and more bans, in 1938 the November pogroms and finally the **Holocaust**. After the end of the Second World War in 1945, the laws were abolished.

gewusst: The laws were written in great haste, some of them only shortly before the party rally.
Because races could not be determined scientifically, the National Socialists had to fall back on the religion of people's ancestors.

teile.einleitung: An autocracy is a form of rule in which one person or a small group governs alone. The people cannot check the government or remove it through free elections.
wichtigste: “Autocracy” literally means “self-rule”.
The Russian tsars called themselves “autocrats”.
A military junta is a government made up of officers.
An oligarchy is rule by a few powerful people.
What matters is the lack of control over power by the people.
Autocratisation means that democratic features are being dismantled.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from Greek: **“autos”** means self, and **“kratos”** means power. So an autocrat rules alone and without checks. The Russian **tsars** bore the title “Autocrat of All the Russias”. In Russian this is “samoderzhets”. Until 1905 their power was not limited by any constitution.

There are different forms. A **military junta** is a group of officers who rule together after a coup. The Spanish word “junta” means assembly or committee. Examples are Argentina from 1976 to 1983 and Greece from 1967 to 1974. In an **oligarchy** a small group of rich and powerful people rules; the word comes from the Greek “oligoi”, meaning “few”.

Autocracies also have armies, taxes and capitals. What matters is that the government is not checked by **free elections**, the **separation of powers** and **independent courts**. In Switzerland, on the other hand, the people elect parliament and can have a say in decisions through votes. The Federal Council has seven members so that nobody decides alone.

In 1999 the political scientist **Barbara Geddes** divided autocracies into military regimes, one-party regimes and personalist regimes. The **V-Dem** project at the University of Gothenburg distinguishes between closed autocracies, electoral autocracies, electoral democracies and liberal democracies. **Autocratisation** means a process in which free elections, freedom of the media or the separation of powers are gradually weakened.

gewusst: V-Dem stands for “Varieties of Democracy”.
In an electoral autocracy there are elections, but they are not free and fair.

teile.einleitung: Austrofascism is the name for the authoritarian rule in Austria from 1933 to 1938. It is also called the Corporate State. Federal Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss shut down parliament and banned the other parties.
wichtigste: In March 1933 Dollfuss used a crisis in the National Council to govern without parliament.
He relied on an enabling act from 1917.
The Fatherland Front replaced the parties.
In February 1934 there was fighting with the Social Democrats.
Dollfuss was shot by Nazis in July 1934.
His successor was Kurt Schuschnigg.

abschnitte.text: In March 1933, after a dispute over the rules of procedure, all three **presidents of the National Council** resigned. Federal Chancellor **Engelbert Dollfuss** spoke of parliament having “shut itself down” and prevented it from meeting again. He governed with emergency decrees. For this he relied on the **War Economy Enabling Act** of 1917 from the First World War.

In 1933 Dollfuss founded the **Fatherland Front** as a single unified organisation, and other parties were banned one after another. Its badge was the **crutch cross** (Kruckenkreuz), which was meant to set it clearly apart from the symbols of the Nazis. The **May Constitution** of 1934 began with “In the name of God, the Almighty” and described Austria as a **Christian corporate state**. Instead of parties, bodies representing the professions were to have a say, and elections no longer took place.

In February 1934 government troops and the **Heimwehr** (Home Guard) fought against the Social Democrats’ **Republican Protection League**. The uprising began in Linz and was crushed with artillery, which was also used against council housing blocks in Vienna. After that Social Democracy was banned. Political opponents were held without trial in the **Wöllersdorf detention camp**.

Against Hitler’s Germany Dollfuss relied mainly on **Italy** under Mussolini. On 25 July 1934 Austrian Nazis broke into the Federal Chancellery and shot Dollfuss, but their **July Putsch** failed. His successor **Kurt Schuschnigg** continued the Corporate State. When Italy moved closer to Germany from 1936, this protection was lost. In March 1938 Austria was annexed by Germany.

gewusst: Experts still debate today whether to speak of “Austrofascism”, the “Corporate State” or a “chancellor dictatorship”.
Many opponents of the Corporate State, but also many of its supporters, were persecuted by the Nazis after 1938.

teile.einleitung: Miklós Horthy ruled Hungary as regent from 1920 to 1944. Before that he had been an admiral. His rule was authoritarian, and his country was allied with National Socialist Germany in the Second World War.
wichtigste: Before 1920, Horthy was an admiral in the Austro-Hungarian navy.
From 1920 to 1944 he was Regent of Hungary.
In the Treaty of Trianon in 1920, Hungary lost around two thirds of its territory.
In 1921 he prevented King Charles IV from returning to the throne.
After the German occupation in 1944, around 437,000 Jews were deported.
Horthy died in exile in Estoril, Portugal, in 1957.

abschnitte.text: Horthy was an officer in the **Austro-Hungarian navy** and became an admiral. After the First World War, Austria-Hungary fell apart. There was unrest in Hungary. Horthy led an army against the communist Soviet Republic. This period is called the **White Terror**, because there was a lot of violence against communists and Jews. In 1920 Horthy became **regent**, meaning someone who stands in for a king.

Hungary officially remained a kingdom but had no king. The former king **Charles IV** tried twice to return in 1921. Horthy prevented this. He ruled in an **authoritarian** way: there was a parliament, but the opposition had little chance.

In the **Treaty of Trianon** of 1920, Hungary lost around two thirds of its territory. Many Hungarians felt this was a great injustice. Through the **Vienna Awards** of 1938 and 1940, Hungary got back parts of Slovakia and Northern Transylvania with the help of Germany and Italy. In the Second World War, Hungary fought on Germany's side.

As early as 1920, Hungary passed the **numerus clausus law**. It limited the number of Jewish students at universities and is considered one of the first antisemitic laws in Europe between the wars. Later, further laws against Jews followed. After the **German occupation** in March 1944, around 437,000 Jews were deported by July, mostly to **Auschwitz**. In July, Horthy had the deportations stopped.

In October 1944, Horthy announced a **ceasefire** with the Soviet Union. Germany then forced him to resign. Power was taken over by **Ferenc Szálasi** of the **Arrow Cross**, a fascist party. Horthy was taken prisoner by the Germans. After the war he lived in **exile** in Portugal, where he died in Estoril in 1957.

gewusst: At that time Hungary had no access to the sea, but it was ruled by an admiral.
Horthy's remains were brought to Hungary in 1993 and buried there.

teile.einleitung: Exile means living far from home because you are not safe there. People go into exile because they are being persecuted, often by a dictatorship. Throughout history many famous writers, scientists and politicians have had to live in exile.
wichtigste: Exile is living far from home because you are not safe there.
The word comes from the Latin “exilium”, meaning banishment.
People often flee into exile from dictatorships.
After 1933 many people fled from Germany, including Albert Einstein and Thomas Mann.
Some governments carry on working in exile; they are called governments in exile.
Switzerland was a country of exile for many persecuted people.
Life in exile is often hard, because you lose your language, friends and work.

abschnitte.text: The word **exile** comes from the Latin “exilium” and means banishment. People go into exile when they have to leave their home because they face persecution, prison or even death there. Sometimes a person is expelled from their country, and sometimes they flee themselves. People in exile are called **exiles** or emigrants. They often hope to be able to return one day.

As far back as ancient Rome people were banished, for example the poet **Ovid**, who was sent to the Black Sea. The French emperor Napoleon was banished to the island of **Elba** in 1814. After his return and his defeat at Waterloo he was sent to the remote Atlantic island of St Helena. He died there in 1821.

After 1933 hundreds of thousands of people fled from the Nazis in Germany. The physicist **Albert Einstein** went to the USA. The writer **Thomas Mann** lived first in Küsnacht near Zurich and then in the USA. People also fled from the Soviet Union, from Spain under Franco and from many other dictatorships. The Dalai Lama, the religious leader of the Tibetans, has lived in exile in India since 1959.

When a country is occupied, sometimes the whole government flees abroad. In the Second World War, for example, the governments of Poland, Norway and the Netherlands carried on working from **London**. This is called a **government in exile**. It wants to show that it remains the lawful representative of its country.

abschnitte.titel: Switzerland as a country of exile
abschnitte.text: Over the course of history Switzerland took in many persecuted people, for example the **Huguenots** from France in the 16th and 17th centuries. The Russian revolutionary Lenin lived in Zurich during the First World War. In the Second World War tens of thousands of refugees found protection, but many Jewish refugees were turned away at the border. Today Switzerland grants **asylum** to persecuted people.

In exile people often have to learn a new language and start all over again. Many miss their family, friends and home very much. Some exiles wrote famous books about this experience. At the same time they bring new ideas to the country that takes them in. In this way exiles shaped science and art in the USA and in Europe.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who lives in exile.
Protection that a state grants to persecuted people from other countries.
A punishment in which someone has to leave their home.
A government that works for its country from abroad.

gewusst: After the war Thomas Mann returned to Switzerland and is buried in Kilchberg on Lake Zurich.
The Dalai Lama has lived in exile in the Indian town of Dharamsala for more than 60 years.

teile.einleitung: The Gulag was the huge system of prison camps in the Soviet Union. The prisoners had to work there without pay under harsh conditions, often in freezing cold. Millions of people suffered in these camps, and many did not survive them.
wichtigste: The Gulag was the system of forced labour camps in the Soviet Union.
Prisoners had to work without pay under harsh conditions.
The abbreviation stands for “Main Administration of Camps” in Russian.
The camp system was at its largest under Joseph Stalin.
Many camps were in Siberia and the far north.
Altogether about 18 million people passed through the camps.
The writer Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn made the Gulag known around the world.

abschnitte.text: The word **Gulag** is a Russian abbreviation and means “Main Administration of Camps”. This authority was founded in 1930 and ran hundreds of prison camps. Today the word stands for the whole camp system. In the camps prisoners had to do **forced labour**, that is, work without pay and against their will.

abschnitte.titel: Who was sent to the camps?
abschnitte.text: The Gulag held criminals, but also a great many **political prisoners**. Even a joke about Stalin or a contact abroad could be enough. Farmers who resisted collectivisation were sent away, as were priests, artists and scientists. Prisoners of war and entire ethnic groups were also taken to camps or special settlements.

Many camps were in **Siberia**, on the Kolyma in the Far East or north of the Arctic Circle, for example in Vorkuta and Norilsk. In winter the temperature there often fell below minus 40 degrees. The prisoners felled trees, dug for gold and coal in mines and built canals, railways and roads. There was too little food and warm clothing. Hunger, disease and exhaustion caused many deaths.

The Soviet Union used the prisoners as cheap labour. The **White Sea-Baltic Canal** was built from 1931 to 1933 almost entirely by prisoners, often with the simplest tools. Cities such as Magadan and Norilsk were also built with forced labour. Thousands of people died on such building projects.

The writer **Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn** spent eight years in the camps himself. In 1962 his story “One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich” about everyday life in the camp was published. Later he wrote the great work **“The Gulag Archipelago”**, which was published in the West in 1973. In 1970 he received the Nobel Prize in Literature. In 1974 he was expelled from the Soviet Union and lived in Zurich for a while.

After Stalin's death in 1953 many prisoners were released and the camp system was greatly reduced. However, there were political prisoners in the Soviet Union until the 1980s. A former camp near Perm became the museum **Perm-36**. Experts estimate that at least 1.5 million people died in the Gulag; some estimates are considerably higher.

begriffe.erklaerung: Work that people have to do against their will and usually without pay.
Someone who is locked up because of their opinions or political views.
The forced merging of farms into large state-controlled enterprises.
A group of islands; Solzhenitsyn compared the scattered camps to one.

gewusst: After being expelled from the Soviet Union, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn first lived in Zurich for about two years.
The city of Magadan in Russia's Far East was founded in the 1930s as a centre for the camps on the Kolyma.

teile.einleitung: Nicolae Ceaușescu was the dictator of Romania from 1965 to 1989. He had himself worshipped like a hero, while many people in his country went hungry and cold. In December 1989 he was overthrown by a popular uprising and executed together with his wife Elena.
wichtigste: Nicolae Ceaușescu was born in 1918 and ruled Romania from 1965.
He was head of the Communist Party and from 1974 also President.
There was a huge personality cult around him and his wife Elena.
His secret police, the Securitate, watched and persecuted the population.
In the 1980s there was a shortage of food, electricity and heating.
In December 1989 he was overthrown by a popular uprising.
On 25 December 1989, he and his wife were executed after a quick trial.

abschnitte.text: Nicolae Ceaușescu was born in 1918 in the village of **Scornicești** in Romania. As a young man he joined the communists and was imprisoned several times because of this. In 1965 he became head of the **Romanian Communist Party** and thus the most powerful man in the country. In 1974 he also made himself President.

abschnitte.titel: Popular in the West at first
abschnitte.text: Romania belonged to the Eastern Bloc, but Ceaușescu often acted independently of the Soviet Union. In 1968 he publicly criticised the invasion of **Czechoslovakia** by Warsaw Pact troops. For this reason, he was long regarded in Western countries as a comparatively open politician. In his own country, however, his rule became harsher and harsher.

Ceaușescu had himself called “Conducător”, meaning leader, and celebrated everywhere. His wife **Elena** was also given a lot of power and had herself honoured as a great scientist. The secret police, the **Securitate**, spied on people, and critics were locked up. Even typewriters had to be registered with the police.

In the 1980s Ceaușescu wanted to pay back all foreign debts and had a lot of goods exported to do so. As a result, food was rationed and flats stayed cold in winter. At the same time, he had the enormous **People's Palace** built in Bucharest, for which a whole district of the city was demolished. Today the building is the seat of the Romanian parliament.

In December 1989, protests began in the city of **Timișoara** and spread quickly. On 21 December, Ceaușescu was booed by the crowd during a big speech in Bucharest. The next day he fled by helicopter but was caught. On 25 December 1989, he and his wife were shot in **Târgoviște** after a short military trial.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ruler who governs alone and does not allow criticism or free elections.
The secret police in communist Romania.
When a ruler is worshipped excessively, with pictures, statues and songs of praise.
The communist states in Eastern Europe that were closely tied to the Soviet Union.

gewusst: The Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest is one of the largest buildings in the world.
The speech of 21 December 1989 was broadcast live on television, so the whole country saw Ceaușescu being booed.
Romania was the only country in the Eastern Bloc where the upheaval of 1989 was very bloody.

teile.einleitung: The Hitler Youth, HJ for short, was the youth organisation of the Nazi party in Germany. Its purpose was to bring up children and young people as loyal followers of Hitler. From 1939 all young people had to be members.
wichtigste: Boys joined the German Young People at the age of 10.
Girls were organised in the League of Young Girls and the League of German Girls.
From 1936 the Hitler Youth was by law the “state youth”, alongside the family home and school.
From 1939 membership was compulsory.
The Reich Youth Leaders were Baldur von Schirach and, from 1940, Artur Axmann.
Towards the end of the war young people were used as anti-aircraft helpers and in the Volkssturm.

abschnitte.text: The Hitler Youth was organised by age and sex. Boys aged 10 to 14 belonged to the **German Young People**, and after that to the **Hitler Youth** proper. Girls aged 10 to 14 were in the **League of Young Girls**, and from 14 to 18 in the **League of German Girls** (BDM). They all wore uniforms and had to take part in meetings, marches and camps.

The main aim was to bring up young people in line with **Nazi ideology**. They were to obey Hitler and believe in the ideas of the National Socialists, including their hatred of Jews. With **field exercises**, camps and marches the boys were prepared for war. The girls were mainly to be prepared for the role of housewife and mother.

From 1933 **Baldur von Schirach**, as Youth Leader of the German Reich, led the Hitler Youth and turned it into a mass organisation. Other youth organisations were banned or absorbed. The law of 1 December **1936** made the Hitler Youth the “**state youth**” alongside the family home and school. From **1939** **compulsory youth service** applied, and all young people had to be members. In 1940 **Artur Axmann** took over the leadership and focused the Hitler Youth more and more on the war.

Not everyone joined in. The **Edelweiss Pirates** were nonconformist youth groups, mainly in the Rhineland and the Ruhr. They met up, went hiking and sang their own songs. They wanted to be free and were persecuted for it.

abschnitte.titel: At the end of the war
abschnitte.text: Towards the end of the war young people also had to operate **anti-aircraft guns**; they were called **Flak helpers**. In the **Volkssturm** even children and teenagers were sent into battle, and many of them were killed. After the war the victorious powers banned the Hitler Youth in 1945.

gewusst: Many Edelweiss Pirates wore an edelweiss as their badge.
Baldur von Schirach was sentenced to 20 years in prison at the Nuremberg trials.

teile.einleitung: The Democracy Index is a ranking that shows how democratic the states of the world are. It is published by the research division of the magazine “The Economist”. Every country is given a score between 0 and 10.
wichtigste: It is published by the Economist Intelligence Unit of the magazine “The Economist”.
The index first appeared in 2006.
It rates 165 states and 2 territories, so 167 in total (as of 2025).
Each country is rated in five areas using a total of 60 indicators.
Norway has been in first place since 2010, and Afghanistan is in last place (as of 2025).
Switzerland is regarded as a full democracy.

abschnitte.text: The **Economist Intelligence Unit** is the research division of the British magazine **“The Economist”**. It first published the **Democracy Index** in 2006. Almost all the countries in the world are rated in it. As of 2025 there are 165 states and 2 territories, 167 in total.

Each state is rated in **five areas**: electoral process and pluralism, functioning of government, **political participation**, political culture and **civil liberties**. For this there are 60 questions in total, the **indicators**. Economic data is not rated. An overall score between 0 and 10 is calculated from the areas.

Depending on their score, countries are divided into four groups: **full democracies**, **flawed democracies**, **hybrid regimes** and **authoritarian regimes**. A hybrid regime has elections, but serious shortcomings in freedom and the rule of law. According to the 2025 index, only about 6.6 per cent of the world’s population live in a full democracy. Many large states are regarded as flawed democracies or authoritarian regimes.

**Norway** has topped the ranking since 2010 and in 2025 scored about 9.8 out of 10. In last place is **Afghanistan** under the Taliban, with only about 0.25 points. There are neither elections nor civil liberties there. **Switzerland** scores about 9.3 points and so is one of the full democracies (as of 2025).

The rating is also based on assessments by experts and on surveys. That is why individual scores can be disputed. Other organisations such as **Freedom House** or the **V-Dem** project measure democracy with their own methods. If you compare several rankings, you get a more accurate picture.

gewusst: The ranking is drawn up again every year, so you can see whether a country is becoming more or less democratic.
A country with more than 8 points is regarded as a full democracy.

teile.einleitung: Augusto Pinochet was a Chilean general who ruled Chile as a military dictator from 1973 to 1990. He came to power in a coup during which the elected president, Salvador Allende, died. Under his rule thousands of people were killed, tortured or disappeared without trace.
wichtigste: Augusto Pinochet was born in Valparaíso in 1915 and died in Santiago de Chile in 2006.
On 11 September 1973 the army under his leadership overthrew the socialist president Salvador Allende.
Pinochet banned parties, restricted freedom of the press and had opponents persecuted.
More than 3,000 people were murdered or disappeared, and tens of thousands were tortured.
In a referendum in 1988 the majority voted against him.
In 1990 he handed over the government to an elected president.
In 1998 he was arrested in London, but he was never convicted.

abschnitte.text: **Augusto Pinochet** was a career officer and rose to the very top of the Chilean army. In August 1973 President Salvador Allende appointed him commander-in-chief of the army. Only a few weeks later he led the coup against that very president. After that he headed a **military junta** and made himself president.

Chile lies on the west coast of South America and is more than 4,000 kilometres long but very narrow. In 1970 the socialist **Salvador Allende** was democratically elected president. His reforms, economic problems and resistance from at home and abroad led to a deep crisis. On 11 September 1973 the army attacked the presidential palace, **La Moneda**, in Santiago with aircraft, and Allende took his own life there.

After the coup tens of thousands of people were arrested, and many were held in the National Stadium in Santiago. The secret police, the **DINA**, persecuted opponents even abroad. Many victims were secretly abducted and never seen again; they are known as the **disappeared**. Hundreds of thousands of Chileans fled into exile, some of them to Switzerland.

Pinochet relied on a free **market economy** and sold many state-owned companies to private owners. He was advised by economists who had studied in Chicago and were therefore called the Chicago Boys. At times the economy grew strongly, but many poor people hardly benefited. To this day people argue about how this policy should be judged.

In 1980 Pinochet had a new **constitution** adopted, which provided for a referendum on whether he would stay in office. On 5 October 1988 about 56 per cent voted No and so rejected him. In 1990 the elected president Patricio Aylwin took office, but Pinochet remained head of the army until 1998. In October 1998 he was arrested in London at the request of a Spanish judge, and he was involved in court cases until his death in 2006, without ever being convicted.

begriffe.erklaerung: When the army or a small group overthrows the government by force.
A government made up of generals and senior officers.
Living abroad because you are persecuted in your home country.
A ruler who decides everything alone and tolerates no opposition.

gewusst: The 1988 referendum was won with a cheerful campaign for No that used a rainbow as its symbol.
The National Stadium in Santiago, where thousands of prisoners were held in 1973, is today also a place of remembrance.
In Chile, 11 September is still a day on which the victims of the dictatorship are remembered.

teile.einleitung: In a one-party state only a single party is allowed to govern. Other parties are banned or have no say. Anyone who thinks differently is usually not allowed to found a new party, which is why the one-party system is a typical feature of dictatorships.
wichtigste: In a one-party state only one party is allowed to govern.
Founding new parties is usually forbidden.
In elections there is no real choice.
The party controls the government, the media, schools and often the economy too.
Examples are Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union.
Today China, North Korea, Cuba and Vietnam, among others, have a one-party system.
The opposite is a multi-party system, as in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: A **party** is a group of people with similar political goals. In a **one-party state** only a single party has the right to govern. It fills all the important posts in the state. Anyone who thinks differently is not allowed to found a party of their own; this is usually forbidden. Anyone who tries anyway risks prison.

Elections often take place in one-party states too. But people can only vote for candidates of the ruling party or approve a **single list**. The results are often over 99 per cent approval. Such elections are **sham elections**, because the result has been fixed in advance. They are only meant to make it look as though the people agree.

In Germany the Nazis banned all other parties in July 1933, and after that only the **NSDAP** remained. In the **Soviet Union** the Communist Party ruled alone from the 1920s until 1990. In the GDR the SED held power, even though other parties still existed for show. These so-called bloc parties, however, had to obey the SED.

Today China, for example, is governed by the **Communist Party of China**. North Korea, Cuba, Vietnam and Laos also have one-party systems. In China there are still a few small parties, but they are not allowed to challenge the Communist Party. The party also decides what appears in newspapers, on the internet and in school books.

Without other parties there is no **opposition** to criticise the government’s mistakes in public. The government cannot be voted out peacefully. Power stays with the same people for a long time, which encourages abuse of power and corruption. In a multi-party system such as Switzerland’s, on the other hand, citizens can choose between different ideas.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of people who pursue shared political goals.
Parties that are not in government and that criticise and check the government.
A ballot paper with only candidates chosen by the government on it.
An election in which the result has been fixed in advance.

gewusst: The Communist Party of China has about 100 million members (as of 2024), which makes it one of the largest parties in the world.
In Nazi Germany, from July 1933, there was a law that expressly banned the founding of new parties.

teile.einleitung: The Great Terror was a wave of persecution in the Soviet Union under Joseph Stalin, mainly in the years 1936 to 1938. It was aimed at real and suspected opponents of Stalin and is also called the “Great Purge”. Hundreds of thousands of people were shot, and many more were sent to prison camps.
wichtigste: The Great Terror was a wave of persecution against real and suspected opponents of Stalin.
It is also called the “Great Purge”.
It reached its peak in 1937 and 1938.
The secret police, the NKVD, carried out the arrests.
In show trials the accused had to confess to invented crimes.
In 1937 and 1938 alone, about 680,000 people were shot.
Those affected included politicians, officers, farmers, artists and quite ordinary people.

abschnitte.text: **Joseph Stalin** had ruled the Soviet Union as a dictator since the end of the 1920s. He distrusted many people, including in his own party. With the **Great Terror** he wanted to get rid of everyone who might become dangerous to him. It also struck many who had nothing at all against him. Nobody could feel safe.

On 1 December 1934 the popular party leader **Sergei Kirov** was murdered in Leningrad. Stalin used the murder as an excuse for ever harsher persecution. From 1936 the number of arrests rose sharply. From 1936 the head of the secret police was **Nikolai Yezhov**, which is why in Russia this period is also called the “Yezhovshchina”.

From 1936 to 1938 three big **show trials** took place in Moscow. The accused were former comrades of Lenin such as Grigory Zinoviev, Lev Kamenev and Nikolai Bukharin. Under torture and threats they confessed to crimes they had never committed. Most were sentenced to death and shot. The trials were meant to show the people and other countries that there were traitors everywhere.

The terror also struck the **Red Army**. Many high-ranking officers, including Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky, were shot in 1937. In addition, farmers, workers, teachers, artists, priests and members of minorities were arrested. Often a wrong remark or a report by a neighbour was enough. Sometimes authorities even had to reach fixed numbers of arrests.

In 1937 and 1938 around 1.5 million people were arrested. About 680,000 of them were shot, and many others were sent to the prison camps of the **Gulag**. The families of those convicted were often punished as well. At the end of 1938 Stalin had Yezhov removed, and later Yezhov himself was shot. The weakening of the army had disastrous effects in the Second World War.

For a long time people in the Soviet Union were hardly allowed to talk about the terror. In 1989 the organisation **Memorial** was founded to research the fates of the victims. It was dissolved by Russian courts in 2021 and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022. Every year people in Moscow read out the names of victims at the Solovetsky Stone.

begriffe.erklaerung: Here: the persecution and elimination of supposed enemies.
A trial in which the verdict has been decided in advance.
The Soviet secret police under Stalin.
The system of prison camps in the Soviet Union.

gewusst: Nikolai Yezhov, who led the terror, was himself later arrested and shot in 1940.
Stalin had executed opponents retouched out of old photos, as if they had never existed.

teile.einleitung: Authoritarianism describes a form of rule in which a leadership exercises power without real control by the people. Unlike totalitarian systems, however, authoritarian regimes do not try to control every part of people’s lives. The term also refers to the attitudes of people who prefer strong authorities.
wichtigste: In 1964 the researcher Juan Linz described authoritarian regimes using the example of Franco’s Spain.
Authoritarian regimes allow limited pluralism.
Instead of a fixed ideology they rely more on mentalities.
They usually do without intensive mass mobilisation.
The Estado Novo in Portugal ended in 1974 with the Carnation Revolution.
Pinochet’s rule in Chile ended after he lost a referendum in 1988.

abschnitte.text: In 1964 the political scientist **Juan Linz** published a study of Spain under **Franco**. For him this regime was neither a democracy nor a totalitarian system. According to Linz, authoritarian regimes allow **limited pluralism**, for example the Church, the army or business associations. They rely more on **mentalities** such as order, nation or religion than on a fully worked-out ideology.

Totalitarian systems want to mobilise the masses constantly for their goals. Authoritarian regimes, on the other hand, usually do without **intensive mass mobilisation**. They rely instead on the population staying passive and not concerning itself with politics. Criticism is still dangerous, though, and opponents are often persecuted.

In Portugal **António de Oliveira Salazar** built up the **Estado Novo**. It ended on 25 April 1974 with the **Carnation Revolution**, a largely bloodless military coup. Soldiers put carnations in the barrels of their rifles. In Chile General **Augusto Pinochet** ruled from 1973. In 1988 a majority voted in a **referendum** against him serving another term, and in 1990 the country returned to democracy.

Researchers also study why people find anti-democratic ideas appealing. In 1950 a group around **Theodor W. Adorno** published the study **“The Authoritarian Personality”** with the **F-scale**; the F stands for fascism. Later **Bob Altemeyer** developed the **Right-Wing Authoritarianism** scale. It measures submission to authorities, rejection of people who deviate and clinging to conventions.

gewusst: The Carnation Revolution got its name because the population gave the soldiers red carnations.
Today 25 April is a public holiday in Portugal, Freedom Day.

teile.einleitung: Emergency laws give a government special powers in a crisis. They are meant to help it act quickly. But history shows that without checks they can also open the way to a dictatorship.
wichtigste: Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution allowed the Reich President to issue emergency decrees.
The Reichstag Fire Decree suspended fundamental rights in February 1933.
The Enabling Act allowed Hitler to pass laws without parliament.
In 1939 the Swiss Federal Council was given special powers, the full powers regime.
In March 2020 the Federal Council declared the extraordinary situation because of Covid.
In 2023 the Federal Council used emergency law for the takeover of Credit Suisse by UBS.
In a democracy, emergency law is time-limited and is checked.

abschnitte.text: In a war, an epidemic or a serious crisis, a state sometimes has to act very quickly. Then the government can use **emergency law**. It may issue rules without going the long way through parliament. In a democracy, emergency law is **time-limited** and is **checked** by parliament and the courts. In a dictatorship, on the other hand, it often becomes permanent.

In the Weimar Republic, **Article 48** of the constitution allowed the Reich President to issue **emergency decrees**. After the Reichstag fire, the government issued the **Reichstag Fire Decree** in February 1933. It suspended important fundamental rights, such as freedom of expression. In March 1933 the **Enabling Act** followed. It allowed Hitler's government to pass laws without parliament. This is how the dictatorship came about.

In the Federal Republic of Germany, the Bundestag passed the **emergency laws** in **1968**. They set out what applies in war or in disasters. Many people, especially students, protested against them because they were thinking of 1933. The laws therefore contain strict limits and checks.

At the start of the **Second World War** in 1939, the Federal Assembly gave the Federal Council special powers. This is called the **full powers regime**. The Federal Council could decide many things alone, for example about the supply of food. After the war, the full powers were gradually withdrawn. Today the **Federal Constitution** only allows the Federal Council to issue time-limited emergency ordinances.

In March 2020, because of the **coronavirus**, the Federal Council declared the **extraordinary situation** under the **Epidemics Act**. For example, it closed schools and many shops. In March 2023 it used emergency law for the **takeover of Credit Suisse by UBS**. In both cases there were debates in parliament afterwards about whether this had been right.

gewusst: The Enabling Act was extended several times and remained in force until the end of the Second World War.
In Switzerland, the extraordinary situation because of Covid lasted until June 2020.

teile.einleitung: Corporatism is a system in which workers and employers are grouped together in associations controlled by the state. Corporatism is especially well known from fascist Italy under Mussolini.
wichtigste: Fascist corporatism wanted to overcome class struggle.
From 1926, only fascist syndicates were allowed to represent workers.
Strikes and lockouts were banned in 1926.
The Carta del Lavoro of 1927 was the founding text of the system.
In 1934, the economy was divided into 22 corporations.
In 1939, the Chamber of Fasces and Corporations replaced the elected Chamber of Deputies.

abschnitte.text: According to its own teaching, fascist **corporatism** wanted to overcome the **class struggle** between workers and employers. Both sides were to be grouped together in **corporations** according to branches of the economy. They were to work together under the direction of the state. In reality, the system served mainly to control the workers.

A law of 1926 recognised only the **fascist syndicates** as representatives of the workers. Free **trade unions** thus lost any legal basis. At the same time, **strikes and lockouts** were banned. In a lockout, employers stop the workers from working. Labour disputes were now decided by state labour courts.

abschnitte.titel: Carta del Lavoro and the ministry
abschnitte.text: In 1926, Mussolini set up the **Ministry of Corporations**, the Ministero delle Corporazioni. At times he ran it himself. In April 1927, the **Carta del Lavoro** came into force. It described the cooperation of labour and capital under the supervision of the state and is regarded as the founding text of fascist corporatism.

In 1934, **22 corporations** were created, one for each area such as agriculture, industry or services. In 1939, the elected Chamber of Deputies was abolished. It was replaced by the **Chamber of Fasces and Corporations**. Its members were no longer elected but appointed by virtue of their posts in the party and the corporations.

gewusst: Not a single member elected by the people sat in the Chamber of Fasces and Corporations.
In fascist Italy, strikes and lockouts were banned alike.

teile.einleitung: Aung San Suu Kyi is a politician from Myanmar, formerly Burma. For decades she fought non-violently against military rule and was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for it. Later she was strongly criticised for her silence about the persecution of the Rohingya.
wichtigste: Aung San Suu Kyi comes from Myanmar.
Her father, Aung San, was a hero of independence.
She spent about 15 years under house arrest.
In 1991 she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
Her party is called the National League for Democracy (NLD).
From 2016 to 2021 she was State Counsellor.
After the military coup of 2021 she was arrested and convicted.

abschnitte.text: Aung San Suu Kyi was born in Rangoon in 1945. Her father, General **Aung San**, led Burma to independence from Great Britain. He was murdered in 1947, when his daughter was two years old. She later studied in England and lived abroad for a long time.

abschnitte.titel: House arrest and the Nobel Prize
abschnitte.text: In 1988 she returned to Burma and founded the **National League for Democracy**, NLD for short. The military government placed her under **house arrest** in 1989. Up to 2010 she was locked up in her house in Rangoon for about 15 years in total. The NLD won the election in 1990, but the army did not recognise the result. In 1991 she was awarded the **Nobel Peace Prize**, and her sons accepted it on her behalf.

In November 2010 she was released. In 2015 the NLD won the election clearly. However, the constitution of 2008 barred her from becoming president, because her sons have **foreign citizenship**. That is why the post of **State Counsellor** was created for her in 2016. In this way she led the government, but the army kept a lot of power.

The **Rohingya** are a Muslim minority in Myanmar. From 2017 hundreds of thousands of them fled from violence by the army. Aung San Suu Kyi largely remained silent about it. In 2019 she even defended Myanmar before the **International Court of Justice** in The Hague, after Gambia had brought a case against the country for genocide. Many former supporters were disappointed by this.
On 1 February 2021 the army staged another coup. Aung San Suu Kyi was arrested the same day. In several trials she was sentenced to many years in prison. The army dissolved the NLD in 2023.

gewusst: Because she was under house arrest, she could only give her Nobel Prize speech in person in Oslo in 2012.
Until 1989 Myanmar’s official name was Burma.

teile.einleitung: The National Security Law for Hong Kong came into force on 30 June 2020. It was passed by the government in Beijing. The Chinese government sees it as protection for peace and order; critics see it as the end of many freedoms in Hong Kong.
wichtigste: The law came into force on 30 June 2020.
It punishes secession, subversion, terrorism and collusion with foreign forces.
Beijing set up its own Office for Safeguarding National Security in Hong Kong.
According to Article 38, the law also applies to foreigners outside Hong Kong.
47 activists were charged because of an unofficial primary election.
In March 2024, an additional security law under Article 23 was added.

abschnitte.text: Hong Kong was a British colony for a long time. In 1997 it went back to **China**. It was agreed that Hong Kong could keep its own rules for 50 years. The principle is called **“One country, two systems”**. For this, Hong Kong has its own constitution, the **Basic Law**. In 2019 there were large protests against a planned law on extradition to China.

After the protests, Beijing passed the **National Security Law**. It came into force on **30 June 2020**. It makes four acts punishable: **secession**, **subversion**, **terrorism** and **collusion with foreign forces**. The penalties can be as high as life imprisonment. The law also created an **Office for Safeguarding National Security**, which reports directly to Beijing.

According to **Article 38**, the law also applies to foreigners outside Hong Kong. For example, anyone who calls for Hong Kong's independence abroad could be charged when they enter the territory. Many countries criticised the law. Some suspended their extradition agreements with Hong Kong.

On the day the law was passed, the party **Demosisto** of the activist **Joshua Wong** dissolved itself. In 2021 the first defendant was convicted, partly because of the slogan **“Liberate Hong Kong, revolution of our times”**. 47 pro-democracy activists, the **Hong Kong 47**, were charged because of an unofficial primary election in 2020. Several newspapers stopped publishing.

The governments in Beijing and Hong Kong say that the law brought back **stability** after the unrest. Critics say that it severely restricts **freedom of expression** and freedom of assembly. In March 2024, Hong Kong's parliament also passed its own security law under **Article 23** of the Basic Law.

gewusst: The “One country, two systems” agreement officially applies until the year 2047.
The exact text of the security law was only published on the day it came into force.

teile.einleitung: In politics, the opposition means the people or parties who disagree with the government and are not part of it. It criticises the government, makes its own proposals and keeps a check on those in power. In a democracy the opposition is welcome; in a dictatorship it is persecuted.
wichtigste: Opposition means people or parties who disagree with the government.
The word comes from the Latin “opponere”, which means “to set against”.
In a democracy, the opposition has the right to criticise the government openly.
It keeps a check on the government and can come to power itself at the next election.
In dictatorships, opposition figures are often arrested, persecuted or forced into exile.
Because of concordance, Switzerland has no classic opposition party.
The Swiss people can act as an opposition themselves through referendums and popular initiatives.

abschnitte.text: The word **opposition** comes from the Latin “opponere”, which means “to set against”. In politics it refers to everyone who is not part of the **government** and has different ideas. Usually these are parties in parliament, but also groups and individuals outside it. Its most important task is to criticise the government and propose alternatives.

In many democracies, the parties that have won an election form the government, and the others are in opposition. In Great Britain there is even an official **shadow cabinet** that shows who would govern. The opposition asks questions, uncovers mistakes and in this way **keeps a check** on power. After the next election it may form the government itself.

In Switzerland, the largest parties sit together on the **Federal Council**; this is called **concordance**. That is why there is no large opposition party as in other countries. Even so, parties in parliament often vote against proposals from the Federal Council. In addition, the people can stop laws with a **referendum** and bring in their own ideas with popular initiatives.

Dictators do not tolerate any opposition, because it could endanger their power. Opposition parties are banned, and their members are arrested or threatened. Many opposition figures have to go into **exile**, meaning flee abroad. Even so, in almost every dictatorship there are brave people who stand up to those in power, secretly or openly.

**Nelson Mandela** fought against racial segregation in South Africa and spent 27 years in prison for it; later he became president. In Myanmar, Aung San Suu Kyi led the opposition to military rule and was under house arrest for many years. In Poland in the 1980s, the trade union Solidarność became a strong opposition to the communist government. Examples like these show that an opposition can change a country.

begriffe.erklaerung: The people who lead a country and carry out decisions.
A Swiss principle under which the large parties sit together in the government.
When someone has to leave their home country because they are persecuted there.
A group from the opposition that shows who would become a minister if it won the election.

gewusst: In Great Britain, the largest opposition party is officially called “His Majesty's Loyal Opposition”.
Swiss voters go to the polls several times a year and can thus also vote against decisions of the government and parliament.

teile.einleitung: A letter to the editor is a letter to a newspaper or magazine. In it, readers give their opinion, often about an article they have read.
wichtigste: With a letter to the editor, you tell the newspaper your opinion.
The editorial team decides which letters are published.
Usually you have to give your name.
A good letter to the editor is short and objective.
Writing a letter to the editor means using your freedom of expression.
Children are allowed to write letters to the editor too.

abschnitte.titel: What is a letter to the editor?
abschnitte.text: In a **letter to the editor**, readers write their opinion to the newspaper. They are often replying to a **newspaper article**. They say whether they agree or not. Some letters are printed in the newspaper. Today letters to the editor are often sent by email.

The **editorial team** is the team that makes the newspaper. It chooses which letters are printed. It may also shorten long letters. Usually it prints letters only with the writer's **name and place of residence**. Completely anonymous letters rarely appear.

abschnitte.titel: How to write a good letter to the editor
abschnitte.text: A letter to the editor is addressed to the editorial team. That is why people often begin with **“Dear Editor”**. A good letter to the editor is **short and objective**. You name the article you are replying to and explain your opinion with reasons. Short, polite letters are more likely to be printed. No newspaper prints insults.

abschnitte.titel: A piece of freedom of expression
abschnitte.text: Anyone who writes a letter to the editor expresses their opinion in public. This is protected by **freedom of expression**. In Switzerland, it is written in the **Federal Constitution**. In dictatorships, people are often not allowed to say what they think freely. **Children** are allowed to write letters to the editor too, and children's magazines are happy to print letters from children.

gewusst: In many newspapers, the letters pages are among the most read pages.
A letter to the editor is freedom of expression in action.

teile.einleitung: The word “dictator” comes from ancient Rome. There the dictator was a special office with great power, which was only given in times of emergency. Unlike today’s dictators, a Roman dictator had to give up his power again after a short time.
wichtigste: The word “dictator” comes from ancient Rome.
The dictator was an office with great power in times of emergency.
The term of office was limited to a maximum of six months.
The dictator was appointed by a consul.
Cincinnatus is regarded as a model, because he voluntarily gave up his power early.
Sulla and Caesar abused the office in order to rule themselves.
Today “dictator” means a sole ruler without any checks.

abschnitte.text: In the **Roman Republic** the state was normally led by two consuls, who were elected anew every year. In great danger, for example in a war or an uprising, a **dictator** could be appointed, however. For a short time he had almost unlimited power, so that action could be taken quickly. The name comes from the Latin word “dictare”, which means “to say” or “to command”.

The dictator was appointed by a consul on the decision of the **Senate**. His term of office lasted at most six months. Once the danger was over, he often stepped down earlier. As his deputy he chose a **Master of the Horse**, in Latin magister equitum. As a sign of his power he was accompanied by 24 attendants, the lictors, carrying bundles of rods.

The most famous story is about **Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus**. According to tradition, he was ploughing his field when he was made dictator in 458 BC, because a Roman army was trapped. He defeated the enemy and gave up his office after only 16 days. After that he returned to his farm. That is why he is still regarded today as an example of a politician who does not abuse power.

From the late 3rd century BC the office was not given out for a long time. In the 1st century BC the general **Sulla** had himself appointed dictator without a time limit and persecuted his opponents. Later **Gaius Julius Caesar** made himself dictator, and in 44 BC even dictator for life. Shortly afterwards, on 15 March 44 BC, he was murdered. After that the office was abolished.

In ancient Rome “dictator” was at first an honourable office regulated by law. But because of Sulla and Caesar the word took on a bad flavour. Today it is used for a **sole ruler** who governs without elections and without checks. The word “dictatorship” for such a form of rule comes from it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state without a king, in which elected people govern.
One of the two highest offices in the Roman Republic.
The council of experienced men in ancient Rome, which had a strong influence on politics.
Attendants who accompanied senior Roman officials and carried bundles of rods.

gewusst: The American city of Cincinnati is indirectly named after the Roman dictator Cincinnatus.
After the end of his term of office, a Roman dictator was in principle not allowed to be punished for his decisions.

teile.einleitung: Ioannis Metaxas was a Greek general and politician. From 1936 he ruled Greece as a dictator until he died in January 1941. He is also known for his “No” to Mussolini in 1940.
wichtigste: On 4 August 1936 Metaxas suspended parts of the constitution.
His dictatorship is therefore called the “4th of August Regime”.
King George II supported the dictatorship.
The regime copied features of fascist states, such as the state youth organisation EON.
In 1940 Metaxas rejected Italy's ultimatum, which is remembered on Ochi Day on 28 October.
Metaxas died in Athens in January 1941.

abschnitte.text: On **4 August 1936** Metaxas dissolved parliament and suspended parts of the constitution. The excuse was a planned **general strike** that Communists had announced. Metaxas claimed the state was in danger. He declared a state of emergency and banned the parties. King **George II**, who had returned in 1935, signed the necessary decrees.

Metaxas proclaimed the goal of a **“Third Hellenic Civilisation”**. After ancient Greece and Byzantium, a third great era was to follow. For this the regime adopted the symbols and forms of fascist states. The youth organisation **EON** was meant to bring up young people in line with the regime.

Under Metaxas, Communists in particular were persecuted. The security minister **Konstantinos Maniadakis** forced prisoners to make public **declarations of repentance**. In them they had to renounce their beliefs in order to be released. Many other opponents were banished to islands.

In 1940 Mussolini demanded that Italian troops be allowed to occupy important places in Greece. Metaxas refused. “Ochi” means “No” in Greek. The Greek army then pushed the Italians back into Albania. Today this is remembered on the national holiday of **Ochi Day** on 28 October. Before that, the fortified **Metaxas Line** had been built to protect the border with Bulgaria.

gewusst: In April 1941 the German Wehrmacht partly got round the Metaxas Line by going through Yugoslavia.
Metaxas died while the war against Italy was still going on, a few months before the German attack.

teile.einleitung: On 1 February 2021, the military took power in Myanmar. It removed the elected government and arrested leading politicians. Many people resisted with protests, strikes and later also with weapons.
wichtigste: The army justified the coup with alleged electoral fraud.
President Win Myint and Aung San Suu Kyi were arrested.
The military first declared a state of emergency for one year.
The junta governed through the State Administration Council.
Many employees went on strike in the Civil Disobedience Movement.
Removed members of parliament formed the National Unity Government.

abschnitte.text: Myanmar had already experienced long military rule in the past. In 1962, General **Ne Win** overthrew the civilian government. Only from 2011 did the country open up a little. In the election in November 2020, the party of **Aung San Suu Kyi** won clearly. The army claimed that there had been **electoral fraud**. Observers found no evidence of this.

On the morning of 1 February 2021, the military intervened. It arrested President **Win Myint**, Aung San Suu Kyi and other politicians. The military declared a **state of emergency**, at first for one year, and later extended it several times. The junta governed through a body called the **State Administration Council**. At its head was General Min Aung Hlaing.

After the coup, hundreds of thousands took to the streets. As a symbol they showed the **three-finger salute**. Doctors, teachers and civil servants stopped working. This **Civil Disobedience Movement** was meant to show that the junta cannot govern without the people. The army took very harsh action against the protests.

Removed members of parliament founded a rival government, the **National Unity Government**. Many young people joined armed groups. Together with groups of ethnic minorities, they fought against the army. From October 2023, the junta lost large areas in the north of the country to a rebel alliance's **Operation 1027**.

gewusst: The three-finger salute comes from the film series “The Hunger Games”.
Operation 1027 is named after its start date, 27 October 2023.

teile.einleitung: Francisco Franco was a Spanish general who ruled Spain as a dictator from 1939 to 1975. He came to power after a bloody civil war. Only after his death did Spain become a democracy again.
wichtigste: Francisco Franco ruled Spain as a dictator from 1939 to 1975.
He was born in Ferrol in north-western Spain in 1892 and died in Madrid in 1975.
In the Spanish Civil War from 1936 to 1939 he led the rebels.
Hitler and Mussolini supported him in the civil war.
He had himself called “Caudillo”, which means leader.
His opponents were persecuted, imprisoned or executed.
After his death Spain became a democracy under King Juan Carlos I.

abschnitte.text: **Francisco Franco** was born on 4 December 1892 in Ferrol in the region of Galicia. He became an officer and quickly made his career in the war in Morocco. At the age of only 33 he became a general, one of the youngest in Europe. He was a strict Catholic and rejected democracy, communism and regional self-government.

In July 1936 part of the army staged a coup against the democratically elected government of the **Second Spanish Republic**. This led to the **Spanish Civil War**, which lasted until 1939. Franco quickly became the leader of the rebels. Germany and Italy sent him soldiers, aircraft and weapons. In 1937 German aircraft destroyed the Basque town of Guernica, which the painter Pablo Picasso captured in a famous picture.

After his victory in 1939 Franco ruled as **Caudillo** with almost unlimited power. Only one party was allowed, the Falange. Tens of thousands of opponents were executed, and many hundreds of thousands were sent to prisons and camps or fled into **exile**. The languages of the Catalans and Basques were suppressed in public life. Newspapers and books were censored.

In the **Second World War** Spain officially remained neutral, but sent volunteers to fight on Germany’s side against the Soviet Union. After the war Spain was at first isolated internationally. In the Cold War, however, the USA worked with Franco because he was against communism. From the 1960s the economy grew strongly, partly thanks to many tourists.

Franco chose **Juan Carlos** as his successor as king. Franco died in Madrid on 20 November 1975. After that Juan Carlos I led Spain to democracy; this transition is called the **Transición**. In 1977 free elections took place, and in 1978 Spain was given a new democratic constitution. In 2019 Franco’s body was moved out of a large monument and reburied, which was much debated in Spain.

begriffe.erklaerung: Spanish for leader; this is what Franco had himself called.
A war between groups within the same country.
A violent overthrow, usually by the army.
Spain’s peaceful transition from dictatorship to democracy after 1975.

gewusst: Franco ruled Spain for about 36 years, longer than most European dictators of the 20th century.
Picasso’s painting “Guernica” about the destruction of the town was only allowed to be brought to Spain after Franco’s death.

teile.einleitung: Freedom of the press means that newspapers, radio, television and online media are allowed to report freely on what is really happening. The state may not tell them what to write and may not censor them. Free media are so important for democracy that they are often called the “fourth estate”.
wichtigste: A free press means that newspapers may write about what is really happening.
In Switzerland, Article 17 of the Federal Constitution guarantees media freedom and forbids censorship.
Free media keep a check on the powerful and uncover wrongdoing.
In dictatorships, the media are censored and journalists are persecuted.
The organisation Reporters Without Borders publishes a press freedom ranking every year.
3 May is World Press Freedom Day.
Journalists may keep their sources secret; this is called protection of sources.

abschnitte.titel: What is freedom of the press?
abschnitte.text: Originally, the **press** meant printed newspapers, but today radio, television and the internet are included too. Freedom of the press means that these media may report independently and express their opinions. The state may not check articles beforehand or ban them; that would be **censorship**. Freedom of the press is closely linked to freedom of expression.

In Switzerland, **Article 17 of the Federal Constitution** guarantees the freedom of the press, radio and television. It states explicitly that censorship is forbidden. **Editorial confidentiality** is also protected, so journalists do not have to reveal who told them something. Even so, there are rules: anyone who spreads lies or defames someone can be punished.

Free media inform the population so that people can make good decisions in elections and votes. They uncover **scandals**, for example bribery or abuse of power. That is why, alongside parliament, the government and the courts, they are called the **fourth estate**. Without a free press, the powerful could hide their mistakes more easily.

abschnitte.titel: Freedom of the press in dictatorships
abschnitte.text: In dictatorships, the state controls newspapers, broadcasters and often the internet too. Only what the government likes is reported, and criticism is forbidden. Journalists who write the truth anyway are threatened, imprisoned or even killed. As a result, many people do not find out what is really happening in their own country.

abschnitte.titel: Freedom of the press around the world
abschnitte.text: The organisation **Reporters Without Borders** was founded in France in 1985. Every year it publishes a ranking that shows how free the media are in around 180 countries. At the top there are usually northern European countries such as Norway, and at the bottom countries such as North Korea or Eritrea. In 1993 the UN declared **3 May** World Press Freedom Day.

begriffe.erklaerung: When the state controls and forbids what may be published.
A name for the media, because they keep a check on the powerful.
The right of journalists not to reveal their informants.
A person who researches news and writes reports for the media.

gewusst: The invention of printing by Johannes Gutenberg around 1450 made it possible for the first time to spread texts quickly to many people.
As early as 1766, Sweden was one of the first countries in the world to introduce a law on freedom of the press.

teile.einleitung: Nicolás Maduro became President of Venezuela in 2013 as the successor to Hugo Chávez. Under his government the country fell into a severe economic crisis, and millions of people emigrated. His rule and the elections in Venezuela are highly disputed internationally.
wichtigste: Maduro succeeded Hugo Chávez in 2013.
Before he became a politician, he worked as a bus driver.
From about 2016, Venezuela experienced hyperinflation.
By 2025, almost 8 million people had left the country.
In 2019 Juan Guaidó declared himself interim president.
In 2025 the opposition politician María Corina Machado received the Nobel Peace Prize.

abschnitte.text: As a young man, Maduro worked as a **bus driver** in the capital Caracas and was active in a trade union. Later he became a politician and a supporter of President **Hugo Chávez**. Among other things, he was foreign minister. When Chávez died in 2013, Maduro became his **successor** and narrowly won the presidential election.

Venezuela has very large **oil reserves**. When the oil price fell and the economy was badly managed, the country got into difficulty. From about 2016 there was **hyperinflation**: prices rose so fast that money was worth almost nothing. There was a shortage of food and medicines. By 2025, almost **8 million** people had left the country.

In December 2015 the opposition clearly won the **parliamentary election**. Maduro wanted to get round parliament. In 2017 he had a **Constituent Assembly** elected, which was dominated by his supporters. The opposition boycotted this election. Many countries criticised what he did.

In January 2019 the president of parliament, **Juan Guaidó**, declared himself interim president. Many countries recognised him, but Maduro stayed in power. In the presidential election in July 2024, the electoral authority declared Maduro the winner without showing detailed results. The opposition presented **evidence of its victory**. That is why this election is highly disputed.

In 2025 the Venezuelan opposition politician **María Corina Machado** received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. The Nobel Committee honoured her peaceful efforts for democracy. Maduro's supporters, on the other hand, see themselves as defenders of the country against foreign influence, especially from the USA.

gewusst: Because of inflation, many zeros have been removed from Venezuela's currency several times.
Venezuela is estimated to have the largest oil reserves in the world.

teile.einleitung: The People Power Revolution was a peaceful popular uprising in the Philippines in February 1986. In only four days, hundreds of thousands of people forced the long-time ruler Ferdinand Marcos to leave.
wichtigste: The uprising lasted from 22 to 25 February 1986.
It is also called the EDSA Revolution, after a large road in Manila.
Cardinal Jaime Sin called people out onto the streets via Radio Veritas.
Defence Minister Enrile and General Fidel Ramos turned away from Marcos.
Marcos left the country, and Corazon Aquino became president.

abschnitte.text: **Ferdinand Marcos** had been President of the Philippines since 1965. From 1972 he ruled under **martial law** and suppressed the opposition. In 1983 the opposition politician Benigno Aquino was murdered. His widow **Corazon Aquino** stood against Marcos in the election in February 1986. Marcos declared himself the winner, but many accused him of **electoral fraud**.

On **22 February 1986**, Defence Minister **Juan Ponce Enrile** and General **Fidel Ramos** turned away from Marcos. They barricaded themselves with their troops in two military camps in Manila. Ramos was later president himself from 1992 to 1998.

Cardinal **Jaime Sin** called on people via the church radio station **Radio Veritas** to protect the rebel soldiers. Hundreds of thousands then streamed onto **Epifanio de los Santos Avenue**, **EDSA** for short. They stood in front of the tanks with prayers and flowers. Many soldiers refused to shoot at the crowd.

On **25 February 1986**, Marcos left the presidential palace and was flown out to the USA. Corazon Aquino became the first female president of the Philippines. The peaceful uprising made the words **People Power** famous all over the world. It became a model for other non-violent movements.

gewusst: The colour yellow became the symbol of the movement around Corazon Aquino.
After fleeing, Marcos lived in Hawaii, where he died in 1989.

teile.einleitung: Desaparecidos means “the disappeared” in Spanish. This is the name for people who were abducted by state agencies and never reappeared. There were particularly many during the military dictatorship in Argentina from 1976 to 1983.
wichtigste: “Desaparecido” is the Spanish word for “disappeared”.
The last military dictatorship in Argentina lasted from 1976 to 1983.
General Jorge Rafael Videla led the junta from 1976.
Human rights groups speak of up to 30,000 disappeared people.
The former ESMA is now a memorial site.
30 August is the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances.

abschnitte.text: In **enforced disappearance** people are arrested by the police, the army or the secret services. The state then denies knowing anything about them. The families do not find out where their relatives are or whether they are still alive. This was meant to spread fear and cover every trace. Such crimes happened in several countries in Latin America, for example in Chile too.

In March 1976 the army in Argentina overthrew the government. General **Jorge Rafael Videla** became the first president of the **military junta**. The regime persecuted political opponents, students, trade unionists and many others. Human rights groups speak of **up to 30,000** disappeared people, and a state commission was able to document about 9,000 cases individually. After the defeat in the **Falklands War** there were free elections again in 1983.

The **ESMA** in Buenos Aires was actually a naval school. During the dictatorship it was a secret **torture centre**; about 5,000 people were held prisoner there, and most of them were murdered. In the so-called **death flights**, prisoners were thrown from aircraft over the Río de la Plata or the sea. In this way they were never to be found.

Since 1977 the **Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo** have gathered in Buenos Aires. Wearing white headscarves, they demand information about their disappeared children. Later many of those responsible were put on trial. Videla was sentenced to life imprisonment and died in prison in 2013. The former ESMA is now a **memorial site**, and since 2023 the museum has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: The UN has made 30 August the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances.
The white headscarves of the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo are now painted on the ground of the square.

teile.einleitung: Hugo Chávez was a Venezuelan officer and politician. From 1999 until his death in 2013 he was President of Venezuela. His supporters saw him as a fighter for the poor; his critics accused him of weakening democracy.
wichtigste: Chávez became known across the country in 1992 through a failed coup attempt.
In 1998 he won the presidential election.
With the constitution of 1999 the country was named the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela.
A coup against him in April 2002 failed after about two days.
In the programme “Aló Presidente” he spoke directly to the people.
In 2009 the limit on terms of office was lifted.

abschnitte.text: Hugo Chávez was born in 1954 and was a **paratrooper officer**. On 4 February 1992 he led a **coup attempt** against President Carlos Andrés Pérez. The attempt failed and Chávez went to prison. But a short television address made him known throughout the country. In 1998 he won the **presidential election** and took office in 1999.

Chávez called his political project the “**Bolivarian Revolution**”, after the independence hero **Simón Bolívar**. With the new **constitution of 1999** the country was now called the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela. With money from **oil** the government paid for health and education programmes. At the same time it nationalised many companies. Supporters praised the help for the poor; critics warned of the consequences for the economy.

In April 2002, after mass protests, Chávez was removed by a **coup**. The head of the employers' association, **Pedro Carmona**, became interim president. He immediately dissolved parliament and the courts. After mass protests by Chávez supporters and parts of the military changing sides, Chávez returned after about two days.

In the television programme “**Aló Presidente**” Chávez often spoke directly to the people for hours. He announced decisions there and took phone calls. Critics accused him of weakening independent media, the courts and the opposition. In February 2009 the people voted to lift the **limit on terms of office**. This allowed Chávez to stand again in 2012. He died in March 2013.
