gewusst: In his television address in 1992 Chávez said he had not achieved his goals “por ahora”, meaning “for now”. The words became famous.
Chávez named his whole political project after Simón Bolívar, who fought against Spanish rule in the 19th century.

teile.einleitung: In a good state, nobody has all the power alone. Power is shared among several people, bodies and levels. This way they can keep a check on each other, and abuse of power becomes more difficult.
wichtigste: Shared power prevents one person from becoming too powerful.
There are three branches of power: making laws, governing and administering justice.
Switzerland is a federal state with 26 cantons.
The Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities each have their own tasks.
The Federal Council has seven members and makes decisions together.
In 2025, four parties were represented in the Federal Council: SVP, SP, FDP and the Centre.

abschnitte.text: The idea of the **separation of powers** is old. The French thinker **Montesquieu** described it in the 18th century. The **legislature** makes the laws; this is parliament. The **executive** governs and carries out the laws; this is the government. The **judiciary** is the courts, which administer justice. None of these branches should dominate the others.

Switzerland is a **federal state**. This means that the Confederation and the 26 **cantons** share power. Each canton has its own constitution, its own parliament and its own government. In many German-speaking cantons the government is called the **Regierungsrat**, and in French-speaking Switzerland often the **Conseil d'État**. The more than 2000 municipalities also have a lot of say. Their government is often called the **municipal council**, and in towns the **town council**. This sharing of power is called **federalism**.

The Swiss national government is the **Federal Council** with seven members. It has no boss who decides alone. The members discuss and decide as a group. Afterwards, they all represent the decision to the outside world, even those who were against it. This is called the **principle of collegiality**. The President of the Confederation only chairs the meetings for one year.

Members of different parties sit on the Federal Council. In 2025 there were two from the SVP, two from the SP, two from the FDP and one from the Centre. The way the seats are shared among the large parties is often called the **magic formula**. In this way, many opinions are represented in the government. In addition, the people can have their say through **initiatives** and **referendums**. This is also a form of shared power.

In a **dictatorship** there is no real sharing of power. One person or a small group controls the government, parliament and the courts at the same time. Criticism is often suppressed, and there are no independent newspapers. That is why the separation of powers is seen as an important protection for people's **freedom**.

gewusst: The Swiss Federal Supreme Court is not based in Bern but in Lausanne.
Switzerland does not have a single person as head of state: the whole Federal Council forms the government together.
Germany, Austria and the USA are federal states too.

teile.einleitung: The November pogroms of 1938 were organised acts of violence against Jews in the German Reich. During the night of 9 to 10 November, synagogues burned, shops were destroyed and many people were arrested. They are seen as an important step towards the Holocaust.
wichtigste: The worst pogroms took place during the night of 9 to 10 November 1938.
For a long time the trivialising name “Kristallnacht” was widely used for them.
An assassination in Paris of the diplomat Ernst vom Rath served as the pretext.
Joseph Goebbels gave the hate speech in Munich that set off the pogrom.
Synagogues were set on fire.
Around 30,000 Jewish men were taken to concentration camps.

abschnitte.text: In October 1938, Germany expelled thousands of Jews with Polish citizenship to Poland. This is called the **“Polenaktion”** (Polish action). Among those affected were the parents of the young **Herschel Grynszpan**, who lived in **Paris**. In despair he shot the German diplomat **Ernst vom Rath**, who died shortly afterwards. The National Socialists used this act as a pretext.

On the evening of 9 November 1938, **Joseph Goebbels** gave a **hate speech** in Munich. After that, members of the SA, the SS and the party set off. They set **synagogues**, the Jewish houses of worship, on fire. They destroyed Jewish shops and homes. The police and the fire brigade did not step in to protect the Jews. Hundreds of people lost their lives.

For a long time the events were called **“Reichskristallnacht”** (Night of Broken Glass). The word “crystal” comes from the many **broken panes of glass** lying in the streets. Today this name is considered **trivialising**, because it sounds as if only glass was broken. That is why people speak of the **November pogroms** or the Pogrom Night. A pogrom is a violent hunt against a group of people.

After the pogroms, around **30,000 Jewish men** were taken to **concentration camps**. The German Jews were also forced to pay a so-called “atonement payment” of **one billion Reichsmarks**. So they had to pay themselves for the damage that others had done. Many Jewish shops were taken away from their owners. More and more Jews tried to flee Germany.

At that time many Jewish refugees also sought protection at the Swiss border. But Switzerland took in only a few. The St Gallen police commander **Paul Grüninger** let hundreds of refugees enter the country in 1938 and 1939 in spite of a ban. He was dismissed and convicted for this. Only in 1995 was he rehabilitated by a court, meaning declared innocent.

gewusst: 9 November is a special date in German history: the Berlin Wall also fell on a 9 November.
In many towns today, memorial plaques remember the destroyed synagogues.

teile.einleitung: A monarchy is a state headed by a king, a queen, a prince or an emperor. In the past, monarchs often ruled alone. Today, in most of Europe's monarchies, elected parliaments hold the real power.
wichtigste: Monarchy means “rule by one”; “mono” means alone.
In a monarchy, power is usually inherited.
In an absolute monarchy, the king rules without limits.
In Great Britain today, parliament makes the laws.
In 2025, Charles III was King of Great Britain.
Liechtenstein, a neighbour of Switzerland, is a principality.

abschnitte.text: The word **monarchy** comes from Greek. “Mono” means **alone**, and “archein” means **to rule**. So a monarch is someone who rules alone. The position is usually inherited within a family, often by the eldest child. The family is called a **dynasty** or royal house. The opposite is a **republic**, like Switzerland.

In an **absolute monarchy**, the king rules completely alone and without limits. He makes the laws, governs and administers justice. A famous example is the French king **Louis XIV**, the “Sun King”. He is said to have said: “I am the state”. He had the magnificent palace of **Versailles** enlarged.

Today most monarchies in Europe are **parliamentary** or **constitutional monarchies**. The king is at the top, but an elected **parliament** makes the laws. The monarch mainly has ceremonial tasks; for example, he welcomes guests from abroad. This is the case in **Great Britain**, where **Charles III** was king in 2025. Spain, Sweden, Norway and the Netherlands are also kingdoms.

The neighbouring country of **Liechtenstein** is a **principality**. At its head is a prince. He has more power there than most kings in Europe; for example, he can reject laws. At the same time there is a parliament and, similar to Switzerland, there are popular votes. Liechtenstein pays with the **Swiss franc**.

There are still around 40 monarchies in the world. Some are still almost absolute monarchies today, for example **Saudi Arabia**. The **Vatican** is also led by a monarch: however, the Pope is not determined by inheritance but elected.

gewusst: Louis XIV reigned for 72 years, longer than almost any other king in Europe.
The British king is also head of state of other countries such as Canada and Australia.

teile.einleitung: Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a Protestant theologian and pastor from Germany. He opposed National Socialism and was in contact with the military resistance. Shortly before the end of the war he was executed.
wichtigste: Bonhoeffer was a Protestant theologian, pastor and university teacher.
He belonged to the Confessing Church.
Through the Abwehr intelligence service he was in contact with the resistance.
From April 1943 he was in prison.
On 9 April 1945 he was executed in Flossenbürg concentration camp.
In prison he wrote the poem “Von guten Mächten wunderbar geborgen” (“By gracious powers so wonderfully sheltered”).

abschnitte.text: Dietrich Bonhoeffer was born in Breslau in 1906 and grew up in Berlin. He studied **theology**, the study of God and faith. While still young he became a pastor and university teacher. He made contacts with Christians in many countries. He was strongly influenced by the Swiss theologian **Karl Barth**.

The Nazis wanted to bring the Protestant Church into line. Its supporters, the **“German Christians”**, backed the regime. Opposing this was the **Confessing Church**, to which Bonhoeffer belonged. For it he ran the **preachers’ seminary in Finkenwalde**, where young pastors were trained. As early as 1933 he wrote in the essay “The Church and the Jewish Question” that, in the last resort, the Church must **“jam a spoke in the wheel itself”**, in other words stop the unjust state directly.

His brother-in-law **Hans von Dohnanyi** worked for the **Abwehr** intelligence service under Wilhelm Canaris. Bonhoeffer was formally employed there. On trips abroad, including to Switzerland, he made contacts for the resistance. In April 1943 he was arrested. On **9 April 1945**, a few weeks before the end of the war, he was executed in **Flossenbürg concentration camp** in the Upper Palatinate.

In December 1944, from prison, he sent the poem **“Von guten Mächten wunderbar geborgen”** (“By gracious powers so wonderfully sheltered”) as a Christmas greeting to his fiancée and his family. It was later set to music and is now a frequently sung hymn. In 1951 his friend **Eberhard Bethge** published his letters from prison under the title **“Widerstand und Ergebung”**, known in English as “Letters and Papers from Prison”. The book is one of the most influential theological texts of the 20th century.

gewusst: The hymn “Von guten Mächten” is also sung in many Swiss churches, often on New Year’s Eve.
Bonhoeffer lived and worked as a pastor in London for some time.

teile.einleitung: Freedom of expression means that you are allowed to say openly what you think, even if the government does not like it. It is a fundamental right and one of the most important features of a democracy. It is often missing in dictatorships, where criticising the government can be punished.
wichtigste: Freedom of expression means that you may express and spread your opinion freely.
In Switzerland, Article 16 of the Federal Constitution protects freedom of opinion and information.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 also mentions freedom of expression.
In a dictatorship you usually may not say freely what you think about the government.
Anyone who criticises it there risks prison, a ban from working or worse.
Freedom of expression has limits: insults, defamation and calls to hatred are forbidden.
Freedom of expression also means putting up with other opinions.

abschnitte.text: Freedom of expression is the right to **express freely** your own thoughts, views and judgements. You can do this by speaking, in a text, on a poster, in a song or on the internet. It also includes **freedom of information**, meaning the right to get information from different sources. Nobody may be forced to hold a particular opinion.

In Switzerland, freedom of expression is set out in **Article 16 of the Federal Constitution**. So you may criticise the government, the Federal Council or a party without being punished. This is important for direct democracy, because there is a lot of discussion before votes. The European Convention on Human Rights, which Switzerland joined in 1974, also protects this right.

In dictatorships, the government does not want to hear criticism. Anyone who speaks out against those in power can be arrested and then becomes a **political prisoner**. There is often **censorship**, which controls newspapers, books, films and websites. Many people therefore do not even dare to talk openly among friends, because informers might be listening.

Even in a democracy you may not say everything. Anyone who insults other people or spreads lies about them can be reported for **defamation**. In Switzerland, the **anti-racism law** also forbids demeaning people because of their origin or religion. The limit is where the rights of others are violated.

Having your own opinion is good; backing it up with arguments is even better. Listen too when someone has a different opinion, because you can learn a lot from it. On the internet, remember: many people can read what you write, so stay fair and respectful. Also check whether a piece of information is true before you pass it on.

begriffe.erklaerung: An important right that every person has and that is protected by the state.
When the state controls and forbids what may be published.
The most important law in Switzerland, which also contains the fundamental rights.
When someone insults another person or tells damaging lies about them.

gewusst: At Speakers' Corner in London's Hyde Park, anyone has been allowed to stand on a box and make a speech since the 19th century.
Children also have freedom of expression; this is written in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.

teile.einleitung: The Baath Party is an Arab party that was founded in Damascus in 1947. It combined the dream of a united Arab nation with socialism. In Syria and Iraq it ruled as the state party for decades.
wichtigste: “Baath” means rebirth in Arabic.
The party was officially founded in Damascus in 1947.
Its main founders were Michel Aflaq and Salah al-Din al-Bitar.
Its motto is “Unity, Freedom, Socialism”.
In 1966 it split into a Syrian and an Iraqi wing.
In Iraq it ruled from 1968 to 2003.

abschnitte.text: **Baath** means rebirth or renewal. What is meant is the rebirth of a united Arab nation. The two Syrian teachers **Michel Aflaq** and **Salah al-Din al-Bitar** had studied in Paris. Aflaq came from a Christian background, al-Bitar from a Muslim one. In April 1947 the founding congress took place in **Damascus**.

The motto is **“Unity, Freedom, Socialism”**. Unity means uniting all Arabs, and freedom means liberation from foreign rule. Socialism stands for an economy steered by the state. The idea of a common state for all Arabs is called **Pan-Arabism**. The party was expressly secular, in other words not religious in its outlook.

In Syria the party came to power in a coup in 1963. After another coup in Syria in 1966 it split into a **Syrian** and an **Iraqi wing**. After that Damascus and Baghdad remained enemies. In Syria Hafez al-Assad ruled with the Baath Party from 1970, and later his son Bashar. With Assad’s fall in December 2024 the party also lost power there.

In July 1968 the Baath Party came to power permanently in Iraq through a coup under **Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr**. His deputy was **Saddam Hussein**, who became president himself in 1979. Both Baathist states became dictatorships with powerful intelligence services. After the US invasion in 2003, party members were removed from state posts. This policy is called **de-Baathification**. Critics believe that it left many experts unemployed and fuelled the insurgency.

gewusst: One of the party’s co-founders was a Christian, even though most members were Muslims.
Syria and Iraq were both ruled by Baath parties and yet were enemies for a long time.

teile.einleitung: Malala Yousafzai comes from Pakistan and campaigns for all girls to be allowed to go to school. Even as a child she spoke bravely about this right. At the age of 17 she received the Nobel Peace Prize.
wichtigste: Malala was born in Pakistan on 12 July 1997.
She fights for the right of all girls to education.
At the age of 11 she wrote an online diary for the BBC.
In 2012 she was attacked by the Taliban and seriously injured.
In 2014, at 17, she received the Nobel Peace Prize.
She studied at the University of Oxford.

abschnitte.text: Malala grew up in the **Swat Valley** in the north of Pakistan. Her father ran a school. From 2007, the **Taliban** gained power there. This radical group wanted to forbid girls to go to school. Many girls' schools were closed or destroyed.

At the age of 11, Malala wrote an **online diary** for the British broadcaster the **BBC**. She used a different name so that nobody knew who she was. In it she wrote about life under the Taliban and about her love of school. Later she also appeared openly in the media and became well known.

In October 2012, the Taliban attacked Malala on her way home from school. She was seriously injured. She was taken to **Great Britain**, where she was treated in Birmingham. She recovered and has lived in Great Britain ever since. The attack caused outrage all over the world.

On her 16th birthday, 12 July 2013, Malala gave a famous speech at the **UN in New York**. She said that one child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world. The UN declared **12 July** “Malala Day”. Together with her father she founded the **Malala Fund**, which makes it possible for girls to go to school.

In 2014, Malala received the **Nobel Peace Prize**, together with Kailash Satyarthi from India. She was only 17 years old, which made her the youngest prize-winner in the history of the Nobel Prize. After that she studied Philosophy, Politics and Economics at the University of **Oxford**. She graduated in 2020.

gewusst: Malala is still the youngest person ever to have received a Nobel Prize.
Her book “I Am Malala” has been translated into many languages.

teile.einleitung: The “Great Firewall” is the system China uses to control and censor the internet in the country. Many foreign websites and services are blocked there. The name is a play on words with the Great Wall of China.
wichtigste: The Great Firewall is part of the “Golden Shield” project, which started in 1998.
The computer scientist Fang Binxing is seen as the “father of the Great Firewall”.
Deep packet inspection is used to check the content of data packets.
DNS manipulation makes blocked sites unreachable.
Since 2019 Wikipedia has been blocked in China in all language versions.
Since 2019 Russia has been building a so-called “sovereign internet”.

abschnitte.text: In 1998 China's Ministry of Public Security started the “**Golden Shield**” project. It includes police surveillance and filtering systems. The best-known part is the “**Great Firewall**”. A firewall is really a protective program for computers. Here it is used to keep out unwanted content. The computer scientist **Fang Binxing** is seen as the “father of the Great Firewall”, and he was often fiercely criticised for it online.

The Great Firewall uses several techniques. With **DNS manipulation**, the name service gives a false answer when asked for an internet address, and the blocked site leads nowhere. With **deep packet inspection**, not only the sender and destination but also the contents of data packets are checked. This makes it possible to track down banned keywords and disguised connections such as a **VPN**. A VPN is a kind of protected tunnel through the internet.

Many well-known services are blocked in China, such as Google, Facebook and YouTube. In 2010 Google no longer wanted to go along with the censorship of its search results and redirected its Chinese site to **Hong Kong**. However, this site is blocked in mainland China. Since April **2019** **Wikipedia** has been blocked in all language versions. Censorship also targets mockery: because users compared pictures of **Winnie the Pooh** with head of state Xi Jinping, such pictures were removed for a time.

Other states also control the internet more tightly. In 2019 Russia passed the **sovereign internet law**. Providers have to route data traffic through nodes controlled by the state. In this way the regulator **Roskomnadzor** can block content centrally. In an emergency the Russian network is even supposed to be able to disconnect from the worldwide internet. In Switzerland, by contrast, the Federal Constitution protects freedom of expression and freedom of information.

gewusst: The name “Great Firewall” refers to the Great Wall of China.
Anyone in China who wants to open blocked sites usually needs a VPN, which the state also tries to block.

teile.einleitung: Juche is the official state ideology of North Korea. The word is usually translated as “self-reliance”: the country is not to depend on anyone.
wichtigste: Juche means self-reliance or independence.
The doctrine demands political, economic and military independence.
In 1972 Juche was written into the constitution.
The Juche calendar begins in 1912, the year Kim Il-sung was born.
The Juche Tower in Pyongyang is 170 metres high.
Since 2012 the party has spoken of Kimilsungism-Kimjongilism.

abschnitte.text: According to the official doctrine, Juche has three principles. **Chaju** stands for political independence, **Charip** for economic self-sufficiency and **Chawi** for military self-defence. In this way North Korea is to become independent of foreign powers. **Hwang Jang-yop** is regarded as the most important person to have worked out the doctrine. In 1997 he fled to South Korea via the South Korean embassy in Beijing.

In 1972 Juche was written into the **constitution** as the guiding ideology. Step by step it pushed out **Marxism-Leninism**. In 2009 even the word “Communism” disappeared from the constitution. Since 2012 the party has spoken of **Kimilsungism-Kimjongilism**. This makes the teachings of the two dead leaders binding.

North Korea has its own **Juche calendar**. Juche year 1 is 1912, the year Kim Il-sung was born. The calendar was introduced in 1997. The **Juche Tower** stands in Pyongyang. It was opened in 1982 for Kim Il-sung's 70th birthday and is 170 metres high.

After the collapse of the Soviet Union, North Korea lost important help. Together with bad harvests, this led to a severe **famine** in the mid-1990s. In North Korea this period is called the “Arduous March”. Estimates speak of hundreds of thousands of deaths.

gewusst: The Juche Tower is made of 25,550 granite blocks, one for each day of Kim Il-sung's life up to its opening.
Hwang Jang-yop was the highest-ranking defector from North Korea.

teile.einleitung: North Korea is a country in East Asia and is regarded as one of the strictest dictatorships in the world. Since it was founded in 1948 it has been ruled by the same family, the Kims. The people there are almost completely controlled by the state and have hardly any contact with the rest of the world.
wichtigste: North Korea is in the north of the Korean Peninsula, and its capital is Pyongyang.
The state was founded in 1948 and has about 26 million inhabitants.
Since its founding, the Kim family has ruled: Kim Il-sung, Kim Jong-il and, since 2011, Kim Jong-un.
When a dictator dies, a family member often takes over power, as in North Korea.
The Songbun system divides the population according to the political loyalty of their family.
Free media, travel abroad and criticism of the government are forbidden.
North Korea has nuclear weapons and has carried out several nuclear tests since 2006.

abschnitte.text: North Korea is on the **Korean Peninsula** and borders China, Russia and South Korea. The capital is **Pyongyang**. The country is about three times the size of Switzerland and very mountainous. Between North and South Korea lies a strictly guarded **Demilitarised Zone** about four kilometres wide.

After the Second World War, Korea was divided, and in 1948 two states came into being. From 1950 to 1953, North and South Korea fought the **Korean War**, which only ended with a ceasefire. The founder of the state, **Kim Il-sung**, ruled until his death in 1994, and then his son Kim Jong-il followed. Since the end of 2011, his son **Kim Jong-un** has been in power.

In North Korea there is only one permitted ideology, which is called **Juche** and emphasises the country's self-reliance. Radio and television show only state programmes, and the worldwide internet is blocked for ordinary people. Anyone who criticises the government can be sent to a labour camp together with their whole family. In the 1990s, a great many people died in a severe famine.

The **Songbun system** divides the population according to the political loyalty of their family. Anyone whose ancestors were loyal to the party belongs to the “core” and has advantages. Those who come from “hostile” families get worse schools, jobs and housing. This classification is inherited, and children can hardly change it.

The rulers of the Kim family are worshipped like heroes. Their pictures hang everywhere, and in Pyongyang there are huge bronze statues of Kim Il-sung and Kim Jong-il. Adults often wear badges with the faces of the leaders. Children already learn songs and stories about the Kims at school.

Since 1953, Swiss officers have worked in the **Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission** on the border between North and South Korea. They are meant to help monitor the ceasefire. It is also known that Kim Jong-un went to school in the Bern area as a teenager. Switzerland has also provided humanitarian aid in North Korea for a long time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A form of rule in which one person or group decides alone and does not allow free elections.
A system in North Korea that classifies people according to how loyal their family is to the state.
The state ideology of North Korea, which emphasises independence and loyalty to the leader.
An agreement to stop fighting without peace having been made yet.

gewusst: For decades North Korea had its own calendar, which began with Kim Il-sung's year of birth, 1912.
At night North Korea is almost completely dark on satellite images, because there is little electricity.

teile.einleitung: A government in exile is a government that works from abroad. It cannot work in its own country, for example because of an occupation or a dictatorship. Even so, many other states recognise it as the lawful representative.
wichtigste: A government in exile works from abroad.
In the Second World War several governments in exile were based in London.
In 1940 Charles de Gaulle called for resistance from London.
Queen Wilhelmina and King Haakon VII led their countries from London.
The Tibetan government in exile has its seat in Dharamsala in India.

abschnitte.titel: What is a government in exile?
abschnitte.text: **Exile** means that someone cannot live in their home country. A **government in exile** therefore carries on working abroad. Many states recognise it as the **lawful representative** of its country if power there has been taken over through occupation or violence. In this way the government in exile can, for example, conclude treaties or command troops of its own.

abschnitte.titel: London in the Second World War
abschnitte.text: When Germany occupied many countries in Europe, several governments fled to **London**. They included the governments of **Poland**, **Norway** and the **Netherlands**. Queen **Wilhelmina** of the Netherlands encouraged her people to hold out through radio broadcasts. King **Haakon VII** of Norway refused to cooperate with the occupiers and went to London with the government in 1940.

On 18 June 1940 General **Charles de Gaulle** spoke on the **BBC** from London. He called on the French people to resist the German occupation. After that he founded **“Free France”**. After the liberation in 1944 he returned to Paris.

In 1959 an uprising against Chinese rule in Tibet failed. The **Dalai Lama** fled to India. The **Tibetan government in exile** was set up in **Dharamsala** in northern India. From the 1960s **Switzerland** also took in Tibetan refugees. Today one of the largest Tibetan communities in Europe lives here.

gewusst: The appeal of 18 June 1940 is now one of the most famous speeches in French history.
Since 1968 there has been a Tibetan monastery in Rikon in the canton of Zurich.

teile.einleitung: In internet censorship a state decides which websites and news people are allowed to see. Dictatorships in particular block websites, monitor conversations or even switch off the internet completely.
wichtigste: With the “Great Firewall” China blocks many foreign sites such as Google, YouTube or Facebook.
In North Korea most people may only use the sealed-off national network Kwangmyong.
In an internet shutdown a government switches off the internet completely or partly.
Many people get round blocks with a VPN.
Turkey blocked Wikipedia from 2017 to 2019.
Russia blocked Facebook and Instagram in March 2022.

abschnitte.text: China runs one of the biggest censorship systems in the world. It is called the **Great Firewall**. The name refers to the Great Wall of China. The system blocks many foreign sites such as Google, YouTube or Facebook. Instead, people use Chinese services, which the state can control more easily.

In an **internet shutdown** the government switches off the internet completely or partly. This often happens during protests. It makes it harder for demonstrators to coordinate, and pictures do not get out of the country. In January 2011, during the protests in Tahrir Square, Egypt cut almost all connections. In 2022, during the protests after the death of Jina Mahsa Amini, Iran slowed down the internet and blocked Instagram and WhatsApp.

Often states block only individual websites. Turkey blocked **Wikipedia** in April 2017. Only after a ruling by the Constitutional Court was the site unblocked at the end of 2019. In March 2022, shortly after the attack on Ukraine, Russia blocked **Facebook and Instagram**. The government wanted to restrict critical information about the war in this way.

abschnitte.titel: North Korea: a network for its own country only
abschnitte.text: In North Korea the worldwide internet is forbidden for almost everyone. At most, people may use **Kwangmyong**. This is an **intranet**, a network that only works inside the country. It contains only content that the state allows. Contact with the outside world is therefore hardly possible.

Many people in dictatorships use a **VPN**. A VPN sends data in encrypted form via a server abroad. This often makes it possible to open blocked sites anyway. Some governments therefore also try to block VPN services. In Switzerland the Federal Constitution protects **freedom of expression and freedom of information**.

gewusst: Turkey blocked Wikipedia for almost three years.
Despite switching off the internet in 2011, the Egyptian government could not stop the protests.

teile.einleitung: Rafael Leónidas Trujillo ruled the Dominican Republic in the Caribbean as a dictator from 1930 to 1961. He had himself called “El Jefe”, the boss, and ruled through fear and a large personality cult.
wichtigste: Trujillo ruled from 1930 to 1961.
From 1936 the capital Santo Domingo was called Ciudad Trujillo.
In 1937 he had thousands of people from Haiti murdered in the border area.
In 1960 the Mirabal sisters were murdered on his orders.
On 30 May 1961 Trujillo was shot dead in an assassination.

abschnitte.text: **Rafael Trujillo** was an officer and came to power in **1930**. He remained the country's strongman for over 30 years, and at times he let others govern as president. He had himself called **“El Jefe”** and officially “Benefactor of the Fatherland”. Statues and signs in his honour stood everywhere. In **1936** the capital Santo Domingo was renamed **Ciudad Trujillo**.

In 1937 Trujillo had thousands of Haitians murdered in the border area with **Haiti**. Estimates vary widely, but many experts put the number of deaths at around 20,000. Soldiers are said to have made people say the Spanish word **“perejil”**, parsley. Anyone who pronounced it with a Creole accent was considered Haitian. That is why the crime is called the **Parsley Massacre**.

The sisters **Patria**, **Minerva** and **María Teresa Mirabal** fought against the dictatorship. On **25 November 1960** they were murdered by Trujillo's men. Their death caused great outrage. Today, on this day, the UN also remembers the sisters with the **International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women**.

On **30 May 1961**, Trujillo was shot dead in his car by conspirators. Soon afterwards his regime collapsed, and the capital got its old name back. The Peruvian writer **Mario Vargas Llosa** tells the story of Trujillo's last days in his novel **“The Feast of the Goat”** from the year 2000.

gewusst: “The Goat” was a mocking nickname for Trujillo.
Under Trujillo, even the country's highest mountain, Pico Duarte, bore his name.

teile.einleitung: Competitive authoritarianism is a term from political science. It describes states in which elections do take place, but the government bends the rules so much that the opposition can hardly compete fairly.
wichtigste: The term was coined by Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way in 2002.
The opposition fights on an “uneven playing field”.
Unlike in closed dictatorships, the opposition can in principle win elections.
Competition takes place in four arenas: elections, parliament, the courts and the media.
Such governments often use tax investigations and lawsuits against critical media.
A well-known example is Peru under Alberto Fujimori.

abschnitte.text: In 2002, the political scientists **Steven Levitsky** and **Lucan Way** published an essay on **competitive authoritarianism** in the “Journal of Democracy”. A book on the subject followed in 2010. “Competitive” means that there is real competition. “Authoritarian” means that the government does not allow its power to be fairly limited.

In such states, **elections** take place and the opposition is allowed to take part. But the state systematically favours the government. Media, money and the courts create an **uneven playing field**. Even so, the opposition can in principle win. This distinguishes these regimes from completely closed dictatorships and can make them unstable.

According to Levitsky and Way, there are four areas in which the opposition can challenge the government: **elections, parliament, the courts and the media**. At the same time, the rulers try to increase their advantages in exactly these areas. Instead of open violence, they often use seemingly legal means. These include **tax investigations**, libel suits or taking away licences. In this way they keep up the appearance of the rule of law.

On 5 April 1992, the Peruvian president **Alberto Fujimori** had Congress dissolved and the courts reorganised. This is called a **self-coup**, because a president stages a coup against his own system. After that, Fujimori governed with elections. However, these were distorted by bribery and control of the media.

gewusst: In 2018, Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt published the book “How Democracies Die”, called “Wie Demokratien sterben” in German.
Regimes of this kind can actually lose power through an election.

teile.einleitung: The Reichstag fire was a large fire in the German parliament building in Berlin during the night of 27 to 28 February 1933. The National Socialists under Adolf Hitler used the fire to persecute their opponents and to abolish important fundamental rights. It is therefore seen as a decisive step on the road to the Nazi dictatorship.
wichtigste: On the evening of 27 February 1933, the Reichstag building in Berlin burned.
Adolf Hitler had only been Reich Chancellor since 30 January 1933.
The young Dutchman Marinus van der Lubbe was arrested at the scene.
The Nazis claimed that the communists had been planning an uprising.
The very next day, the Reichstag Fire Decree abolished important fundamental rights.
After that, thousands of political opponents were arrested.
Whether van der Lubbe acted alone is still disputed among experts today.

abschnitte.text: Late in the evening of **27 February 1933**, the **Reichstag building** in Berlin was in flames. The large debating chamber with the dome burned out completely. The 24-year-old Dutchman **Marinus van der Lubbe** was arrested in the building. He said that he had set the fire alone to protest against the government.

Only a few weeks earlier, on 30 January 1933, **Adolf Hitler** had been appointed Reich Chancellor. There were still other parties, and a Reichstag election had been set for 5 March 1933. But the National Socialists wanted all the power for themselves. The fire therefore suited them very well.

Hitler and his supporters immediately claimed that the communists wanted to start an overthrow. As early as 28 February, Reich President Paul von Hindenburg signed the so-called **Reichstag Fire Decree**. It suspended fundamental rights such as freedom of expression, freedom of the press and the right of assembly. The police could now hold people without a court ruling.

In the days that followed, thousands of communists, social democrats and other opponents were arrested. Many were taken to the first **concentration camps**. On 23 March 1933, the Reichstag passed the **Enabling Act**, which allowed the government to pass laws without parliament. In this way, Germany became a dictatorship within a few months.

abschnitte.titel: Trial and coming to terms with the past
abschnitte.text: At the end of 1933 a trial took place in Leipzig, at which van der Lubbe was sentenced to death; he was executed in 1934. Communists who were charged with him, including the Bulgarian Georgi Dimitrov, were acquitted. Experts still argue today about whether van der Lubbe acted alone or whether he had helpers. In 2008 the verdict against him was officially overturned by the German courts.

begriffe.erklaerung: The parliament of the German Reich and the building in which it met.
A rule issued by the government without a vote in parliament.
A law of 1933 that allowed Hitler's government to make laws without parliament.
Camps in which the National Socialists held opponents and persecuted people prisoner.

gewusst: The Reichstag building is now the seat of the German Bundestag and has had a glass dome that visitors can walk up since 1999.
The Reichstag Fire Decree remained in force throughout the whole period of National Socialism until 1945.

teile.einleitung: A children's magazine is a publication with news, knowledge and entertainment made especially for children. It explains the world in a way that children can understand well.
wichtigste: Children's magazines are made for children.
“Spick” is a well-known Swiss children's magazine.
A monthly magazine comes out once a month.
“logo!” is a news programme for children on the German channel ZDF.
In a school newspaper, children write the articles themselves.
Good children's news is true and easy to understand.

abschnitte.text: A **children's magazine** brings reports, puzzles, pictures and knowledge for children. It explains difficult things in simple language. In Switzerland, for example, **“Spick”** is well known. Some magazines come out every week, others once a month. A **monthly magazine** comes out once a month, a **daily newspaper** every day.

**Children's news** explains what is happening in the world. This helps children understand the world better, join in conversations and form their own opinions. On German television there is the programme **“logo!”** from ZDF for this. Children's news should also tell the **truth**. Good children's news is true and easy to understand.

An **interview** is a conversation in which a reporter asks someone questions. The reporter writes down or records the answers. Interviews are often found in children's magazines. Reporters also check whether a piece of news is correct before they report on it.

In a **school newspaper**, children write their own reports and interviews. This way they learn how **journalists** work. They look for topics, ask questions and design pages. Newspapers and free media are important because they are allowed to report on everything. In dictatorships this is often not allowed.

gewusst: Many children's magazines also print letters and drawings from their young readers.
Even children can work like real journalists on a school newspaper.

teile.einleitung: A personality cult is the excessive worship of a ruler as if he were a hero without faults. It includes huge pictures, statues, songs and holidays in his honour. Dictators in particular use personality cults to secure their power.
wichtigste: In a personality cult, a ruler is worshipped excessively.
Huge pictures, statues and monuments of the ruler are typical.
Some dictators build huge statues of themselves to look powerful.
Schoolbooks, newspapers and films show the leader as wise and faultless.
In a personality cult, criticising the leader is forbidden and often punished.
Famous examples are Joseph Stalin, Mao Zedong and the Kim family in North Korea.
The term became well known through a speech by Nikita Khrushchev in 1956.

abschnitte.text: In a **personality cult**, a single person is at the centre of the whole state. This person is shown as clever, brave, kind and infallible, almost like a superhuman being. Their picture can be seen everywhere: in schools, offices, on banknotes and on the walls of buildings. Anyone who doubts this is seen as a **traitor**.

A personality cult is built up with **propaganda**. This includes statues, portraits, songs, poems, parades and holidays in honour of the leader. Towns, streets or mountains are often named after him. Even children learn at school to be grateful to the leader.

A dictator has not come to power through free elections. With the personality cult, he wants to show that he is the only right person for the country. If people worship him or are afraid to criticise him, his **power** is secure. Mistakes and problems are therefore blamed on others.

There was an enormous cult around **Joseph Stalin** in the Soviet Union, with cities such as Stalingrad. In China, a large portrait of **Mao Zedong** still hangs on the Gate of Heavenly Peace in Beijing today. In Romania, Nicolae Ceaușescu had himself celebrated as “Conducător”. In North Korea, the Kims have been worshipped like heroes for decades, and their huge bronze statues stand in Pyongyang.

In 1956, the Soviet party leader **Nikita Khrushchev** gave a secret speech entitled “On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences”. In it he criticised the crimes of his predecessor Stalin and the worship of him. After that, many Stalin statues in the Soviet Union were removed and places were renamed. Since then, the term personality cult has been known all over the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: Excessive worship of a ruler, often encouraged by the ruler himself.
Deliberately influencing people, often with one-sided or false information.
A picture that shows a person's face or figure.
A ruler who decides alone and does not tolerate criticism.

gewusst: In Turkmenistan, the ruler Saparmurat Niyazov even named months after himself and his mother.
After dictatorships end, statues of the ruler are often pulled down by the people, like many Lenin statues after 1989.

teile.einleitung: Estado Novo means “New State” in Portuguese. This was the name of the dictatorship in Portugal that António de Oliveira Salazar built up. It lasted from 1933 until the Carnation Revolution in 1974.
wichtigste: Salazar became head of the Portuguese government in 1932.
The constitution of 1933 founded the Estado Novo.
The only permitted political organisation was the União Nacional.
The blue pencil became the symbol of censorship.
Portugal was a founding member of NATO in 1949 and of EFTA in 1960.
The dictatorship ended on 25 April 1974 with the Carnation Revolution.

abschnitte.text: **António de Oliveira Salazar** was finance minister from 1928 and took over the government in **1932**. The constitution of 1933 founded the **Estado Novo**. In the referendum on it, **abstentions were counted as Yes votes**. In this way the constitution achieved apparently overwhelming approval. The only permitted organisation was the **União Nacional**, which provided all the members of parliament at elections.

Censors struck out unwanted passages in newspapers and books with a **blue pencil**. In Portugal the “lápis azul” still stands for censorship today. The secret police, the **PIDE**, persecuted opponents. Many political prisoners were sent to the **Tarrafal** camp in the Cape Verde Islands. Because of its deadly climate it was called the “camp of slow death”.

In the Second World War Portugal remained neutral. In 1943, however, it let **Great Britain** use bases in the **Azores**, based on its old alliance with England. Because of this important location, Portugal became a **founding member of NATO** in 1949 despite the dictatorship. In 1960, together with **Switzerland**, Austria, Great Britain and other states, it founded **EFTA**, the European Free Trade Association.

In the presidential election of 1958 General **Humberto Delgado** challenged the regime. After the rigged election he went into exile and was murdered in Spain in 1965 by PIDE agents. From 1961 Portugal fought long **colonial wars** in its African colonies. In 1968 Marcelo Caetano succeeded the ailing Salazar. On **25 April 1974** officers overthrew the regime in the **Carnation Revolution**, largely without bloodshed.

gewusst: A song on the radio, “Grândola, Vila Morena”, was the secret starting signal on the night of the Carnation Revolution.
After 1974 Angola and Mozambique also became independent.

teile.einleitung: Freedom means being allowed to decide for yourself what you think, say and do. It is one of the most important human rights. In a dictatorship, people's freedom is severely restricted.
wichtigste: You are free if you are allowed to decide for yourself.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 says: all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.
Human rights apply to all people.
My freedom ends where the freedom of others begins.
The Statue of Liberty in New York was a gift from France.
William Tell is a Swiss hero of freedom from legend.

abschnitte.text: Imagine a bird whose cage is opened. It can decide for itself where to fly. **Freedom** is a bit like that: you may say what you think, choose your religion, meet other people and move about freely. But freedom has limits. My freedom ends where the **freedom of others** begins. I may do a lot, but I must not harm other people.

In 1948 the UN adopted the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights**. Its first article says: all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. Human rights apply to **all people** in the world; nobody is left out. In Switzerland the **Federal Constitution** protects many freedoms, for example freedom of expression and freedom of religion.

In the past there were **slaves** in many countries. They belonged to other people and had to work for their owners. Today slavery is banned everywhere. People are not free in a **dictatorship** either: anyone who criticises the government can be punished. Newspapers may not write freely, and there are no free elections.

The **Statue of Liberty** stands in New York Harbour. France gave it to the USA, and it was unveiled in 1886. In her raised hand she holds a **torch** whose light is meant to show the way to freedom. In Switzerland, **William Tell** is seen as a hero of freedom. In the legend he fights against the bailiff Gessler and stands for the freedom of the Swiss Confederates.

gewusst: The Statue of Liberty was built in France, taken apart into pieces and shipped to New York.
Friedrich Schiller made the legend of William Tell world famous with his play in 1804.

teile.einleitung: Joseph Goebbels was one of the most important men in National Socialist Germany. As Propaganda Minister from 1933 he controlled newspapers, radio and films in order to influence people in the party's interest.
wichtigste: From 1933 Goebbels was Reich Minister of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda.
He had studied German language and literature and had a doctorate.
From 1926 he led the Nazi party in Berlin as Gauleiter.
On 10 May 1933 he gave a speech at the book burning in Berlin.
In 1943 he asked in the Berlin Sportpalast: “Do you want total war?”
In May 1945 he took his own life in Berlin.

abschnitte.text: Goebbels studied **German studies**, that is German language and literature. In 1921 he finished in Heidelberg with a doctorate and liked to call himself “Dr Goebbels”. From 1926 he was **Gauleiter** of the Nazi party in Berlin. He built up the party there with marches and the newspaper “Der Angriff” (The Attack).

From 1933 Goebbels was **Reich Minister of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda**. **Propaganda** means deliberately influencing people with one-sided messages. Goebbels controlled newspapers, radio and films. The cheap **People's Receiver** radio meant that many families could afford a radio. In this way millions heard the speeches of the party leadership.

On **10 May 1933** students in Berlin and many university towns burned books by Jewish authors and authors who criticised the regime. In Berlin Goebbels gave a speech at the event. Artists, musicians and journalists had to be members of the **Reich Chamber of Culture** to be allowed to work. Anyone who was not admitted, for example Jews, was no longer allowed to practise their profession.

In 1943 the German army had suffered a heavy defeat at **Stalingrad**. In the Berlin **Sportpalast** Goebbels asked: “Do you want total war?” He wanted to get the population to make even greater efforts for the war. The hand-picked audience cheered on command. On 1 May 1945 Goebbels and his wife took their own lives in the Führerbunker in Berlin.

gewusst: The People's Receiver was deliberately cheap so that propaganda reached as many homes as possible.
The Sportpalast speech is seen as a well-known example of how propaganda stages enthusiasm.

teile.einleitung: Abuse of power means that someone uses their power to harm others or to gain advantages for themselves. This can be a dictator, but also a boss, a coach or an older child in the playground. That is why there are rules and checks that limit power.
wichtigste: Abuse of power means that someone uses their power to harm others.
It can happen in politics, at work, in sport, at school or in the family.
Dictatorships are based on abuse of power without any checks.
Separation of powers, elections and free media limit power in a democracy.
In Switzerland, abuse of office by officials is a criminal offence.
Ombudsman offices help if you feel you have been treated unfairly by the authorities.
Children and young people can call the number 147 if they have problems.

abschnitte.text: **Power** means that someone can decide things for others or make decisions about them. Parents, teachers, police officers and politicians have power so that they can carry out their tasks. We speak of **abuse of power** when someone uses this power for the wrong purposes. They then harm others or gain unfair advantages for themselves. Often the people affected find it hard to defend themselves.

In a **dictatorship**, abuse of power is an everyday thing, because there are no checks. Rulers have critics arrested, rig elections or enrich themselves from state assets. There can be abuse of power in democracies too, for example through **corruption**, meaning bribery. In 1887, the English historian Lord Acton wrote the famous sentence that power tends to corrupt and absolute power corrupts absolutely.

Abuse of power does not only happen in politics. A boss can treat employees unfairly or put them under pressure. A coach can humiliate children in sport, or older pupils can intimidate younger ones. **Bullying** often has to do with power too, because a group acts against a single person. Nobody has to put up with something like this.

In a state under the rule of law, power is shared out among different bodies; this is called the **separation of powers**. Regular elections make sure that politicians can be voted out. Free media uncover wrongdoing. Courts check whether the authorities are keeping to the law. Term limits also prevent someone from having too much power for too long.

The Swiss Criminal Code explicitly forbids **abuse of office**. Officials who use their position to harm someone or to enrich themselves can be punished. In many cantons and cities there are **ombudsman offices** that you can turn to if you have problems with the authorities. The first of these was set up in the city of Zurich in 1971.

If someone uses their power to put pressure on you, it is not your fault. Talk to someone you trust, for example your parents, a teacher or the school social worker. The **Pro Juventute** helpline is there for you around the clock on the phone number 147. You can also chat or send a message there. It also helps to write down what happened so that you can prove it later.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ability to decide things for others.
When someone accepts money or gifts and in return uses their power unfairly.
When an official uses their position to harm someone or to gain advantages.
A neutral office that helps if you feel you have been treated unfairly by the authorities.

gewusst: From 1971, the city of Zurich was the first municipality in Switzerland to have an ombudsman office.
The word “ombudsman” comes from Swedish, where such offices have existed since 1809.

teile.einleitung: Francoism is the name for the dictatorship of General Francisco Franco in Spain. It began after the Spanish Civil War in 1939 and ended with Franco’s death in 1975. During this time there were no free elections and no freedom of opinion.
wichtigste: Francisco Franco ruled Spain as a dictator from 1939 to 1975.
He had himself called “Caudillo”, which means leader.
The only permitted party was the Falange.
In the Second World War Spain officially remained neutral.
Catalan and Basque were suppressed in public.
From the 1960s tourism grew strongly.
After Franco’s death in 1975 Spain became a democracy.

abschnitte.text: In 1936 parts of the army rose up against the elected government of the **Second Spanish Republic**. This led to the **Spanish Civil War**, which lasted until 1939. General Francisco Franco led the rebel troops. He received help from Hitler’s Germany and from fascist Italy. After his victory in 1939 he ruled Spain as a dictator.

Franco had himself called “**Caudillo**”, the Spanish word for leader, rather as Mussolini called himself “Duce”. He was head of state and commander-in-chief at the same time. All parties except the **Falange** were banned, and Franco controlled this state party. Newspapers and radio were **censored**, and opponents were persecuted and imprisoned. The Catholic Church was closely linked with the regime.

Franco wanted a unified Spain with only one language. That is why **Catalan** and **Basque** were suppressed for a long time in schools, offices and in public. In the Basque Country the underground organisation **ETA** was formed in 1959. It fought with violence for an independent Basque Country and carried out many attacks. In 1973 it killed Franco’s head of government, Luis Carrero Blanco. ETA only dissolved itself in 2018.

In the **Second World War** Spain officially remained neutral, even though Franco was close to Hitler. However, he sent the volunteer **Blue Division** to fight against the Soviet Union. After the war Spain was at first isolated, but in the Cold War it moved closer to the USA. From the 1960s millions of tourists from northern Europe travelled to Spain’s beaches. **Tourism** brought a lot of money into the country.

Franco died in Madrid on 20 November 1975. After that **Juan Carlos** became king, and Spain peacefully became a democracy. Near Madrid Franco had a huge memorial with a tall cross built, the **Valley of the Fallen**. Political prisoners also had to work on it. Franco was buried there, but was reburied elsewhere in 2019. Today the place is called the **Valle de Cuelgamuros**.

gewusst: Franco’s rule lasted almost 40 years.
The cross above the memorial near Madrid is about 150 metres high.

teile.einleitung: Auschwitz was the largest concentration and extermination camp of the National Socialists. Around 1.1 million people were murdered there, the vast majority of them Jews. Today Auschwitz is a memorial and a symbol of the Holocaust.
wichtigste: Auschwitz is near the town of Oświęcim in the south of present-day Poland.
The Birkenau section of the camp was an extermination camp.
Above the gate of the main camp are the words “Arbeit macht frei” (“Work sets you free”).
The first and longest-serving commandant was Rudolf Höss.
The Red Army liberated the camp in January 1945.
27 January is International Holocaust Remembrance Day.

abschnitte.text: Auschwitz is near the town of **Oświęcim** in the south of present-day **Poland**. During the Second World War the area was occupied by Germany. The camp consisted of several parts. The **main camp** was the first part, and **Auschwitz II**, called **Birkenau**, was an extermination camp.

Around **1.1 million people** were murdered at Auschwitz, the vast majority of them Jews. No other camp had so many victims. At Birkenau, most were killed straight after arrival. Above the gate of the main camp are the words **“Arbeit macht frei”**, meaning “Work sets you free”. This sentence was a cruel lie meant to deceive and mock the prisoners.

Many prisoners had their **prisoner number** tattooed on their forearm. Auschwitz was the only camp where this was done systematically. People were no longer meant to have names, only numbers. The first and longest-serving commandant was **Rudolf Höss**. He was sentenced in Poland in 1947 and executed.

In **January 1945**, soldiers of the **Red Army** reached the camp. They still found around 7000 survivors. Before that, the SS had driven most of the prisoners on **death marches**. The day of liberation, **27 January**, has been the international day of remembrance for the victims of the Holocaust since 2005. In Switzerland too, the victims are remembered on this day.

gewusst: In 2005, the UN declared 27 January International Holocaust Remembrance Day.
Today many school classes from all over Europe visit the Auschwitz memorial.

teile.einleitung: Benito Mussolini was an Italian politician who ruled Italy as a fascist dictator from 1922. He founded the fascist movement and had himself called “Duce”, meaning leader. As an ally of Adolf Hitler he led Italy into the Second World War, at the end of which, in 1945, he was shot.
wichtigste: Mussolini was born in Predappio in northern Italy in 1883.
As a young man he lived in Switzerland from 1902 to 1904.
In 1919 he founded the fascist movement, whose supporters wore black shirts.
After the March on Rome in October 1922 he became head of government.
From 1925 he turned Italy into a dictatorship.
In 1940 Italy entered the Second World War on Germany’s side.
In April 1945 Mussolini was shot by partisans at Lake Como.

abschnitte.text: **Benito Mussolini** was the son of a blacksmith and a teacher. At first he himself worked as a teacher and journalist and was a member of the Socialist Party. From 1902 to 1904 he lived in **Switzerland**, including in Lausanne, where he got by doing odd jobs and was arrested several times. Because he campaigned for Italy to enter the First World War, he was expelled from the party in 1914.

In 1919 Mussolini founded the **Fasci di combattimento** in Milan, from which the fascist party emerged. The name comes from the Latin fasces, a bundle of rods that was a sign of power in ancient Rome. **Fascism** rejects democracy and demands that everyone submit to a strong leader and to the nation. Mussolini’s gangs of thugs, the **Blackshirts**, violently attacked political opponents.

In October 1922 thousands of fascists marched to Rome to put pressure on the government. King Victor Emmanuel III then appointed Mussolini prime minister. From 1925 he banned other parties, restricted the press and ruled as a **dictator**. In 1929 he concluded the Lateran Treaties with the Catholic Church, which created the state of Vatican City.

In 1935 Italy invaded **Abyssinia**, today’s Ethiopia, and even used poison gas. In 1936 Mussolini allied himself with Hitler in the so-called Berlin-Rome Axis. In June 1940 Italy entered the **Second World War**, but suffered many defeats. In 1938 Italy also introduced laws against Jews.

After the Allies landed in Sicily, Mussolini was removed from power and arrested in July 1943. German paratroopers freed him, and after that he led a state in northern Italy that depended on Hitler, the Republic of Salò. In April 1945 he tried to flee towards Switzerland in disguise, but was recognised by **partisans** at **Lake Como**. On 28 April 1945 he was shot, and his body was publicly displayed in Milan.

begriffe.erklaerung: An ideology that wants an all-powerful leader and a strictly controlled nation.
Italian for leader; this is what Mussolini had himself called.
Fighters who secretly fight against an occupation or a dictatorship.
A ruler who decides everything alone and tolerates no opposition.

gewusst: In Lausanne Mussolini also attended lectures at the university, which later gave him an honorary doctorate that caused a lot of criticism.
The word “fascism” became known all over the world through Mussolini.
Mussolini was captured only a few kilometres from the Swiss border.

teile.einleitung: Propaganda is the deliberate influencing of people so that they adopt a particular opinion or do a particular thing. It often spreads one-sided or false information and appeals to feelings such as fear, pride or hatred. Dictatorships use propaganda to secure their power.
wichtigste: Propaganda is the deliberate influencing of people, often with one-sided or false information.
The word comes from the Latin “propagare”, which means to spread.
Propaganda uses posters, films, speeches, songs and today also social media.
It appeals above all to feelings and greatly simplifies complicated things.
Under National Socialism, Joseph Goebbels ran a special Ministry of Propaganda.
Dictatorships use propaganda to justify their rule and to create enemy images.
If you check sources and read different media, you can see through propaganda more easily.

abschnitte.text: Propaganda wants to steer people in a particular direction. Unlike factual information, it is not about showing all sides fairly. Instead, only suitable facts are shown, others are left out, or even **lies** are told. Often an **enemy image** is created, meaning a group that is supposed to be to blame for everything.

The word comes from the Latin **“propagare”**, which means “to spread” or “to extend”. In 1622 Pope Gregory XV founded an office in Rome for spreading the faith, the “Congregatio de Propaganda Fide”. For a long time the word therefore had no negative meaning. Only through the propaganda of the First and Second World Wars did it get its bad reputation.

Under **National Socialism**, from 1933 there was a Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda under **Joseph Goebbels**. It controlled newspapers, radio, films and art. A cheap radio, the “Volksempfänger” (people's receiver), was meant to bring Hitler's speeches into every home. In the Soviet Union, China and North Korea too, posters, films and schoolbooks have been and are used for propaganda.

Propaganda repeats simple messages again and again until people believe them. It works with powerful images, music and feelings instead of arguments. It is often claimed that “everyone” thinks something, so that you go along with it. Critics are made fun of or called **traitors**.

Today propaganda also spreads through social media, videos and chat messages. False reports are often called **fake news**. Sometimes automatic programs, so-called bots, spread such content thousands of times. Tip: always ask yourself who is spreading a message, what intention might lie behind it and whether other sources report the same thing.

begriffe.erklaerung: Deliberately influencing the opinions of many people, often in a one-sided or false way.
A bad, often false picture of a group that is presented as an opponent.
Deliberately false news that is made to look real.
Where a piece of information comes from, for example a newspaper or a specialist book.

gewusst: Advertising uses some tricks that propaganda also uses, for example repeating a message over and over.
In the First World War, almost all the countries involved used colourful posters to recruit soldiers.

teile.einleitung: The term “Machtergreifung” (seizure of power) describes how Hitler and the National Socialists came to power in Germany in 1933 and quickly expanded it. Many historians prefer to speak of a “Machtübertragung” (transfer of power), because conservative elites handed power to Hitler.
wichtigste: On 30 January 1933, Reich President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Hitler Reich Chancellor.
Apart from Hitler, only two NSDAP members sat in the first cabinet.
After the Reichstag fire of 27 February 1933, the communists were the first to be persecuted.
Only the SPD voted against the Enabling Act.
On 2 May 1933, the trade unions were smashed.
From August 1934, Hitler called himself “Führer and Reich Chancellor”.

abschnitte.text: On **30 January 1933**, Reich President **Paul von Hindenburg** appointed Hitler Reich Chancellor. Apart from Hitler, only **Wilhelm Frick** and **Hermann Göring** in the first cabinet belonged to the NSDAP. Most of the ministers were conservatives. Vice-Chancellor **Franz von Papen** believed they could “box Hitler in” and tame him. This **taming strategy** failed within a few months.

Late in the evening of **27 February 1933**, the **Reichstag building** in Berlin caught fire. The National Socialists claimed that the communists had set it alight. They used the fire as an excuse to move against their opponents. Thousands of members of the **KPD** were arrested.

With the **Enabling Act**, the government could pass laws without parliament. Only the **SPD** voted against it, even though armed SA men stood in the chamber. Its chairman **Otto Wels** explained the no vote in a famous speech. On **2 May 1933**, the SA and SS occupied the trade union buildings throughout the country. The trade unions were replaced by the German Labour Front.

During the **Gleichschaltung** (bringing into line), states, clubs and associations were made subject to the party. They were given National Socialist leaders. After Hindenburg's death in **August 1934**, Hitler combined the two highest offices. He now called himself **“Führer and Reich Chancellor”**. This placed all power in his hands.

**“Machtergreifung”** is a term from Nazi propaganda. It pretends there was a heroic victory. In fact, Hitler was brought into government by conservative circles around the Reich President. That is why many historians prefer to speak of a **“Machtübertragung”**, a transfer of power.

gewusst: In Hitler's first cabinet, the National Socialists were in the minority in terms of numbers.
In only about a year and a half, the Weimar Republic was turned into a Führer state.

teile.einleitung: The Cultural Revolution was a campaign by Mao Zedong in China that lasted from 1966 to 1976. It was directed against supposed enemies and old traditions. Young Red Guards humiliated teachers and officials, destroyed temples and works of art, and millions of people suffered.
wichtigste: The Cultural Revolution was Mao's campaign against supposed enemies and old traditions.
It lasted from 1966 to 1976.
School pupils and students formed the Red Guards.
Old customs, works of art and temples were destroyed.
Many teachers, artists and politicians were persecuted and humiliated.
Millions of young people were sent to work in the countryside.
The Cultural Revolution ended after Mao's death in 1976.

abschnitte.text: In May 1966, **Mao Zedong** proclaimed the Cultural Revolution. He claimed that enemies of communism were hiding in the party, in schools and in culture. In truth, after failures such as the Great Leap Forward, Mao wanted to win back his power. To do this, he turned to young people and called on them to fight against authority.

Millions of school pupils and students joined the **Red Guards**. They carried the little red book of Mao quotations with them, which in German is often called the **“Mao Bible”**. At huge rallies in Tiananmen Square in Beijing, they cheered Mao. They forced teachers, professors and party officials to confess supposed mistakes at public meetings. Many were beaten, and some were killed.

The Red Guards were supposed to fight the **“Four Olds”**: old ideas, old culture, old habits and old customs. In the process, temples, monasteries, churches, books and art treasures were destroyed. In Tibet too, many Buddhist monasteries were damaged. Schools and universities stayed closed for years.

Senior politicians were persecuted too. The head of state **Liu Shaoqi** was overthrown and died in captivity in 1969. The later leader **Deng Xiaoping** was banished and had to work in a factory. From 1968, millions of young people from the cities were sent to work in the countryside. The number of deaths is estimated at hundreds of thousands to several million.

Mao died on 9 September 1976. Shortly afterwards, the so-called **Gang of Four** was arrested, a group of radical leaders that included Mao's widow Jiang Qing. This brought the Cultural Revolution to an end. In 1981, the Communist Party of China officially described it as a serious mistake. However, an open examination of this period is still only possible to a limited extent in China today.

begriffe.erklaerung: Groups of school pupils and students who fought for Mao during the Cultural Revolution.
A small red book with sayings of Mao Zedong, called the “Mao Bible” in German.
Four radical politicians who were arrested after Mao's death.
A planned action intended to achieve a particular goal.

gewusst: The little red book of Mao quotations is one of the most printed books in the world.
During the Cultural Revolution, many young people could not go to school or university for years.

tfxuge1.t: Candles as a sign of protest

teile.einleitung: A burning candle is a powerful sign of peaceful protest. People in dictatorships and democracies have used candles to show that they stand up for their rights without violence.
wichtigste: Candles show that you do not want violence.
If you are carrying a candle, you have no hand free for stones or sticks.
In 1989 many people in Leipzig carried candles at demonstrations.
In 1988 the Candle Demonstration for freedom of religion took place in Bratislava.
The symbol of Amnesty International is a candle with barbed wire.
Chains of lights and vigils are quiet forms of protest.

abschnitte.text: A small flame lights up the darkness. That is why a candle often stands for **hope** of a better future. It also shows: we are **peaceful**. You hold the candle in one hand and shield the flame from the wind with the other. So you have no hand free for stones or sticks.

In autumn 1989 tens of thousands of people in **Leipzig** in the GDR demonstrated against the dictatorship. Many carried candles. They also placed them in front of buildings of the **secret police**. The protests remained peaceful and helped to bring about the end of the GDR.

In 1988 thousands of people stood in a square in **Bratislava** holding candles. At that time the city belonged to **Czechoslovakia**, which was ruled by the Communists. The people demanded **freedom of religion**. The police drove them away with water cannon. The protest is seen as a brave sign against the dictatorship.

In a **chain of lights** many people stand side by side in a row holding candles or lamps. In 1992 hundreds of thousands of people in **Munich** protested in this way against **hostility towards foreigners**. At a **vigil** people stand quietly in one place, often with candles. They remember an injustice or demand something. Such gatherings also take place in Swiss cities.

The human rights organisation **Amnesty International** has a **candle with barbed wire** as its symbol. The candle stands for hope, the barbed wire for imprisonment. Amnesty works for people who have been locked up because of their opinions.

gewusst: Hundreds of thousands of people took part in the chain of lights in Munich in 1992.
The candle in barbed wire is one of the best-known symbols of human rights.

teile.einleitung: In autumn 1989 hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets in the GDR. They demanded freedom and democracy, and they did so without violence. This Peaceful Revolution led to the fall of the Berlin Wall and to the reunification of Germany.
wichtigste: The GDR was the eastern part of Germany and a dictatorship.
In Leipzig people demonstrated every Monday after the prayer for peace in St Nicholas Church.
The chants “We are the people!” and “No violence!” became famous.
On 9 October 1989 around 70,000 people demonstrated in Leipzig.
On 9 November 1989 the Berlin Wall opened.
Since 3 October 1990 Germany has been one country again.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War Germany was divided. In the east the **GDR**, the German Democratic Republic, was created. Despite its name it was a dictatorship: the SED party decided everything, and there were no free elections. The secret police, the **Stasi**, spied on the population, and travelling to the West was almost impossible. In 1989 many people fled to the West via Hungary, and discontent grew.

In Leipzig people met every Monday for the **prayer for peace** in **St Nicholas Church**. Afterwards they marched through the city together. These gatherings grew into the **Monday demonstrations**. Many people carried candles in their hands. Soon people were demonstrating in other cities of the GDR too.

The demonstrators chanted “**We are the people!**”. With this they showed that the people, not the government, should decide. Another chant was “**No violence!**”. People did not want to give the police any reason to attack. On **9 October 1989**, despite great fear, around 70,000 people turned up in Leipzig. The police and the army did not step in because there were so many of them.

abschnitte.titel: Fall of the Wall and unity
abschnitte.text: On the evening of **9 November 1989** the **Berlin Wall** opened. It had divided the city for almost 30 years. That night people from East and West celebrated together. In March 1990 the first free elections took place in the GDR. On **3 October 1990** the GDR and the Federal Republic became one country again. Today this day is the Day of German Unity.

gewusst: The Wall also opened because of a mistake: at a press conference an SED politician said the new travel rules applied “immediately, without delay”.
Because of the Monday demonstrations, Leipzig is also called the “City of Heroes”.

teile.einleitung: A peaceful transfer of power means that whoever loses an election hands over the government to the winners without violence. This is at the heart of democracy. Some dictatorships also came to an end peacefully.
wichtigste: In a democracy, the losers of an election accept the result.
George Washington stepped down voluntarily in 1797 after two terms.
In 1801 the governing party in the USA changed peacefully for the first time.
New US presidents take office on 20 January.
In Poland in 1989, the government and the opposition negotiated change at the Round Table.
In Chile, Pinochet lost a referendum in 1988.
After Franco, Spain became a democracy during the Transición.

abschnitte.text: In a **democracy** the people decide who governs. For this to work, the losing side has to accept the result. It hands over office to the winners in an orderly way, without violence. This is called a **peaceful transfer of power**. In a dictatorship, by contrast, rulers often cling to power. In Switzerland the Federal Assembly elects the Federal Council, and changes happen calmly and in an orderly way.

**George Washington** was the first President of the USA. In 1797 he stepped down voluntarily after two terms and gave up a third. With this he set an important example. In 1801 **Thomas Jefferson** took over from John Adams, who belonged to a rival party. Adams accepted his defeat and handed over office. Since 1937 a new president's term has begun on **20 January** after the election.

Poland was ruled by the Communists until 1989. The trade union **Solidarność** campaigned for more freedom. In 1989 the government and the opposition sat down at a **Round Table**. They agreed on partly free elections. This began a peaceful path to democracy in Poland.

In Chile, General **Augusto Pinochet** ruled as a dictator. In 1988 he let the people vote on whether he should continue to govern, and the majority voted “No”. In 1989 **Patricio Aylwin** won the presidential election and took office in March 1990. In Spain the dictator Franco died in 1975. During the **Transición** the country became a parliamentary monarchy without civil war, with free elections and the constitution of 1978.

gewusst: Washington giving up a third term later became the rule: since 1951 a US president may be elected no more than twice.
In 1988 Pinochet's opponents campaigned for the “No” with a cheerful rainbow.

teile.einleitung: The Holocaust was the genocide of the European Jews by the National Socialists during the Second World War. Around six million people were murdered. In Hebrew this crime is called the Shoah.
wichtigste: Around six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust.
Shoah is the Hebrew word for it and means “catastrophe”.
From September 1941 Jews in the German Reich had to wear a yellow star.
The mass murder was organised at the Wannsee Conference in January 1942.
The Sinti and Roma were also victims of genocide.
The Swiss Paul Grüninger and Carl Lutz saved many people.

abschnitte.text: The word **Holocaust** comes from the Greek “holokaustos” and refers to a sacrifice that is completely burnt. Because the word recalls a sacrifice, many people prefer the Hebrew term **Shoah**. It means “catastrophe” or “great disaster”. The National Socialists murdered around **six million** Jews, about two thirds of the Jews in Europe.

From as early as 1933 Jews in Germany were **excluded** and deprived of their rights. They lost their jobs, their businesses and their rights. From September 1941 in the German Reich they had to wear a **yellow star** with the word “Jude” (Jew) on it. In the occupied territories Jews were locked up in **ghettos**. The largest was in **Warsaw**; at times more than 400,000 people lived there in extremely cramped conditions. In 1943 the inhabitants fought back in the Ghetto Uprising.

From 1941 the **Einsatzgruppen** (mobile killing units) shot hundreds of thousands of Jews behind the Eastern Front. On **20 January 1942** representatives of ministries and the SS met in a villa on the Wannsee in Berlin. At this **Wannsee Conference** they discussed how to carry out the so-called “Final Solution”, the murder of the Jews of Europe.
