People from all over Europe were deported to **extermination camps** such as Auschwitz-Birkenau and murdered there. Hundreds of thousands of **Sinti and Roma** were also victims of genocide; many Roma call it the Porajmos.

Switzerland took in refugees during this time, but also turned many Jewish refugees away at the border. In 1938 the St Gallen police commander **Paul Grüninger** let hundreds of refugees into the country even though it was forbidden. He was dismissed and convicted and was only rehabilitated in 1995. In 1944 the diplomat **Carl Lutz** issued **letters of protection** in Budapest and so saved tens of thousands from deportation. Both are honoured as “**Righteous Among the Nations**”.

On **27 January 1945** Soviet soldiers liberated the Auschwitz camp. Since 2005 this day has been the UN's International Holocaust Remembrance Day. Memorials, museums and the accounts of survivors keep the memory alive. They are meant to help make sure that something like this never happens again.

gewusst: The Yad Vashem memorial in Jerusalem honours people who rescued Jews as “Righteous Among the Nations”.
Carl Lutz set up numerous safe houses in Budapest, including the well-known “Glass House”.

teile.einleitung: In a political purge, a government removes people it sees as a danger from the party, the state or the army. In dictatorships this was often done through arrests, show trials and murders.
wichtigste: Political purges are meant to get rid of opponents and possible rivals.
Under Stalin they reached their peak in the Great Terror of 1937 and 1938.
NKVD Order No. 00447 set fixed quotas of victims.
The leadership of the Red Army was also purged.
In 1934 Hitler had the SA leadership around Ernst Röhm murdered.
In 1956 Khrushchev criticised Stalin's crimes in his secret speech.

abschnitte.text: The word **purge** sounds harmless, but it means something terrible. Rulers remove people they distrust from their posts. Often their own supporters who have become too powerful are hit too. In dictatorships, those affected are often arrested, convicted in **show trials** or killed. The aim is to secure the ruler's own power and to intimidate everyone.

In the Soviet Union in the 1930s, **Joseph Stalin** had hundreds of thousands of people killed and even more sent to camps. The peak in 1937 and 1938 is also called the “Yezhovshchina”, after the head of the secret police **Nikolai Yezhov**. **Order No. 00447** of July 1937 told the regions how many people were to be arrested. Yezhov himself was removed in 1938 and shot in 1940.

In 1937, Marshal **Mikhail Tukhachevsky** was convicted in a secret trial of an alleged conspiracy and shot. After that, thousands of officers were arrested. This greatly weakened the **Red Army** shortly before the Second World War. Stalin also persecuted opponents abroad: **Leon Trotsky** was murdered by a Soviet agent in Mexico in 1940.

At the end of June 1934, **Adolf Hitler** had the leadership of the SA and other rivals murdered, including **Ernst Röhm**. The National Socialists called the killings the “Röhm Putsch”, even though there was no putsch. After that, Hitler's power was secure, and the **SS** rose.

abschnitte.titel: Coming to terms with the past, and the present
abschnitte.text: In 1956, at the 20th Congress of the CPSU, **Nikita Khrushchev** criticised the personality cult and the persecution under Stalin in the **secret speech**. Many victims were then rehabilitated, meaning declared innocent. Purges still happen today: in North Korea in 2013, **Kim Jong-un** had his uncle **Jang Song-thaek**, who was seen as the second most powerful man, executed.

gewusst: Many perpetrators of Stalin's purges later became victims themselves.
Stalin had people who had fallen out of favour retouched out of photos afterwards.

teile.einleitung: Belarus, which used to be called White Russia (Weissrussland) in German, is a country in Eastern Europe between Russia, Ukraine, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. Since 1994 Alexander Lukashenko has ruled there with an iron fist. Because there are no free elections and critics are persecuted, Belarus is often called “Europe’s last dictatorship”.
wichtigste: The capital of Belarus is Minsk.
Belarus has about 9 million inhabitants (as of 2024).
The country became independent in 1991 after the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Alexander Lukashenko has been president since 1994.
The official languages are Belarusian and Russian.
Belarus is the only country in Europe where the death penalty is still carried out.
After the election in 2020 there were huge protests, which were brutally suppressed.

abschnitte.text: **Belarus** has no access to the sea and is about five times the size of Switzerland. The country is flat and has many forests, lakes, rivers and marshes. In the primeval forest of **Białowieża** on the border with Poland live wisents, the largest land animals in Europe. The Chernobyl nuclear accident in neighbouring Ukraine in 1986 contaminated large parts of southern Belarus.

For centuries the area belonged to the **Grand Duchy of Lithuania** and later to Poland-Lithuania and the Russian Empire. From 1922, as the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic, it was part of the **Soviet Union**. The country suffered particularly badly in the Second World War, when about a quarter of the population died. In 1991 Belarus declared its independence.

In 1994 **Alexander Lukashenko** was elected president; it is so far the only presidential election generally recognised as free. Since then he has kept extending his power and has changed the constitution in his own favour. Independent newspapers, parties and organisations are suppressed. Many parts of the economy still belong to the state today, much as in Soviet times.

In the presidential election in August 2020 **Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya** stood against Lukashenko after her husband had been arrested. The government declared Lukashenko the winner, but many people believed that the election had been rigged. Hundreds of thousands demonstrated peacefully for weeks, often with white-red-white flags. The police arrested tens of thousands, and many people fled abroad.

Most people speak **Russian** in everyday life, even though Belarusian is the country’s original language. Belarus is closely linked with Russia and forms a so-called Union State with it. In 2022 Russian troops also attacked Ukraine from Belarusian territory. The Belarusian human rights campaigner **Ales Bialiatski** was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022.

begriffe.erklaerung: A form of rule in which one person or group decides everything alone and suppresses criticism.
When the results of an election are deliberately reported falsely.
A punishment in which a person is killed by the state.
A large wild ox, related to the American bison; also called the European bison.

gewusst: The name Belarus literally means “White Russia”, but it is not certain where the word “white” comes from.
The Białowieża Forest is one of the last large primeval lowland forests in Europe and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The National Library in Minsk is shaped like a giant diamond.

teile.einleitung: Gleichschaltung is the name for the way in which the National Socialists brought the whole of Germany under their control from 1933. Parties, clubs and media were dissolved or brought under Nazi control. In the end the whole country was to follow only one opinion, namely that of Adolf Hitler.
wichtigste: Gleichschaltung means that everything was brought under Nazi control.
It began in 1933, shortly after Hitler came to power.
Parties, clubs and media were dissolved or controlled.
The trade unions were smashed on 2 May 1933.
From July 1933 the Nazi party was the only party allowed.
Art, schools and youth groups were also brought into line.
Gleichschaltung destroyed diversity and free opinion in Germany.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the word come from?
abschnitte.text: The word **Gleichschaltung** actually comes from electrical engineering. There it means that several devices run in step with one another. The National Socialists applied this to society. All areas of life were to be “switched into line” with the **Nazi party**. Other opinions no longer had any place.

After the **Enabling Act** of March 1933, the German states such as Bavaria or Prussia lost their independence. They were run by Nazi Reich governors. The SPD was banned in June 1933, and the other parties dissolved themselves under pressure. From 14 July 1933 the Nazi party was by law the only party.

On 2 May 1933 the SA and SS occupied the offices of the **trade unions** and arrested many trade unionists. Their assets were seized. In their place came the **German Labour Front**, which was controlled by the Nazis. Workers could no longer fight freely for better wages.

In March 1933 a Ministry of Propaganda was set up under **Joseph Goebbels**. Newspapers, radio and films were only allowed to spread what the Nazis liked. Anyone who wanted to work as an artist, writer or journalist had to be a member of the **Reich Chamber of Culture**. Jews and opponents of the regime were excluded. The cheap People's Receiver radio made sure that Hitler's speeches reached almost every home.

Sports clubs, choirs, professional associations and youth groups also had to fall into line. Jewish members were excluded. Other youth organisations were banned or absorbed into the **Hitler Youth**. From 1936 the Hitler Youth was the official state youth organisation, and later almost all children and young people had to take part.

Gleichschaltung shows how quickly a democracy can be destroyed. Within a few months there was no free press, no opposition and no independent clubs left in Germany. Today **fundamental rights** such as freedom of association and freedom of the press protect against this. These rights are also set down in the Swiss Federal Constitution.

begriffe.erklaerung: The National Socialist German Workers' Party, Adolf Hitler's party.
An association of employees who work together for better working conditions.
Deliberately influencing people, often with lies and exaggerations.
The youth organisation of the Nazi party.

gewusst: Bringing the most important areas into line took only about a year and a half.
The People's Receiver was built in such a way that foreign stations were hard to pick up.

teile.einleitung: Bonapartism is a term for a form of rule modelled on Napoleon I and Napoleon III. A strong man rules with the support of the army and referendums and pushes parliament aside.
wichtigste: After his coup in 1799 Napoleon Bonaparte became First Consul.
In December 1848 Louis Napoléon was elected president by the people.
On 2 December 1851 he carried out a coup.
Bonapartist rulers had themselves confirmed by referendums.
Karl Marx analysed Bonapartism in 1852.
Louis Napoléon spent part of his youth in Thurgau.

abschnitte.text: In November 1799 **Napoleon Bonaparte** overthrew the government of the Directory. He became **First Consul**. In 1802 he had himself made consul for life through a referendum, and in 1804 he became emperor. Such referendums are called **plebiscites**. With them he appealed directly to the people and bypassed parliament.

His nephew **Louis Napoléon Bonaparte** won France’s first direct presidential election, in which all men were allowed to vote, in December 1848. The constitution banned him from being re-elected. That is why on **2 December 1851** he dissolved the National Assembly in a coup. The date was the anniversary of Napoleon I’s coronation as emperor and of the Battle of Austerlitz. In 1852 he became emperor as **Napoleon III**.

In 1852 **Karl Marx** wrote the work **“The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte”**. The title refers to Napoleon I’s coup. Marx thought that the government could become independent when no class was strong enough to rule on its own. The ruler would appear to stand above all classes. In doing so he would rely particularly on the small farmers, the **smallholding peasants**.

In his youth Louis Napoléon lived with his mother **Hortense** at **Arenenberg Castle** on the Untersee (Lower Lake Constance). The canton of **Thurgau** made him an honorary citizen. Today the castle houses the **Napoleon Museum Thurgau**. In 1838 France demanded that he be expelled from Switzerland, whereupon he left the country.
In the war against Prussia Napoleon III was taken prisoner at **Sedan** on 2 September 1870. Two days later the republic was proclaimed in Paris. With that the **Second Empire** came to an end.

gewusst: “Brumaire” was a month in the calendar of the French Revolution; 18 Brumaire corresponded to 9 November 1799.
Napoleon III was the first president of France elected by the people and at the same time the last French emperor.

teile.einleitung: The Secret State Police, Gestapo for short, was the political police in National Socialist Germany. It tracked down opponents of the regime and persecuted them. In practice it stood above the law and was an important tool of terror.
wichtigste: Gestapo is short for Geheime Staatspolizei, the Secret State Police.
Hermann Göring founded it in Prussia in April 1933.
Its headquarters were at Prinz-Albrecht-Strasse 8 in Berlin.
With “protective custody” it locked people up without a court ruling.
It received many tip-offs through denunciations by fellow citizens.
From 1939 it was part of the Reich Main Security Office.

abschnitte.text: On **26 April 1933** **Hermann Göring**, then Prussian Minister of the Interior, created the Secret State Police Office. Its first head was **Rudolf Diels**. Soon Heinrich Himmler and Reinhard Heydrich took control. The headquarters were at **Prinz-Albrecht-Strasse 8** in Berlin and had their own prison. Later the Gestapo was active throughout the German Reich.

The Gestapo spied on the population and persecuted everyone who was seen as an opponent. With so-called “**protective custody**” it could lock people up for as long as it liked without a court ruling; many were sent to **concentration camps**. Prisoners were often tortured during interrogations. The Prussian Gestapo Law of 10 February 1936 laid down that those affected could no longer take their case to administrative courts. In practice the Gestapo thus stood above the law.

Compared with the size of the population, the Gestapo had relatively few officers. Even so, it found out a great deal. The reason: many arrests were based on **denunciations**. Neighbours, colleagues or acquaintances reported people, sometimes out of conviction, sometimes out of envy or revenge. This created a climate of fear in which hardly anyone spoke openly.

In September 1939 the Gestapo, the criminal police and the security service **SD** were combined into the **Reich Main Security Office**. Its head was Reinhard Heydrich. This authority played a central role in planning the **Holocaust**. Within it, the Gestapo formed Office IV under **Heinrich Müller**, known as “Gestapo Müller”. He disappeared after the end of the war, and what happened to him has still not been clearly established.

After the war, the International Military Tribunal in **Nuremberg** declared the Gestapo a criminal organisation in 1946. On the site of the former headquarters there is now the documentation centre **Topography of Terror**. There visitors learn how the perpetrators worked. The place shows where a police force without any checks can lead.

gewusst: A large share of the tip-offs to the Gestapo came not from informers but from ordinary people.
Next to the Topography of Terror there is still a section of the Berlin Wall.

teile.einleitung: Mahatma Gandhi was an Indian freedom fighter. He fought against British rule over India, but without violence. His ideas have influenced many people all over the world.
wichtigste: Gandhi was born in India on 2 October 1869.
“Mahatma” means “great soul”.
He fought without violence for India's independence from Great Britain.
His method of non-violent resistance is called Satyagraha.
In 1930 he led the famous Salt March.
India became independent in 1947.

abschnitte.text: Gandhi's real name was **Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi**. He studied law in London and became a lawyer. After that he lived for many years in **South Africa**. There he saw how Indians were discriminated against. He began to resist this injustice and developed his ideas of peaceful resistance.

Gandhi's method is called **Satyagraha**. It means something like “holding on to the truth”. Instead of fighting, people refused to obey unjust laws. They went on strike, boycotted British goods and were even prepared to go to prison. Gandhi himself was imprisoned several times. He did not want to hurt his opponent but to convince him.

The British had a **salt monopoly**: only they were allowed to make and sell salt, and it was taxed. In 1930, Gandhi and many followers marched around 385 kilometres to the sea at Dandi. There he made salt from seawater himself. This was forbidden. Thousands followed his example, and the **Salt March** became world famous.

In many pictures, Gandhi is sitting at a **spinning wheel**. He spun yarn himself and wore simple clothes made of hand-woven cloth. In this way he wanted to show that India did not need expensive cloth from Great Britain. The spinning wheel became a symbol of self-reliance and of the **independence movement**.

In 1947, India became **independent**. At the same time, Pakistan was created as a separate state, and there was serious unrest between religious groups. Gandhi worked for peace. On 30 January 1948 he was murdered in Delhi by a Hindu nationalist. In India he is still honoured today as the “Father of the Nation”.

gewusst: Since 2007, Gandhi's birthday, 2 October, has been the UN's International Day of Non-Violence.
Gandhi was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize several times but never received it.
Martin Luther King and Nelson Mandela were inspired by Gandhi's ideas.

teile.einleitung: The Jasmine Revolution was a popular uprising in Tunisia in 2010 and 2011. It overthrew the long-serving president Ben Ali and is seen as the beginning of the “Arab Spring”.
wichtigste: It was triggered by the desperate act of the vegetable seller Mohamed Bouazizi in December 2010.
The protests began in the small town of Sidi Bouzid.
President Ben Ali ruled for about 23 years and fled to Saudi Arabia on 14 January 2011.
In 2014 Tunisia got a new democratic constitution.
The National Dialogue Quartet received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2015.
The name comes from jasmine, Tunisia's national flower.

abschnitte.text: In December 2010 the authorities took away the goods of the young vegetable seller **Mohamed Bouazizi**. In despair he set himself on fire. His act caused great anger. In the small town of **Sidi Bouzid** in the interior of the country, people were the first to take to the streets. Soon the protests spread as far as the capital, Tunis.

**Zine el-Abidine Ben Ali** had come to power in 1987 and ruled in an authoritarian way. After weeks of protests he left the country on **14 January 2011**. He found refuge in **Saudi Arabia**. He lived there in exile until he died in 2019. He had ruled Tunisia for about 23 years.

After the revolution the Tunisians elected a **Constituent Assembly**. In January 2014 it adopted a new democratic **constitution**. In 2013 the country was in danger of plunging into a serious crisis. Then the **National Dialogue Quartet**, made up of the trade union, the employers' association, the human rights league and the bar association, acted as mediator. For this it received the **Nobel Peace Prize** in 2015.

**Jasmine** is very common in Tunisia and is regarded as the national flower. That is why the revolution was named after it. The events in Tunisia encouraged people in other Arab countries to protest too. This wave is called the **Arab Spring**.

gewusst: The protests did not begin in the capital but in a small town in the interior of the country.
The National Dialogue Quartet was made up of four very different organisations.

teile.einleitung: At a demonstration many people take to the streets together and show their opinion in public. They want to draw attention to something that matters to them. In a democracy this is an important right.
wichtigste: At a demonstration people show their opinion in public.
They often carry placards and banners.
The short form is “demo”.
In many Swiss towns you need a permit.
Demonstrations must be peaceful; violence is forbidden.

abschnitte.text: Instead of demonstration people often just say **“demo”**. People walk through the streets together or meet in a square. Their demands are written on **placards** and **banners**. Some give speeches, while others chant together. In this way everyone can see what it is about.

In Switzerland the Federal Constitution protects **freedom of assembly**. For a demonstration in the street you need a **permit** in many towns. This allows the town to divert traffic and make sure everyone is safe. Anyone who uses **violence** or damages things is punished. Demonstrations are only allowed if they are peaceful.

On **14 June 1991** there was the big **women’s strike**. Many women demanded the same rights and the same pay as men. In 2019 many school pupils took to the streets in the **climate strike**. They demanded more protection for the climate. Rallies are also often held on the Bundesplatz in Bern.

In 1930 **Mahatma Gandhi** led the peaceful **Salt March** in India. With it he protested against British rule, always relying on non-violence. In 1963 **Martin Luther King** spoke at a huge demonstration in Washington. There he spoke the famous words “I have a dream”. He fought peacefully for equal rights for black people in the USA.

gewusst: In dictatorships demonstrations against the government are often banned and dangerous.
Another word for demonstration is “rally”.

teile.einleitung: Jean-Bédel Bokassa ruled the Central African Republic from 1966 to 1979. He even made himself emperor and had himself crowned in the style of Napoleon.
wichtigste: Bokassa came to power through a military coup on New Year's Eve 1965/66.
He overthrew his cousin, President David Dacko.
In 1976 he proclaimed the Central African Empire.
In December 1977 he had himself crowned in Bangui.
In 1979 France removed him from power while he was in Libya.
After his return in 1986 he was convicted.

abschnitte.text: Bokassa was head of the army. On New Year's Eve 1965/66 he overthrew his cousin, President **David Dacko**. Because the coup began on New Year's Eve, it is called the **Saint-Sylvestre coup d'état**, after the French word for New Year's Eve. Dacko had been the first president after independence in 1960. After that Bokassa ruled as sole ruler.

In 1976 Bokassa proclaimed the **Central African Empire** and called himself Emperor Bokassa I. He admired **Napoleon** and modelled his coronation on Napoleon's. It took place in December 1977 in the capital, **Bangui**. Bangui lies on the Ubangi River on the border with the Congo. The lavish celebration swallowed up a large part of the state budget, even though the country was desperately poor.

In 1979 schoolchildren protested against expensive compulsory school uniforms. Many of them were arrested and killed, and Bokassa was involved. This crime cost him his power. In **Operation Barracuda**, French troops brought David Dacko back to power. At that time Bokassa happened to be in Libya.
In 1986 Bokassa returned of his own free will. He was put on trial and sentenced to death. However, the sentence was changed to imprisonment. He was released in 1993 and died in 1996.

gewusst: David Dacko was both Bokassa's predecessor and his successor.
Bokassa had himself crowned even though his country was one of the poorest in the world.

teile.einleitung: Paul Grüninger was police commander of the canton of St Gallen. In 1938 and 1939 he saved the lives of several hundred Jewish refugees by letting them into Switzerland against the regulations. For this he lost his job and his pension.
wichtigste: Paul Grüninger was commander of the St Gallen cantonal police.
After the border was closed in August 1938, he backdated the entry dates of refugees.
In this way several hundred people were given the right to stay.
In 1939 he was dismissed without notice, and in 1940 he was convicted.
In 1971 Yad Vashem honoured him as “Righteous Among the Nations”.
In 1995 the St Gallen district court acquitted him after his death.

abschnitte.text: **Paul Grüninger** lived from 1891 to 1972. He was commander of the **St Gallen cantonal police** and therefore also responsible for the border with Austria. After Austria was annexed to the German Reich in March 1938, many Jews fled. Many tried to get into Switzerland across the Rhine near Diepoldsau.

In **August 1938**, the Federal Council decided to **close the border**: refugees without a visa were no longer allowed to enter. Anyone who was caught was to be sent back. For the Jewish refugees this meant great danger. Swiss refugee policy at that time is now considered to have been too harsh.

Grüninger did not follow the instruction. For refugees he entered **earlier entry dates**, from before the border was closed. That way they counted as having entered legally and were allowed to stay. In this way he got **several hundred people** the right to stay. He knew that he was risking his job by doing so.

In 1939 Grüninger was **dismissed without notice** and lost his right to a pension. In 1940 a court convicted him of breach of official duty and gave him a **fine**. After that he lived in poverty. In 1971 the **Yad Vashem** memorial in Israel honoured him as **Righteous Among the Nations**. The St Gallen government rehabilitated him politically in 1993, and in 1995 the **St Gallen district court** acquitted him.

As a young man, Grüninger played football for **SC Brühl** and became Swiss champion with the club in 1915. Later he was its president. Since 2006 the club's stadium has been called the **Paul-Grüninger-Stadion**. In 2014 the film **“Akte Grüninger”** (The Grüninger Case) by Alain Gsponer was released in Swiss cinemas.

gewusst: Grüninger received the honour from Yad Vashem during his lifetime, one year before his death.
The acquittal of 1995 came 23 years after his death.

teile.einleitung: After the presidential election of 9 August 2020, hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets in Belarus. They accused President Alexander Lukashenko of rigging the election. These were the largest protests since the country became independent.
wichtigste: The protests began after the election of 9 August 2020.
Officially, Lukashenko received around 80 per cent of the vote.
The EU and independent observers did not recognise the result.
On 16 August, more than 100,000 people demonstrated in Minsk.
Women in white with flowers became the face of the protests.
The state responded with violence and mass arrests.

abschnitte.text: **Alexander Lukashenko** has ruled Belarus since 1994. In the 2020 election, **Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya** stood against him after her husband had been arrested as a candidate. According to the electoral commission, Lukashenko received around **80 per cent** and Tsikhanouskaya around 10 per cent. The **EU** and independent observers considered the result to be rigged. Shortly afterwards Tsikhanouskaya had to flee abroad.

On election night itself, thousands took to the streets in **Minsk** and other cities. The police responded with violence and mass arrests. On **16 August 2020**, during the “March for Freedom”, well over **100,000 people** filled the centre of Minsk. Even workers at large state enterprises, which were seen as pillars of the regime, went on strike and shouted “Go away!” at Lukashenko.

Many women formed long chains of solidarity in **white clothes** and with **flowers**. In this way they wanted to show that the protest was peaceful. Even so, many women were also arrested. Among them was **Natallia Hersche**, who has both Swiss and Belarusian citizenship. She was sentenced to two and a half years in prison and was released early in February 2022.

In August 2020 the opposition founded a **Coordination Council**, which was to negotiate a peaceful transfer of power. Its members included the winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature **Svetlana Alexievich**. Almost all the members were persecuted. **Maria Kalesnikava** tore up her passport at the Ukrainian border so that she could not be deported. In 2021 she was sentenced to eleven years in prison.

When the state slowed down the internet, the messaging service **Telegram** became important. Channels such as **NEXTA**, which was run from Poland, had millions of subscribers. They spread videos and calls to action. Lukashenko stayed in power, and many opposition figures now live in exile or are in prison.

gewusst: The symbol of the protests was the white-red-white flag, which Belarus briefly had as its national flag in the 1990s.
Maria Kalesnikava was released in December 2025 and taken out of the country.

teile.einleitung: The Carnation Revolution was an almost bloodless overthrow in Portugal on 25 April 1974. Young officers ended a dictatorship that had lasted more than 40 years. It gets its name from the red carnations that people gave to the soldiers.
wichtigste: The Carnation Revolution took place in Portugal in 1974.
It began on 25 April, mainly in Lisbon.
It was led by the Armed Forces Movement, a group of young officers.
A song on the radio was the secret signal to start.
People put red carnations into the soldiers' rifles.
In 1975 Angola and Mozambique became independent.

abschnitte.text: For decades Portugal was ruled by a **dictatorship**, the **Estado Novo**, meaning “New State”. For a long time the most important ruler was **António de Oliveira Salazar**, later followed by Marcelo Caetano. There were no free elections, there was strict censorship and a feared secret police. At the same time, Portugal was fighting expensive **colonial wars** in Africa.

abschnitte.titel: A song as the signal to start
abschnitte.text: Many young officers wanted to end the wars in Africa. They founded the **Armed Forces Movement**. During the night before 25 April 1974, a particular song was played on the radio. This was the secret **signal to start**. Shortly after midnight, a second song followed, “Grândola, Vila Morena”. Now the soldiers occupied important places in **Lisbon**.

Instead of hiding, many people went out into the streets and cheered the soldiers. They put **red carnations** into the barrels of their rifles. This is where the name **Carnation Revolution** comes from. The government quickly gave up. Only a few people died.

After the revolution, Portugal became a **democracy**. Exactly one year later, on 25 April 1975, free elections took place. The colonies in Africa became independent, including **Angola** and **Mozambique** in 1975. Many Portuguese people returned from the colonies.

Today **25 April** is a public holiday in Portugal, **Freedom Day**. Many people wear a red carnation on that day. A large bridge in Lisbon is called “Ponte 25 de Abril”. The Carnation Revolution is seen as an example of how a dictatorship can end almost without violence.

gewusst: Before the revolution, the “Ponte 25 de Abril” bridge was called the Salazar Bridge.
According to tradition, a woman called Celeste Caeiro, who worked in a restaurant, handed out the first carnations.

teile.einleitung: After the Second World War, leading figures of National Socialist Germany had to answer for their actions before an international court. The most important trial took place in Nuremberg in 1945 and 1946 and is regarded as the birth of modern international criminal law.
wichtigste: The trial of the major war criminals began on 20 November 1945.
The verdicts were announced on 1 October 1946.
The four victorious powers, the USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France, formed the court.
Twelve defendants were sentenced to death, and three were acquitted.
For the first time, crimes against humanity were charged in an international trial.
The trial took place in the Nuremberg Palace of Justice.

abschnitte.text: After the end of the war in 1945, the victorious powers did not want simply to punish those responsible but to put them on trial. For this the **USA**, the **Soviet Union**, **Great Britain** and **France** set up the **International Military Tribunal**. Each country provided judges and prosecutors. The defendants had lawyers and were allowed to speak. This was meant to show that even the powerful have to obey the law.

Nuremberg was the city of the National Socialists' great party rallies. The **Palace of Justice** had hardly been destroyed in the war and had its own prison. The hearings took place in **Courtroom 600**. The trial lasted almost a year. Today a memorial there remembers the trials.

Senior politicians, military leaders and officials were charged. The charges included **crimes against peace**, meaning planning wars of aggression, **war crimes** and **crimes against humanity**. The last of these included the murder of millions of Jews and other persecuted people. This last charge was new in international law.

The court passed **twelve death sentences**, one of them against Martin Bormann, who was absent. Seven defendants received prison sentences, and three were acquitted. **Hermann Göring**, the highest-ranking defendant, took his own life in his cell shortly before his execution. **Rudolf Hess**, Hitler's deputy in the party, was sentenced to life imprisonment and died in Berlin-Spandau prison in 1987.

After the main trial, further trials followed in Nuremberg against doctors, lawyers and industrialists. The Nuremberg principles state that anyone who commits the most serious crimes cannot claim to have been following orders. The **International Criminal Court** in The Hague, which has been working since 2002, is built on this. Switzerland is also one of the states that recognise it.

gewusst: Courtroom 600 was still used as a courtroom until 2020.
The speeches at the trial were translated into four languages at the same time. This was the beginning of modern simultaneous interpreting.

teile.einleitung: Gene Sharp was an American political scientist. Throughout his life he researched how people can resist dictatorships without violence. His writings were read by protest movements all over the world.
wichtigste: Gene Sharp lived from 1928 to 2018 and came from the USA.
He was convinced that power depends on the cooperation of those who are ruled.
In a work from 1973 he listed 198 methods of nonviolent action.
His book “From Dictatorship to Democracy” was translated into more than 30 languages.
In 1983 he founded the Albert Einstein Institution.
The Serbian movement Otpor! used his ideas.

abschnitte.text: **Gene Sharp** was born in the USA in 1928 and died in 2018. Among other things he studied **Mahatma Gandhi**. Sharp wanted to show that nonviolent resistance is not only a question of morals. For him it was a **strategy** that can be planned and learned. In 1983 he founded the **Albert Einstein Institution** in Boston, named after the physicist who had worked for peace. It spread his writings around the world.

Sharp started from a simple assumption: **power depends on the cooperation** of those who are ruled. Even a dictator needs officials, soldiers, workers and a population that obeys. If a great many people refuse to cooperate, his power collapses. No ruler can govern alone.

In his work “The Politics of Nonviolent Action” from 1973, Sharp set out **198 methods** of nonviolent action. He divided them into three groups: **protest and persuasion**, for example demonstrations; **non-cooperation**, such as strikes and boycotts; and **nonviolent intervention**, such as blockades or occupations. He also thought “**political jiu-jitsu**” was important. If a regime brutally attacks peaceful people, it often loses support among the population, the security forces and abroad.

In 1993 Sharp wrote the book “**From Dictatorship to Democracy**”, originally for the democratic opposition in **Burma**. It was translated into more than 30 languages. In Serbia the youth movement **Otpor!**, meaning “Resistance!”, based its work on his ideas. It relied on humour, symbols and mass protest and helped to bring down Slobodan Milošević in 2000. Its methods were later taken up by movements in other countries.

gewusst: Sharp's list of 198 methods ranges from strikes and boycotts to symbolic protests.
Gene Sharp was nominated several times for the Nobel Peace Prize.

teile.einleitung: Mao Zedong was the communist dictator of China who was responsible for millions of deaths. He founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and led it until his death in 1976. To this day he is a revered but also highly controversial figure in China.
wichtigste: Mao Zedong was the communist dictator of China.
He lived from 1893 to 1976.
He proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949.
The Long March of 1934 to 1935 made him leader of the communists.
During the Great Leap Forward, millions of people died of hunger.
With the Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976, he had opponents and traditions attacked.
His picture still hangs on the Gate of Heavenly Peace in Beijing today.

abschnitte.text: **Mao Zedong** was born on 26 December 1893 in the village of Shaoshan in Hunan province. His parents were farmers. He became a teacher and was interested in politics from an early age. In 1921 he was one of the participants at the founding meeting of the **Communist Party of China**. In the West, his name used to be written “Mao Tse-tung”.

In China, the communists fought for years against the **Kuomintang** government under Chiang Kai-shek. In 1934 they had to flee from its troops. On the **Long March** they covered more than 10,000 kilometres in about a year, over mountains, rivers and swamps. Only a small part of the participants arrived. During this march, Mao became the most important leader of the communists.

After victory in the civil war, Mao proclaimed the **People's Republic of China** in Beijing on 1 October 1949. The Kuomintang fled to the island of Taiwan. Mao introduced a **one-party system** in which only the Communist Party governed. Landowners had their land taken away, and many of them were killed. Critics were persecuted and put in labour camps.

From 1958, Mao wanted to turn China into an industrial country in a short time with the **Great Leap Forward**. Farmers had to work in people's communes and even make steel in small furnaces in their back yards. Harvests collapsed, but the authorities reported false figures of success. In the famine that followed, an estimated 15 to 45 million people died. It was one of the biggest famines in history.

In 1966, Mao began the **Cultural Revolution** to secure his power. Young Red Guards persecuted teachers, artists and party members. Mao was worshipped like a god, and his quotations were printed millions of times in a little red book. Mao died in Beijing on 9 September 1976.

Mao lies embalmed in a **mausoleum** in Tiananmen Square in Beijing. His large portrait hangs on the Gate of Heavenly Peace, and his picture is on all Chinese banknotes. The Communist Party officially says that Mao did more right than wrong. Historians outside China see him as one of the rulers under whom the most people died in the 20th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: An idea according to which there should be no private property and everything should belong to everyone.
What some communist states call themselves, even if the people are not allowed to vote freely.
A large tomb building for an important person.
A time when very many people do not have enough to eat.

gewusst: Mao's portrait on the Gate of Heavenly Peace is about six metres high.
Mao Zedong is still shown on Chinese banknotes today.

teile.einleitung: Spiritual National Defence was a political and cultural movement in Switzerland. It arose in the 1930s as a response to Fascism and National Socialism. Its aim was to strengthen Switzerland's independence and democratic values.
wichtigste: Originally it was left-wing circles that called for a spiritual defence of democracy.
With the Cultural Message of 9 December 1938 it became official policy of the Federal Council.
Federal Councillor Philipp Etter is seen as its most important supporter.
The Pro Helvetia foundation grew out of the Cultural Message.
In 1938 Romansh became the fourth national language.
The Landi of 1939 in Zurich was its most powerful expression.
During the Cold War it was directed against Communism.

abschnitte.text: In the 1930s National Socialist Germany and Fascist Italy spread a lot of **propaganda**, including in Switzerland. At first it was mainly **left-wing** politicians and intellectuals who called for democracy to be defended with radio, film and culture too. From 1938 the **Federal Council** also supported this idea. It was called **Spiritual National Defence**: as well as the army, culture was to protect the country.

On **9 December 1938** the Federal Council adopted the so-called **Cultural Message**. The person responsible was Federal Councillor **Philipp Etter**, who headed the Department of Home Affairs. The message described Switzerland as a **nation of will**: a country with several languages and cultures that wants to stay together. Etter also stressed Christian conservative values. The message gave rise to the **Pro Helvetia** foundation, which still promotes Swiss culture at home and abroad today.

In 1938 the people agreed by a very large margin that **Romansh** should become the fourth national language. This was also a response to Fascist Italy, where it was claimed that Romansh was just an Italian dialect. With the vote, Switzerland showed that its linguistic diversity belongs together.

In 1939 the **National Exhibition** took place in Zurich, known as the “**Landi**” for short. It showed Switzerland as a diverse, independent nation. The “**Landi spirit**” strengthened unity shortly before the war began. Films contributed too: “**Füsilier Wipf**” from 1938, which Leopold Lindtberg worked on as a director, showed the bond between the people and the army. The film was a big hit with audiences.

After 1945 Spiritual National Defence lived on during the **Cold War**. Now it was directed mainly against **Communism**. Artists and writers increasingly criticised it as narrow and backward-looking. From 1962 official support came to an end. The Pro Helvetia foundation, however, still exists today.

gewusst: The 1938 vote on Romansh as the fourth national language was approved with more than 90 per cent voting Yes.
At the Landi of 1939 a cable car ran right across Lake Zurich.

teile.einleitung: From 1964 to 1985, Brazil was ruled by the military. After a coup against President João Goulart, fundamental rights were restricted and opponents were persecuted. Only after large protests did the country return to democracy.
wichtigste: In 1964 the military staged a coup against President João Goulart.
The first military president was Humberto Castelo Branco.
From 1965 only two parties were allowed: ARENA and MDB.
In 1968 the decree AI-5 abolished important fundamental rights.
In 1970 the Swiss ambassador Giovanni Enrico Bucher was kidnapped.
The military dictatorship ended in 1985.

abschnitte.text: President **João Goulart** wanted reforms, for example in how land was shared out. Many officers, business people and politicians feared that Brazil could become communist. In the spring of 1964, the military overthrew Goulart. The first military president was General **Humberto Castelo Branco**. After him, further generals followed as presidents.

The military banned the old parties. From 1965 only two were allowed: **ARENA**, which was loyal to the government, and the permitted opposition **MDB**. At the end of 1968 the government issued **AI-5**, a decree that abolished fundamental rights. Parliament could be closed, and there was strict **censorship**. Many opponents were arrested, tortured or had to flee abroad. **Dilma Rousseff**, who later became president, was also imprisoned and tortured as a young woman.

From about 1968 to 1973 the economy grew very strongly. This period is called the **economic miracle**, “Milagre econômico” in Portuguese. Large roads, bridges and power stations were built. But the poor benefited little, and Brazil ran up large debts.

abschnitte.titel: A Swiss ambassador as a hostage
abschnitte.text: In December 1970, a left-wing underground group in Rio de Janeiro kidnapped the Swiss ambassador **Giovanni Enrico Bucher**. It demanded the release of political prisoners. After long negotiations, the government let 70 prisoners leave the country. Bucher was freed in January 1971.

From the end of the 1970s, the military slowly relaxed its rule. In 1984, millions of people demanded direct presidential elections with the movement **Diretas Já**. This means “direct elections now”. In 1985 an electoral college chose a civilian president again for the first time. This ended the military dictatorship.

gewusst: Tancredo Neves, the president elected in 1985, fell ill before taking office and died, so José Sarney took over.
From 2012, a truth commission investigated the crimes of the dictatorship.

teile.einleitung: Fleeing means that people leave their home because they are in danger there. Reasons include, for example, war, persecution or a dictatorship. Here you can find out who counts as a refugee, what rights refugees have and what role Switzerland plays.
wichtigste: Refugees flee from war or persecution and seek protection in another country.
Asylum is the protection that a state grants to persecuted people.
The Geneva Refugee Convention of 1951 lays down who is a refugee.
The UN Refugee Agency, UNHCR, has its headquarters in Geneva.
In 1956 many refugees from Hungary were taken in by Switzerland.
People fled from the GDR in adventurous ways, even by balloon.

abschnitte.text: Nobody likes leaving their home. People flee when their life or freedom is threatened. Common reasons are **war**, **persecution** because of religion, origin or political opinion, and oppression by a **dictatorship**. Some flee within their own country; they are called **internally displaced people**. Others cross a border and seek protection in another state.

In 1951 an important agreement was adopted in Geneva: the **Geneva Refugee Convention**. It lays down who counts as a **refugee**. That is a person who has left their country because they are persecuted there because of their origin, religion, nationality, political beliefs or membership of a particular group. The convention also sets out the rights refugees have. Particularly important: nobody may be sent back to a country where they face persecution. Switzerland is also bound by the convention.

Anyone who is persecuted can ask for **asylum** in another country. Asylum means protection from persecution. In Switzerland the **State Secretariat for Migration** (SEM) examines every asylum application. It checks whether a person really is being persecuted. Anyone who is recognised as a refugee may stay and is given protection. Asylum policy is often hotly debated in Switzerland, including in referendums.

The **UN Refugee Agency**, **UNHCR** for short, was founded in 1950 and has its headquarters in Geneva. It helps refugees all over the world, for example with tents, water, food and schools in refugee camps. It also works to make sure that states respect the rights of refugees. UNHCR has been awarded the **Nobel Peace Prize** twice for its work.

In 1956 the Soviet Union crushed an uprising in **Hungary**. Many Hungarians fled, and a large number of them were taken in by Switzerland. Fleeing from the **GDR** was forbidden and very dangerous. **Escape helpers** secretly dug tunnels under the Berlin Wall. In September 1979 two families fled to Bavaria in a home-sewn **hot-air balloon**.

gewusst: In 1979 two families secretly sewed a huge hot-air balloon and flew out of the GDR to Bavaria in it.
UNHCR was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize twice, in 1954 and 1981.
20 June is the UN’s World Refugee Day every year.

teile.einleitung: A kleptocracy is a form of rule in which the leaders of a state make themselves rich. The word literally means “rule by thieves”. Switzerland is affected too, because such money sometimes ends up in Swiss banks.
wichtigste: “Kleptocracy” comes from Greek and means “rule by thieves”.
In 2004, Transparency International named Suharto as the politician with the largest embezzled sums.
Mobutu Sese Seko renamed the Congo Zaire from 1971.
Ferdinand Marcos was overthrown in the Philippines in 1986.
Switzerland returned funds belonging to Sani Abacha to Nigeria.
Since 2016, a federal law has governed the freezing and return of dictators' assets.

abschnitte.text: The word is made up of the Greek **“kleptes”** (thief) and **“kratos”** (rule). It refers to regimes whose leaders enrich themselves from **state assets**. Money that should go to schools, hospitals or roads ends up with the rulers. Anyone who unlawfully takes money that was entrusted to them **embezzles** it.

In 2004, **Transparency International** published a list of the politicians with the largest embezzled sums. In first place was the Indonesian president **Suharto**, estimated at 15 to 35 billion US dollars. **Mobutu Sese Seko** renamed the Congo **Zaire** in 1971. His regime is seen as a textbook example of a kleptocracy and ended in 1997. In the Philippines, **Ferdinand Marcos** was overthrown in 1986 by the “People Power” movement.

**Dictators' assets** are fortunes of rulers that were acquired unlawfully. Since 2016, the **Federal Act on Illicitly Acquired Assets** (SRVG) has governed how Switzerland can freeze and return such money. It replaced the so-called “Lex Duvalier”. A well-known case is the money of the Nigerian military dictator **Sani Abacha**. After court proceedings, Switzerland returned hundreds of millions of dollars to **Nigeria**.

**Transparency International** was founded in Berlin in 1993. Every year the organisation publishes the **Corruption Perceptions Index**. It shows how corrupt the public sector of a country is perceived to be. Countries with strong courts and free media usually score better.

gewusst: Mobutu renamed not only the state but also the Congo River Zaire.
Switzerland returned Sani Abacha's money to Nigeria in several instalments.

teile.einleitung: Torture means deliberately inflicting great pain or suffering on people, for example to force a confession. Today torture is banned worldwide, without any exception. Here you can find out which rules lay this down and who keeps watch over them.
wichtigste: Under international law torture is always forbidden, even in war.
Article 5 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 forbids torture.
Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights forbids torture and inhuman treatment.
The UN adopted the Convention against Torture in 1984, and it came into force in 1987.
In Switzerland the NKVF has been inspecting places of detention since 2010.
26 June is the International Day in Support of Victims of Torture.

abschnitte.text: In the past, torture was a normal part of court proceedings in many countries. It was used to force **confessions**. During the **Enlightenment** in the 18th century criticism grew: a forced confession says nothing about whether someone is really guilty. Little by little, rulers abolished torture. **Maria Theresa** abolished it in the Habsburg lands in 1776.

After the Second World War the ban was set down in important texts. **Article 5** of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 says that nobody may be subjected to torture or cruel treatment. In Europe **Article 3** of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) forbids torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. Switzerland is also bound by the ECHR. This ban is absolute: there is no exception, not even in war.

On 10 December 1984 the UN adopted the **Convention against Torture**, and it came into force in 1987. States that join it must make torture a criminal offence. They may not hand anyone over to a country where they face torture. A UN committee checks whether the states keep to it. Because the convention came into force on a **26 June**, since 1998 this day has been the International Day in Support of Victims of Torture.

The Geneva banker **Jean-Jacques Gautier** had a simple idea: experts should be allowed to visit prisons so that nobody there is badly treated. In 1977 he founded an association for this in Geneva, which today is called the **APT**. His idea found its way into international treaties. An agreement of the Council of Europe in 1987 created the **European Committee for the Prevention of Torture** (CPT). Its experts visit prisons, police stations and clinics in the member states, including Switzerland, and then write reports.

Since 2010 Switzerland has had the **National Commission for the Prevention of Torture** (NKVF). It visits prisons, police stations, psychiatric clinics and other places where people are held. Afterwards it publishes reports with **recommendations** to the authorities. In this way it aims to prevent people from being badly treated.

gewusst: The ban on torture is one of the few rules that apply without exception, even in war.
The idea of having prisons visited by independent experts comes from the Geneva banker Jean-Jacques Gautier.

teile.einleitung: An international arrest warrant makes it possible to arrest wanted people in other countries too. The arrest warrants of the International Criminal Court in The Hague are particularly important. It prosecutes the most serious crimes, such as genocide and war crimes, even if presidents are said to have committed them.
wichtigste: The International Criminal Court is based on the Rome Statute of 1998.
The court has 18 judges but no police force of its own.
In 2009 Omar al-Bashir became the first sitting head of state to receive an arrest warrant.
In 2023 the court issued an arrest warrant against Vladimir Putin.
With a Red Notice, Interpol searches for people worldwide.
In 1998 Augusto Pinochet was arrested in London.

abschnitte.text: The **International Criminal Court** (ICC) is based in **The Hague** in the Netherlands. Its foundation is the **Rome Statute**, which was agreed in Rome in 1998 and came into force in 2002. Switzerland is also a state party. The court prosecutes genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. It has **18 judges**, who are elected by the states parties for nine years.

The court can issue arrest warrants but cannot make arrests itself. It has **no police force of its own**. That is why the states parties have to arrest wanted people and hand them over. As a result, some wanted people only travel to countries that will not hand them over. For worldwide searches there is also **Interpol**. With a **Red Notice**, Interpol asks police forces around the world to arrest a wanted person.

In 2009 the court issued an arrest warrant against a sitting head of state for the first time: **Omar al-Bashir**, the President of Sudan, for crimes in the **Darfur** region. In March 2023 an arrest warrant followed against **Vladimir Putin**, the President of Russia. It concerns the deportation of children from Ukraine to Russia. In March 2025 the former Philippine President **Rodrigo Duterte** was arrested and taken to The Hague. He is accused of killings in the so-called war on drugs.

It is not only the Criminal Court that can issue arrest warrants that apply abroad; national courts can too. In 1998 the Spanish judge **Baltasar Garzón** had the former Chilean dictator **Augusto Pinochet** arrested during a visit to **London**. Pinochet was later allowed to return to Chile for health reasons. Even so, the case is seen as a milestone in international justice: former dictators too can be arrested abroad.

gewusst: The International Criminal Court is not the same as the International Court of Justice, which is also based in The Hague and settles disputes between states.
Omar al-Bashir was the first sitting head of state against whom the Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant.

teile.einleitung: A border fence separates two countries from each other. In dictatorships, fences and walls were often built not to keep foreigners out but to stop the country's own people from escaping. The best-known example is the border of the GDR.
wichtigste: The GDR built walls and fences so that its citizens could not escape.
After the Second World War the Iron Curtain divided Europe into East and West.
Berlin was divided by a wall from 1961 to 1989.
Behind the Berlin Wall lay the guarded death strip.
In June 1989 Hungary and Austria cut through the border fence together.
Korea is still divided into North and South today.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War Europe split into two camps. In the east were the countries under the influence of the **Soviet Union**, in the west the democracies. The border between them was called the **Iron Curtain**. Many sections were secured with fences and watchtowers. Anyone who wanted to flee from the East risked their life.

Many people wanted to leave the **GDR** because they could not live freely there. Until 1961 millions went to the West. So the government built **walls and fences** along the border. Armed **border guards** stood on the watchtowers. Their job was to stop anyone escaping across the border.

From **1961 to 1989** a wall separated East Berlin and West Berlin. Families and friends were torn apart. Behind the wall lay a guarded strip with watchtowers and obstacles, the **death strip**. Border guards shot at people trying to escape there, and many people died attempting to flee. On 9 November 1989 the Wall was opened.

On **27 June 1989** the foreign ministers of **Hungary** and **Austria** together cut through a piece of the border fence. The picture went round the world and became a symbol of the end of the Iron Curtain. Soon afterwards many people fled from the GDR to the West via Hungary. Today memorials recall the former border.

The division is not over everywhere. Since the **Korean War** in the 1950s a strictly guarded border has separated **North Korea** and **South Korea**. Along the border lies a demilitarised zone. It cannot simply be crossed, and many families are still separated today.

gewusst: The expression “Iron Curtain” became well known through a speech by the British politician Winston Churchill in 1946.
The demilitarised zone between North and South Korea is about four kilometres wide.

teile.einleitung: Martin Luther King was an American minister and civil rights activist. He fought without violence for Black people in the USA to have the same rights as white people. His speech “I have a dream” is world famous.
wichtigste: Martin Luther King was born in Atlanta in 1929.
He fought for equal rights for all people.
He learned the idea of non-violent protest from Mahatma Gandhi.
In 1963 he gave the speech “I have a dream” in Washington.
In 1964 he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
In 1968 he was murdered.

abschnitte.text: At that time, **racial segregation** applied in many states in the south of the USA. Black people were not allowed to use the same schools, restaurants or bus seats as white people. In 1955, **Rosa Parks** refused to give up her seat on a bus in Montgomery. After that, Martin Luther King led a long **bus boycott**. In the end, segregation on the buses was banned.

King was a **Baptist minister**. From **Mahatma Gandhi** he learned the idea of protesting without violence. His supporters marched, sang and sat down peacefully, even when they were attacked or arrested. King himself went to prison several times. He was convinced that hatred can only be overcome with love.

On 28 August 1963, around 250,000 people came to a large rally in **Washington**. In front of the Lincoln Memorial, King gave his famous speech. He said: “I have a dream”. He dreamed that one day his children would be judged by their character and not by the colour of their skin.

The **civil rights movement** was successful. In 1964 and 1965, the USA passed important laws against discrimination against Black people, including in voting. In 1964 King received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. He was 35 years old at the time and one of the youngest prize-winners.

On 4 April 1968, Martin Luther King was murdered in **Memphis**. Many people mourned him. Today there is a public holiday in his honour in the USA. It is on the third Monday in **January**, close to his birthday on 15 January.

gewusst: Martin Luther King was named after the German reformer Martin Luther.
Martin Luther King Day is one of only a few US public holidays in honour of a single person.

teile.einleitung: Freedom of religion means that every person may decide for themselves what they believe in. You may have a religion, change it or not belong to any religion at all. In Switzerland, this right is set out in the Federal Constitution.
wichtigste: Everyone may choose for themselves what they believe in.
You may also not belong to any religion.
Nobody may be forced into a faith or into religious education lessons.
Christians pray in church, Muslims in the mosque, Jews in the synagogue.
Freedom of religion applies to everyone, which is why respect is needed.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss **Federal Constitution** contains **freedom of religion and conscience**. Every person may freely choose their religion and practise it alone or with others. You may also belong to **no religion**. Nobody has to join a church or take part in religious ceremonies. The UN Declaration of Human Rights also protects this right.

People of different religions live in Switzerland. **Christians** pray in **church**, and there is one in almost every village. **Muslims** pray in the **mosque**. **Jewish people** meet in the **synagogue**; there is a large one in Basel, for example. There are also temples and other places for further religions.

Church **religious education** is voluntary. Nobody may be forced to attend it. For children, the parents have a say. From the age of 16, young people in Switzerland may decide about their religion themselves. Many schools also have a subject in which you get to know different religions.

Freedom of religion applies equally to all people. That is why **respect** is important: you do not have to share the same faith, but you respect others. Nobody may be laughed at or disadvantaged because of their religion. But the freedom has limits: even in the name of a religion, you may not harm anyone.

In some countries there is no real freedom of religion. Dictatorships often dictate what people may believe or ban religion altogether. Believers are persecuted or punished there. That is why freedom of religion is an important sign of a free state.

gewusst: The synagogue in Basel was opened in 1868.
In Switzerland today, many people do not belong to any religious community, and their share has grown strongly in recent decades.

teile.einleitung: The Frontist movement is the name for far-right groups in Switzerland in the 1930s. They called themselves “Fronts” and took Fascism in Italy and National Socialism in Germany as their models. However, the great majority of the population rejected them.
wichtigste: In 1933 the Fronts had a surge known as the “Spring of the Fronts”.
In Zurich in 1933 they won 10 of the 125 seats on the city council.
Their greeting was “Harus!”.
In 1935 around 72 per cent of voters rejected a total revision of the Federal Constitution.
In the Bern trial the “Protocols of the Elders of Zion” were judged to be a forgery.
In 1940 the Federal Council banned the National Movement of Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of 1933 Adolf Hitler became Chancellor in Germany. After that, numerous **Fronts** were founded in Switzerland too or gained new followers; the best known was the **National Front**. This wave is called the **Spring of the Fronts**. The Fronts rejected democracy and stirred up hatred against Jews. As a greeting they used the call “**Harus!**”, a word of their own modelled on the German and Italian salutes.

abschnitte.titel: Little success at the ballot box
abschnitte.text: In the Zurich city council elections of 1933 the Frontists won 10 of 125 seats. After that they had little success in elections. In 1935 a popular initiative for a **total revision of the Federal Constitution** was put to the vote. The Fronts and conservative groups wanted to rebuild the constitution from the ground up, partly in an authoritarian way. On 8 September 1935 around **72 per cent** of voters rejected the proposal. This is seen as a clear commitment to democracy.

Frontists spread the “**Protocols of the Elders of Zion**”. This antisemitic hate pamphlet claimed that Jews were planning to rule the world. Jewish organisations took the people spreading it to court in Bern. In 1935 the court ruled that the text was a **forgery**. The trial attracted great attention abroad too.

In February 1936 the Jewish student David Frankfurter shot **Wilhelm Gustloff**, the leader of the Nazi party's Swiss branch, in **Davos**. After that the Federal Council banned the national leadership of the Nazi party in Switzerland. After Germany defeated France in 1940, the **National Movement of Switzerland** sought to fall in line with the Nazi regime. The Federal Council banned it on 19 November 1940.

gewusst: The initiative for a total revision of the Federal Constitution failed in 1935 with 72.3 per cent voting No.
As early as 1921 the London newspaper “The Times” showed that large parts of the “Protocols” had been copied from an older French book.

teile.einleitung: A military junta is a group of military officers who have seized power in a country and govern together. The word “junta” comes from Spanish and means something like assembly or council. In the 20th century, military juntas ruled above all in South America, but also in Europe, Africa and Asia.
wichtigste: A junta is a group of military officers who have seized power.
The Spanish word “junta” means assembly, council or committee.
A junta is usually made up of the heads of the army, navy and air force.
Juntas almost always come to power through a coup.
A junta does not allow free elections and restricts fundamental rights.
Well-known juntas existed in Chile, Argentina, Greece and Myanmar.
Often one general within the junta becomes the most powerful man.

abschnitte.text: The word **junta** comes from Spanish and originally simply means “assembly” or “council”. In Spain and Latin America there used to be completely harmless juntas too, for example local councils. Today, however, the word almost always makes people think of a **military junta**. This means a group of officers who rule a country without being elected.

A military junta is often made up of the top commanders of the armed forces. Typically these are the heads of the **army**, the **navy** and the **air force**, and sometimes the police as well. The members share power and decide together. Over time, however, a single general often gains the upper hand and becomes the real dictator.

abschnitte.titel: How a junta comes to power
abschnitte.text: A junta almost always takes power through a **coup**. The officers remove the elected government and dissolve parliament. They then declare that they will only govern temporarily until “order” is restored. In reality, many juntas stay in power for years.

In **Chile**, from 11 September 1973, a junta of four men ruled, soon headed by General Augusto Pinochet. In Argentina a junta ruled from 1976 to 1983, under which thousands of people disappeared. In Greece, the so-called **Colonels** governed from 1967 to 1974. In Myanmar and Thailand the military has also taken power in this century.

Under a junta, parties are banned, newspapers are censored and protests are suppressed. Critics end up in prison or have to flee abroad. Many juntas have committed serious **human rights violations**. After they end, victims and their relatives often fight for justice for decades.

begriffe.erklaerung: Spanish for council or assembly; today usually a ruling group of military officers.
A soldier of higher rank who is allowed to give orders.
All the military troops of a country, meaning the army, navy and air force.
The name for the officers who ruled Greece from 1967 to 1974.

gewusst: In Spanish, the word “junta” is still used today for completely normal bodies, for example for regional governments in Spain.
The Greek junta fell in 1974 after a coup it had supported in Cyprus failed.

teile.einleitung: The KGB was the intelligence service and at the same time the secret police of the Soviet Union. It existed from 1954 to 1991 and spied on people at home and abroad.
wichtigste: KGB means “Committee for State Security”.
It was founded in March 1954, a year after Stalin's death.
Its predecessors included the Cheka and the NKVD.
Yuri Andropov was head of the KGB for a long time and became party leader in 1982.
Vladimir Putin worked for the KGB in Dresden from 1985 to 1990.
In 1991 the KGB was dissolved; inside the country the FSB later followed.

abschnitte.text: KGB is the abbreviation of the Russian “Komitet gosudarstvennoy bezopasnosti”. This means **Committee for State Security**. The KGB spied abroad and at the same time watched over its own population. It was created in March **1954**, a year after Stalin's death.

The first secret police of Soviet power was the **Cheka**. It was founded and led by **Felix Dzerzhinsky** in December 1917. During the Civil War it persecuted opponents of the Bolsheviks with mass terror. Later further services followed, including the **NKVD**. The KGB continued this tradition.

**Dissidents** are people who openly hold a different opinion from the government. The KGB persecuted them harshly. They were often sent to psychiatric hospitals without a trial. For this, psychiatrists used the diagnosis of **“sluggish schizophrenia”**. It had hardly any symptoms and could be found in anyone who thought differently, just as people liked.

**Yuri Andropov** headed the KGB from 1967 to 1982. After Brezhnev's death he became General Secretary of the Communist Party but died as early as 1984. **Vladimir Putin** was stationed as a KGB officer in **Dresden** in the GDR from 1985 to 1990. In 1998 and 1999 he headed the domestic intelligence service, the FSB.

With the end of the Soviet Union, the KGB was dissolved in **1991** and split into several services. From 1995 the **FSB** took over most tasks inside the country. The **SVR** is responsible for abroad.

gewusst: The Cheka of 1917 is seen as the forerunner of the KGB.
A former head of the KGB, Yuri Andropov, later became leader of the Soviet Union himself.

teile.einleitung: Martial law was in force in Taiwan from 1949 to 1987. During this time the Kuomintang ruled alone, and many people were persecuted for political reasons. Today Taiwan is a democracy.
wichtigste: Martial law lasted from 20 May 1949 to 15 July 1987.
At 38 years, it was one of the longest in the world.
The persecution during this time is called the “White Terror”.
The incident of 28 February 1947 is seen as the start of the repression.
The Kuomintang ruled alone, and new parties were banned.
Chiang Ching-kuo lifted martial law in 1987.

abschnitte.text: Under **martial law**, the military and the government take on special powers, and many basic rights no longer apply. In Taiwan it came into force on **20 May 1949**. It was not lifted until **15 July 1987**. At 38 years, it was one of the longest in the world. The **Kuomintang**, the Nationalist Party, had fled to Taiwan under **Chiang Kai-shek** and ruled alone.

There was violence even before martial law. After a dispute over illegal cigarettes, an uprising broke out on **28 February 1947**. The Kuomintang crushed it bloodily, and thousands of people were killed. Today 28 February is a **day of remembrance** in Taiwan.

The political persecution under martial law is called the **White Terror**. Tens of thousands were arrested as supposed communists or separatists, and thousands were executed. Many political prisoners were held on **Green Island** off the east coast. Today a human rights museum there remembers them.

On 10 December 1979, supporters of the magazine “Formosa” demonstrated for human rights in **Kaohsiung**. Their leaders were brought before military courts, and many later became important politicians. On 28 September 1986, the **Democratic Progressive Party** (DPP) was founded, even though new parties were banned. The government tolerated it. In 1987, **Chiang Ching-kuo**, the son of Chiang Kai-shek, lifted martial law. He died in 1988.

gewusst: The DPP was founded when new parties were still banned in Taiwan.
On Green Island, once a place for political prisoners, there is now a human rights museum.

teile.einleitung: From 1967 to 1974 a group of officers ruled Greece as a dictatorship. Because many of them were colonels, it is known as the Regime of the Colonels. After their rule ended, Greece became a democratic republic.
wichtigste: On 21 April 1967 officers staged a coup in Greece.
The most important leader was Colonel Georgios Papadopoulos.
In 1969 Greece left the Council of Europe to avoid being expelled.
In November 1973 the uprising at the Athens Polytechnic was ended by force.
A failed coup in Cyprus led to the collapse in 1974.
Konstantinos Karamanlis led the country back to democracy.
In December 1974 the people voted to abolish the monarchy.

abschnitte.text: During the night before **21 April 1967** troops occupied Athens and arrested leading politicians. At the head was Colonel **Georgios Papadopoulos**, who became head of government. Because the plotters were mainly **colonels**, people speak of the **Colonels' Junta**. A junta is a government of officers.

The colonels abolished civil liberties. Parties were banned, newspapers censored, and many opponents arrested or sent into exile. The famous composer **Mikis Theodorakis**, known for the music to “Zorba the Greek”, was also arrested and his music banned. His songs became symbols of resistance. The **Council of Europe** accused the junta of torture and human rights abuses. Greece left in 1969 to avoid being expelled.

In November 1973 students occupied the **technical university** in Athens, the Polytechnic. They were protesting against the junta. On **17 November** a tank broke through the gate, and people were killed. Shortly afterwards Papadopoulos was removed by other officers. Today 17 November is a day of remembrance in Greece.

In 1974 the junta had the President of **Cyprus** overthrown. Turkey then attacked the island, and the regime in Athens collapsed in July 1974. **Konstantinos Karamanlis** returned from exile in Paris and became Prime Minister. He organised free elections. In December 1974 around two thirds voted against the return of the king, and since then Greece has been a **republic**. In the same year the country rejoined the Council of Europe.

gewusst: The music of Mikis Theodorakis was banned under the junta but was still listened to in secret.
Since 1974 Cyprus has been divided into a Greek part and a Turkish part.

teile.einleitung: In a multi-party system there are several parties that compete freely for the votes of the voters. This is important so that people can choose between different ideas. Switzerland is a good example, because many parties are represented in parliament and even in government.
wichtigste: In a multi-party system there are several parties that are free to stand for election.
People can choose between different ideas.
Anyone can found a new party.
Parties that are not in government form the opposition and keep a check on the government.
A multi-party system is a feature of every democracy.
In Switzerland, several parties share the government; this is called concordance.
The opposite is the one-party system in dictatorships.

abschnitte.text: A **party** is a group of people with similar political ideas. In a **multi-party system** there are many such groups that compete against each other in elections. Anyone can found a new party if they have different ideas. This way voters can choose between different programmes. This is a key difference from a dictatorship, where usually only one party is allowed.

When there are several parties, problems are argued about and discussed openly. Parties that are not in government form the **opposition**. They criticise the government and make their own proposals. If the people are unhappy, they can strengthen other parties at the next election. This makes a **peaceful change of power** possible.

There are many parties in Switzerland. The largest are the SVP, the SP, the FDP, the Centre, the Greens and the Green Liberals. In the 2023 National Council elections, the SVP became the strongest party with about 28 per cent of the vote. The National Council has 200 members from around ten parties. For the National Council there is no nationwide minimum percentage that a party needs.

In the **Federal Council**, the large parties are represented together, instead of one party governing alone. This cooperation is called **concordance**. From 1959 to 2003, the so-called **magic formula** applied: two seats each for the FDP, CVP and SP and one seat for the SVP. Today the SVP has two seats and the Centre one. The parties therefore have to find compromises.

In the **USA** there are many parties, but in practice only two large ones, the Democrats and the Republicans. This is why people speak of a **two-party system**. In Germany, two or three parties usually govern together in a **coalition**. There, a party generally needs at least 5 per cent of the vote in the Bundestag election to get into parliament.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of people with shared political goals.
The parties that are not in government and keep a check on it.
When several large parties govern together and look for compromises.
An alliance of parties that govern together.

gewusst: The magic formula for the Swiss Federal Council stayed unchanged for 44 years.
In Switzerland you can mix candidates from different parties on a ballot paper; this is called panachage.

teile.einleitung: Ferdinand Marcos was president of the Philippines from 1965 to 1986. From 1972 he ruled as a dictator. A peaceful popular uprising overthrew him in 1986.
wichtigste: Marcos ruled the Philippines from 1965 to 1986.
In September 1972 he declared martial law.
In 1983 the opposition leader Benigno Aquino was shot dead.
In 1986 the peaceful People Power Revolution overthrew him.
Corazon Aquino became the first woman president of the Philippines.
The Federal Council had Marcos’s money in Switzerland frozen.

abschnitte.text: **Ferdinand Marcos** was elected president of the **Philippines** in 1965. In September 1972 he declared **martial law**. With it he closed parliament and had opponents arrested. In 1981 he formally lifted martial law, but kept far-reaching special powers. His rule remained authoritarian until 1986.

The Marcos family piled up huge fortunes while many people remained poor. His wife **Imelda Marcos** became known around the world for her **shoe collection**. After the family fled, well over a thousand pairs of shoes were found in the presidential palace. They became a symbol of the extravagance.
