In 1983 the opposition leader **Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino** returned from exile. He was shot dead at Manila airport just as he was getting off the plane. His death sparked big protests. In February 1986 hundreds of thousands gathered peacefully on **EDSA** avenue in Manila. This **People Power Revolution** forced Marcos to leave the country. Aquino’s widow, **Corazon Aquino**, became the first woman president of the Philippines.

With the help of the USA the family was taken to **Hawaii**. Marcos died in Honolulu in 1989. After his fall, in 1986, the **Federal Council** had his accounts in Switzerland frozen. Later the Philippines received about 680 million US dollars back from them. The case shaped the way Switzerland deals with the money of overthrown rulers.

The Marcos family later returned to the Philippines and became politically active again. In 2022 his son **Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr.** clearly won the presidential election. With that the family came back to power 36 years after fleeing.

gewusst: The colour yellow became the symbol of the People Power movement.
Some of Imelda Marcos’s shoes are now on display in a museum in Marikina.

teile.einleitung: Thailand is a kingdom in South-East Asia. Since 1932 the military there has very often staged coups and taken over the government. That is why the country has also had a particularly large number of constitutions.
wichtigste: In 1932 a bloodless coup ended the absolute monarchy.
Since 1932 Thailand has had a new constitution around 20 times.
In 1992 there was the popular uprising known as “Black May”.
In 2006 Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra was overthrown.
In 2014 General Prayut Chan-o-cha staged a coup and became head of government.
The lèse-majesté law strictly punishes criticism of the royal family.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the absolute monarchy
abschnitte.text: Until 1932 the country was called **Siam**, and the king ruled alone. In 1932 a group of officers and officials took power in a **bloodless coup**. Since then Thailand has been a **constitutional monarchy**: the king is subject to a constitution. But the military remained very powerful and intervened again and again.

Since 1932 there have been more than a dozen coups and coup attempts in Thailand. After many coups, the military wrote a new constitution. As a result, Thailand has had a new constitution around **20 times**. On 6 October 1976 there was a **massacre at Thammasat University** in Bangkok, in which protesting students were killed. The same evening, the military staged a coup.

In 1992 the coup general **Suchinda Kraprayoon** became head of government without being elected. Hundreds of thousands protested in Bangkok. The army fired on the demonstrators. These events are called **Black May**. Afterwards Suchinda resigned, and Thailand became more democratic for some years.

In 2006 the military overthrew Prime Minister **Thaksin Shinawatra** while he was in New York. In May 2014 General **Prayut Chan-o-cha** staged a coup. The junta called itself the **National Council for Peace and Order**. Prayut became head of government and remained so even after the 2019 election, until 2023.

In Thailand it is strictly forbidden to insult the king or his family. The **lèse-majesté law** provides for long prison sentences. Critics say the law is used to suppress opinions. The government says it protects the dignity of the monarchy.

gewusst: Since 1939 Siam has officially been called Thailand, which means “land of the free”.
King Bhumibol reigned from 1946 to 2016 and saw many coups during that time.

teile.einleitung: Nonviolent resistance means standing up against injustice without hurting others. People demonstrate, go on strike or hold boycotts to change something. In this way unjust laws have been abolished and dictatorships brought down.
wichtigste: Nonviolent resistance means protesting without violence.
At a demonstration many people show their opinion together.
In a boycott you deliberately do not buy or use something.
In a sit-in blockade people peacefully block a way.
Civil disobedience means openly and peacefully not obeying unjust rules.
Two fingers held up in a V shape are a well-known sign of peace.

abschnitte.text: In **nonviolent resistance** people stand up against injustice without hurting others. They want to show that they are in the right and to convince others. Often a great many people take part together. When a government attacks peaceful people, it often loses the support of the population. Famous examples are **Mahatma Gandhi** in India and **Martin Luther King** in the USA.

At a **demonstration** many people take to the streets together. With placards and chants they show what they want or reject. In Switzerland the Federal Constitution protects the right to assemble peacefully. In a **boycott** many people together go without something, for example certain goods. In this way they put on pressure and want to change something.

In a **sit-in blockade** people sit down, for example on a road or in front of a gate, and peacefully block the way. In a **strike** people stop working together. In a **hunger strike** someone goes without food to draw attention to an injustice. This can be very dangerous for their health.

In **civil disobedience** people deliberately do not keep to a rule they think is unjust. They do this openly and without violence and accept the **punishment**. A well-known example is Gandhi's **Salt March** of 1930. He made salt himself, although at that time in India only the British colonial administration was allowed to make and sell salt. Opinions differ on whether civil disobedience is justified in a democracy.

gewusst: In 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a bus to a white man in Montgomery in the USA. After that many Black people boycotted the buses for more than a year.
The V sign made with two fingers also used to stand for “Victory”.

teile.einleitung: Park Chung-hee ruled South Korea from 1961 to 1979, first as a general and later as president. Under him the poor country became an industrial nation, while at the same time he harshly suppressed his opponents.
wichtigste: Park Chung-hee came to power in a military coup on 16 May 1961.
From 1963 he ruled as an elected president, in an increasingly authoritarian way.
With the Yushin Constitution of 1972 he expanded his power almost without limit.
The economic boom under him is called the “Miracle on the Han River”.
He promoted large family-run conglomerates, the chaebol.
In 1979 he was shot by his own intelligence chief.

abschnitte.text: On **16 May 1961**, a group of officers under **Park Chung-hee** overthrew the government of South Korea. In the same year the military government founded the intelligence service **KCIA**, which watched and persecuted opposition figures. From 1963 Park ruled as elected **President**. However, the elections were not really free and fair.

In 1972 Park had a new constitution introduced. It was called the **Yushin Constitution**; “Yushin” means “renewal”. It allowed him to be re-elected without limit and gave him far-reaching **emergency powers**. Criticism of the government could be severely punished. With this, South Korea was a **dictatorship**.

abschnitte.titel: The Miracle on the Han River
abschnitte.text: The **Han** flows through the capital Seoul. Under Park the economy grew so fast that people speak of the **Miracle on the Han River**. The state steered the economy and especially promoted **exports**. Large family-run conglomerates, the **chaebol**, received cheap loans. They include companies such as Samsung, Hyundai and LG.

In 1970 Park launched the **Saemaul Movement**, the “New Village Movement”. Using materials from the state, villagers built roads, bridges and better houses. Agriculture was also modernised. But the movement also served to win people over to the government.

On **26 October 1979**, **Kim Jae-gyu**, the director of the KCIA, shot Park during a dinner. His motives are still disputed today. In South Korea, Park is still judged in very different ways: as a moderniser or as a dictator. His daughter **Park Geun-hye** became the country's first female president in 2013 and was removed from office in 2017 because of a corruption scandal.

gewusst: Park's wife Yuk Young-soo was killed in 1974 in an attack that was actually aimed at him.
The KCIA intelligence service is now called the National Intelligence Service, NIS for short.

teile.einleitung: A military dictatorship is a form of government in which the army or its generals rule the country without free elections. Usually the military comes to power through a coup. In the 20th century there were many military dictatorships, especially in South America, Africa and Asia.
wichtigste: In a military dictatorship, the army or generals rule the country without free elections.
A military dictatorship usually begins with a coup against the previous government.
Often a group of officers rules together; this is called a military junta.
Fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and freedom of the press are severely restricted.
Well-known examples are Chile under Augusto Pinochet and Argentina from 1976 to 1983.
Many military dictatorships ended through protests, economic crises or lost wars.
Even today there are countries where the military rules, for example Myanmar.

abschnitte.text: In a military dictatorship, power lies with the **army**. A general or a group of officers decides what happens in the country. There is no freely elected **parliament**, or it has no say. Those in power often justify their rule by saying they have to keep order or protect the country from enemies.

Usually the military takes power through a **coup**, meaning a violent overthrow. Tanks roll in, and soldiers occupy government buildings and radio and television stations. Often the previous government is removed, arrested or driven abroad. This often happens at times of economic crisis or great political conflict.

In a military dictatorship, **martial law** or emergency laws often apply. Parties and trade unions are banned, and newspapers are censored. Opponents are arrested, tortured or disappear without a trace. Sometimes there are night-time curfews, and soldiers control the streets.

In **Chile**, General Augusto Pinochet overthrew the elected president Salvador Allende in 1973 and ruled until 1990. In Argentina a military junta ruled from 1976 to 1983, and in Brazil the military governed from 1964 to 1985. In Greece, a group of officers known as the “Colonels” ruled from 1967 to 1974. In **Myanmar**, the military took power again in February 2021.

abschnitte.titel: The end of a military dictatorship
abschnitte.text: Many military dictatorships came under pressure from protests by the population, economic problems or pressure from abroad. In Argentina, defeat in the Falklands War in 1982 led to the end of the junta. In Chile, the people voted in a referendum in 1988 against another term for Pinochet. After the end, there is often the difficult question of how to deal with the crimes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A violent seizure of power, often by the military.
A group of military officers who govern together.
Emergency rules under which the military gets a lot of power and rights are restricted.
A very high rank in the army.

gewusst: In Switzerland there is only a general in times of war; he is elected by the Federal Assembly.
In Chile, a referendum in 1988 finally decided the end of military rule.

teile.einleitung: A dictator is a ruler who decides everything alone and without any checks. Nobody is allowed to contradict him. Both the word and the office already existed in ancient Rome.
wichtigste: A dictator has all the power in a country.
The word comes from Latin.
In ancient Rome there was a dictator for emergencies.
In 44 BC Julius Caesar became dictator for life.
From 1922 Benito Mussolini turned Italy into a dictatorship.

abschnitte.text: The word **“dictator”** comes from Latin. It is connected with **“dictare”**, which means to say aloud or to prescribe. When you write a **dictation**, someone tells you what you have to write down. A dictator tells everyone what they have to do.

In **ancient Rome** a dictator could be appointed in an emergency, for example in a war. He then had all the power for a short time, at most about **six months**. As soon as his task was done, he was supposed to give up power again. In 44 BC **Julius Caesar** had himself made **dictator for life**. In the same year he was murdered.

Today a dictator means a ruler who has not been freely elected and tolerates no checks. **Benito Mussolini** came to power in Italy in 1922 and abolished freedoms step by step. Adolf Hitler in Germany and Joseph Stalin in the Soviet Union were also dictators. A dictator usually does not give up his power voluntarily. He wants to rule **for as long as possible**.

Many dictators have their **picture** hung up everywhere, in schools, offices and on the streets. Everyone is supposed to see and worship him. Newspapers and television may only report good things about him. Anyone who voices criticism can be sent to prison. In Switzerland, on the other hand, a Federal Council with seven members governs, so that nobody decides alone.

gewusst: After his victory, the Roman Cincinnatus is said to have given up power after only a few days and returned to his farm.
The rule of a dictator is called a dictatorship.

teile.einleitung: A dictatorship is a form of state in which a single person or a small group has all the power. The people are not allowed to vote freely, and anyone who criticises openly is often punished. There have been many dictatorships in history, and there are still some today.
wichtigste: In a dictatorship one person or a small group has all the power.
The people are not allowed to vote freely.
The laws are usually made only by the dictator or a small group.
Anyone who openly criticises the ruler is often punished or locked up.
Many dictators have a very large army to protect their power and intimidate critics.
Censorship and propaganda control what people find out.
The opposite of a dictatorship is a democracy.

abschnitte.text: In a **dictatorship** a dictator or a small group rules, for example a party or the army. There are no free elections in which the government could be voted out. Parliament and the courts have either been abolished or have to obey. So the **separation of powers** has been done away with. The ruler can change the laws as he likes.

Dictatorships control newspapers, radio, television and the internet; this is called **censorship**. **Propaganda** is used to praise the ruler and run down opponents. Often there is a secret police that spies on people. Critics end up in prison, have to flee or disappear. Many dictators have themselves worshipped like heroes; this is called a **personality cult**.

In a **military dictatorship** generals rule, often after a coup. In a one-party dictatorship a single party decides everything. A distinction is also made between authoritarian dictatorships, which mainly want obedience, and **totalitarian** dictatorships, which want to control people’s whole lives and thoughts. Some dictatorships hold sham elections in which the result has been fixed in advance.

In the 20th century there were particularly cruel dictatorships. Adolf Hitler ruled in Germany from 1933 to 1945, Joseph Stalin in the Soviet Union and Mao Zedong in China. In Spain Francisco Franco ruled from 1939 to 1975. There were also many military dictatorships in South America, Africa and Asia. Some countries, for example North Korea, are still ruled as dictatorships today.

Some dictatorships end through a war, like Nazi Germany in 1945. Others end through peaceful protests by the people, like the GDR in 1989 after the fall of the **Berlin Wall**. After a dictator’s death a country can also move to democracy, like Spain after 1975. Today there is the International Criminal Court for crimes committed by dictators.

Switzerland has never been a dictatorship since the founding of the federal state in 1848. It has a semi-direct democracy with many referendums. In the Second World War it was surrounded by dictatorships and took in refugees, but also turned many away. Today pupils learn about dictatorships at school so that they can recognise the warning signs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ruler who governs alone and without any checks.
Control over what may be published or said.
A violent overthrow, usually by the army.
When a ruler is worshipped excessively, for example with huge pictures and statues.
A form of rule that wants to control every area of life.

gewusst: Many dictatorships call themselves a “Democratic Republic”, even though there are no free elections there.
The word “dictator” comes from ancient Rome, where it was an emergency office lasting at most six months.

teile.einleitung: Charles de Montesquieu was a French philosopher and writer who lived from 1689 to 1755. He played a decisive part in shaping the idea of the separation of powers. His idea of dividing power in the state into three parts still protects many countries against dictatorship today.
wichtigste: Montesquieu was a French thinker of the Enlightenment.
He lived from 1689 to 1755.
He played a decisive part in shaping the idea of the separation of powers.
His most important book is called “The Spirit of the Laws” and was published in 1748.
Power is to be divided between law-making, government and the courts.
His ideas influenced the Constitution of the USA and many other constitutions.
Switzerland also has a separation of powers, with parliament, the Federal Council and the Federal Supreme Court.

abschnitte.text: Charles-Louis de Secondat, Baron de Montesquieu, was born in 1689 at the **Château de La Brède** near Bordeaux in France. He came from a noble family and studied law. Later he was a judge in Bordeaux. Montesquieu is one of the important thinkers of the **Enlightenment**, a time when reason and freedom were held in high regard. He died in Paris in 1755.

In 1721 Montesquieu published the **“Persian Letters”**. In them two imaginary travellers from Persia describe France and make fun of the king, the Church and society. His main work, **“The Spirit of the Laws”**, was published in Geneva in 1748, without his name on it. In it he compares the laws and forms of state of many countries. The Catholic Church put the book on its list of banned books.

Montesquieu believed that nobody should have too much power, because power is easily abused. That is why the power of the state should be divided into three parts. The **legislature** makes the laws, the **executive** carries them out and governs, and the **judiciary** judges. The three powers check one another. One of his models was England, which he had got to know on his travels.

The founders of the USA took Montesquieu’s ideas into their constitution of 1787. In the French Revolution, too, the separation of powers became an important demand. Today it is a cornerstone of almost all **democracies**. Dictators, on the other hand, usually try to hold all three powers in their own hands.

In Switzerland the **Federal Assembly**, with the National Council and the Council of States, is the legislature. The Federal Council, with seven members, forms the government. The **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne is the highest court. This division also exists in the cantons and municipalities. In addition, the voters can have a say through referendums.

begriffe.erklaerung: Power in the state is divided between several independent parts.
The law-making power, usually parliament.
The power that carries out the laws, in other words the government and the administration.
The power that judges, in other words the courts.
An 18th-century movement that put its trust in reason, knowledge and freedom.

gewusst: Montesquieu’s famous main work was printed in Geneva so that French censorship could not easily stop it.
Montesquieu was also a winegrower and sold wine from his estates near Bordeaux as far away as England.

teile.einleitung: The NSDAP was the party of Adolf Hitler. Its name means National Socialist German Workers' Party. From 1933 it set up a dictatorship in Germany that led to the Second World War and the Holocaust.
wichtigste: The NSDAP was founded in Munich.
In 1923 Hitler tried to seize power with a putsch in Munich.
While imprisoned in Landsberg, he wrote the book “Mein Kampf”.
The symbol of the NSDAP was the swastika.
In the Reichstag election of July 1932 it became the strongest party for the first time.
From July 1933 it was the only permitted party in Germany.
The SA was its fighting force with brown shirts.

abschnitte.text: The party was founded in **Munich** in 1919 under the name German Workers' Party. In 1920 it was renamed the **NSDAP**. Adolf Hitler soon became its most important speaker and then its leader. The party stirred up hatred against Jews, against democracy and against the peace treaty after the First World War. Its symbol was the **swastika**.

abschnitte.titel: The Beer Hall Putsch and “Mein Kampf”
abschnitte.text: In November **1923**, Hitler tried to seize power in Munich with a **putsch**. He wanted to follow Mussolini's example. The putsch failed, and Hitler went to prison in **Landsberg**. There he wrote the book **“Mein Kampf”** (My Struggle). In it he described his ideas, full of hatred against Jews, and his plan to conquer territory in the east.

From 1929, Germany suffered a severe **economic crisis**. Millions of people were unemployed. The NSDAP promised simple solutions and won many votes. In the **Reichstag election of July 1932**, it became the strongest party for the first time. On 30 January 1933, Hitler was appointed Reich Chancellor.

The **SA** was the party's fighting force. Its members wore **brown shirts**, which is why they are also called the “Brownshirts”. They disrupted meetings of other parties and attacked opponents. Later the **SS** became more and more important. It was responsible for surveillance, persecution and the concentration camps.

abschnitte.titel: The only party, and the end
abschnitte.text: In 1933 the other parties were banned or dissolved themselves. From **July 1933** the NSDAP was the **only permitted party**. Germany was now a dictatorship. The rule of the NSDAP led to the **Second World War** and the **Holocaust**, the murder of around six million Jews. After the defeat in 1945, the party was banned.

gewusst: In Germany, displaying the swastika as a symbol of the NSDAP is still generally forbidden today.
By the end, the NSDAP had more than eight million members.

teile.einleitung: The state's monopoly on violence means that only the state may lawfully use force, for example through the police and the courts. Nobody else may use force to get justice for themselves. This ensures peace and security, as long as the state uses its power according to clear rules.
wichtigste: Under the monopoly on violence, only the state may lawfully use force.
This happens mainly through the police, the justice system and the army.
Citizens may not use force to get justice for themselves.
One exception is self-defence when there is immediate danger.
The term was made well known by the German sociologist Max Weber.
In a state under the rule of law, the monopoly on violence is bound by laws.
Dictatorships misuse the monopoly on violence against their own people.

abschnitte.text: The **monopoly on violence** means that only the state may use coercion and force. A monopoly is something that only one party has. If someone steals, you may not punish them yourself but must call the **police**. A court then decides on the punishment. This prevents the stronger person from simply getting their way.

In Switzerland it is mainly the **cantonal police forces** and city police forces that ensure security. Courts give judgements on disputes and crimes. Prisons carry out sentences. The army protects the country and can support the civilian authorities in emergencies. All these bodies have to keep to the **laws**.

In the Middle Ages there was no real monopoly on violence. Nobles fought **feuds** with one another, small private wars, to settle disputes. Whoever was strong got their way; this was called the law of the fist. In 1495 the emperor of the Holy Roman Empire proclaimed the **Perpetual Public Peace**, which banned feuds. Only gradually did the modern state with police and courts become established.

The German sociologist **Max Weber** described the monopoly on violence in 1919 in a famous lecture called “Politics as a Vocation”. For him it is a feature of every modern state. A state that loses its monopoly on violence can no longer protect its citizens. In some countries armed gangs control whole areas; then people speak of a failed state.

So that the state does not misuse its power, the monopoly on violence has to be kept in check. In a **state under the rule of law** the police may only act according to clear rules, and you can defend yourself in the courts. The media and parliament keep a close eye on things. In a dictatorship, by contrast, the police, the secret police and the army use force against people who think differently. That is why the monopoly on violence and the separation of powers belong together.

Taking the law into your own hands is forbidden in Switzerland, even if you feel you have been treated unfairly. However, if you are attacked, you may defend yourself reasonably in **self-defence**. If there is a dispute, you should get help, for example from parents, teachers or the police on the number 117. Police officers must also keep to rules and may only use as much force as necessary.

begriffe.erklaerung: When only one party may have or do something.
A state in which the government too has to keep to the laws.
When someone takes revenge or punishes someone themselves instead of letting a court decide.
The right to defend yourself against an attack.

gewusst: In Switzerland the police are mostly the responsibility of the cantons, not the federal government.
The Perpetual Public Peace of 1495 banned private wars between nobles throughout the Holy Roman Empire.

teile.einleitung: The Berlin Wall was a heavily guarded border that ran right through Berlin from 1961 to 1989. The GDR built it to stop its citizens from fleeing to the West. Its fall on 9 November 1989 became the symbol of the end of the Cold War.
wichtigste: The Wall was built on 13 August 1961.
It separated East Berlin and the GDR from West Berlin.
In total the border installations around West Berlin were about 155 kilometres long.
At least 140 people died at the Berlin Wall.
The GDR called it the “Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart”.
On 9 November 1989 the Wall was unexpectedly opened.
On 3 October 1990 Germany was reunified.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War Germany was divided into four zones, and **Berlin** was also given four sectors. In 1949 two states came into being: the Federal Republic in the West and the communist **GDR** in the East. West Berlin lay like an island in the middle of the GDR. Until 1961 about three million people fled from the GDR to the West, many of them via Berlin.

During the night of 12 to 13 August 1961 soldiers and police sealed off the border with barbed wire. After that a concrete wall was built, which separated families and friends from one day to the next. The GDR government under Walter Ulbricht claimed that the Wall protected against the West and called it the **Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart**. In truth it was meant to stop its own people from leaving.

The border did not consist of just one wall, but of several barriers one behind the other. Between them lay the **death strip**, with watchtowers, dogs, searchlights and alarm systems. The border guards had orders to shoot at people trying to escape. Even so, more than 5,000 people managed to escape, for example through tunnels, hidden in cars or in home-made balloons.

In 1989 more and more people in the GDR protested peacefully for freedom and the freedom to travel. On the evening of 9 November 1989 the politician **Günter Schabowski** announced at a press conference, by mistake, that the new travel rules applied immediately. Thousands streamed to the border crossings until the guards opened the gates. People celebrated on the Wall, and soon the **Mauerspechte** (“wall woodpeckers”) began chipping pieces out of it.

A year later, on 3 October 1990, Germany was **reunified**. Today a line of cobblestones and several memorial sites mark where the Wall ran. At the **East Side Gallery** a long, brightly painted stretch of the Wall has been preserved. At the Bernauer Strasse memorial you can see what the border strip used to look like, and pieces of the Wall now stand in many countries, including Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: German Democratic Republic, the communist state in eastern Germany.
The heavily guarded area behind the Wall, where people trying to escape were shot at.
The joining together of East and West Germany into one state in 1990.
German for “wall woodpecker”: a person who chipped pieces out of the Wall in 1989 and 1990.

gewusst: The best-known border crossing was called Checkpoint Charlie and was meant for foreigners and diplomats.
The Wall stood for 28 years, and since 2018 it has been gone for longer than it stood.
In 1963 US President John F. Kennedy spoke the famous words “Ich bin ein Berliner” (I am a Berliner) in West Berlin.

teile.einleitung: In a book burning, books with unwanted ideas are publicly thrown into the fire. Those who do this want to wipe out ideas and frighten people. The best-known book burning took place in Berlin on 10 May 1933, shortly after the Nazis had come to power.
wichtigste: In a book burning, books with unwanted ideas are burned.
It is a sign of censorship and the suppression of freedom of opinion.
On 10 May 1933 books were burned in Berlin and many other German cities.
The campaign was organised by Nazi students.
It targeted books by Jewish, left-wing and critical authors.
Books have also been burned at other times and in other countries, for example in ancient China.
Today memorials commemorate the book burning of 1933.

abschnitte.text: In a **book burning** people collect books they do not like and burn them publicly. Usually a government or a group with a lot of power is behind it. It is not just about destroying paper. The act is meant to show that certain ideas are forbidden and that people who think differently will be punished. That is why it is seen as a powerful sign of **censorship**.

On the evening of 10 May 1933 a big fire burned on the Opernplatz in Berlin, today’s **Bebelplatz**. Thousands of books were thrown into it while slogans against the authors were shouted. Propaganda minister **Joseph Goebbels** gave a speech there. On the same day there were similar fires in many university towns in Germany. The campaign had been prepared by the German Students’ Union.

Works by writers, scientists and politicians whom the Nazis rejected were burned. They included **Erich Kästner**, Heinrich Mann, Kurt Tucholsky, Bertolt Brecht, Sigmund Freud and Karl Marx. Many of these people were Jewish or had different political views. Erich Kästner, the author of “Emil and the Detectives”, stood in the crowd himself and watched his books burn. Many of the persecuted authors later had to flee into exile.

There were book burnings long before 1933. In ancient China, in the 3rd century BC, Emperor **Qin Shi Huang** had many writings destroyed. In the Middle Ages and the early modern period, books regarded as heresy were burned in Europe. In the 20th century, too, dictatorships destroyed libraries and writings again and again.

On the Bebelplatz in Berlin there is now a special memorial by the artist Micha Ullman. Through a glass panel in the ground you look down into an underground room with **empty bookshelves**. It has room for about 20,000 books, roughly as many as were burned at the time. Every year on 10 May the book burning is remembered in Germany, often with readings from the banned books.

The book burning of 1933 was a warning sign of much worse to come. As early as 1821 the poet **Heinrich Heine** had written that where books are burned, in the end people will be burned too. Sadly, this came true in the Holocaust. Today democracies such as Switzerland protect **freedom of opinion** and freedom of the press in their constitutions.

begriffe.erklaerung: When a government decides what people may read, write or say.
The right to say your own opinion openly.
Targeted promotion of a political idea, often with lies and exaggerations.
A life far from home because you are not safe there.

gewusst: Erich Kästner was the only banned author who watched the Berlin book burning in person.
The memorial on the Bebelplatz can only be seen through a pane of glass in the ground.
Many of the books burned in 1933 are now classics that are read in schools.

teile.einleitung: Internet freedom means that people can use the internet freely. They may look for information, say what they think and share ideas without the state blocking critical websites. But freedom online also means taking responsibility.
wichtigste: With internet freedom the state does not block websites just because they contain criticism.
China blocks many foreign websites with the “Great Firewall”.
In North Korea almost nobody has access to the worldwide internet.
Fake news is deliberately false news.
Before you believe a news story, check where it comes from.
Laws apply on the internet too; cyberbullying is not allowed.

abschnitte.text: On the internet you can look up, learn and share almost anything. **Internet freedom** means that you may use the net freely. The state does not block websites just because they contain criticism. It is closely linked with **freedom of expression** and **freedom of information**. In Switzerland these rights are protected in the Federal Constitution.

Some governments do not want their citizens to be able to read everything. They **block websites**, which then can no longer be opened in the country. In this way they want to hide criticism. **China** blocks many foreign websites; this block is called the “**Great Firewall**”. In **North Korea** only very few people have access to the worldwide internet, and the government controls almost everything.

There is also false news on the internet. News that has been made up on purpose is called **fake news**. It is meant to deceive people or make them angry. That is why it is important to **check** a news story before you believe it or pass it on. Ask yourself: who wrote this? Are other trustworthy **sources** reporting it too?

Freedom online does not mean that everything is allowed. **Laws** apply on the internet too; insults and lies about other people are forbidden. In **cyberbullying** someone is repeatedly insulted or humiliated online. This hurts and is not part of freedom of expression. Anyone who experiences something like this should talk to someone they trust. In Switzerland, for example, the number **147** from Pro Juventute can help.

gewusst: North Korea has its own closed network that is not connected to the worldwide internet.
In Switzerland the phone number 147 for children and young people can be reached around the clock.

teile.einleitung: Georg Elser was a carpenter from Württemberg who in 1939 tried to kill Adolf Hitler with a bomb he had built himself. He acted entirely alone, following his own conscience. Today he is seen as one of the bravest resistance fighters against National Socialism.
wichtigste: Georg Elser was a trained carpenter.
On 8 November 1939 his bomb exploded in the Bürgerbräukeller in Munich.
Hitler had left the hall around 13 minutes earlier.
Elser was caught that same evening at the Swiss border near Konstanz.
He planned and acted without anyone else knowing.
On 9 April 1945 he was murdered in Dachau concentration camp.

abschnitte.text: Georg Elser was born in 1903 and grew up in **Württemberg**. He trained as a **carpenter** and was a very skilled craftsman. Elser rejected the National Socialists. He saw that workers' living conditions were getting worse, freedom was disappearing and Hitler was heading for **war**. So he decided to kill Hitler.

Every year Hitler gave a speech in the **Bürgerbräukeller** in Munich on the anniversary of his attempted coup of 1923. Elser worked secretly in the hall for many nights. He built the bomb with a **time fuse** himself and hid it in a **pillar** behind the speaker's lectern. Nobody else knew, and he planned everything **alone**. That sets him apart from the men of 20 July 1944, who acted as a group.

On the evening of **8 November 1939** Hitler finished his speech earlier than planned. Because of the weather he wanted to travel back by train instead of by plane. He left the hall around **13 minutes** before the explosion. The bomb killed eight people. By then Elser was already on his way to Switzerland. Customs officers stopped him near **Konstanz** and found suspicious objects on him.

For a long time the Gestapo did not believe that one man alone was behind the attack. Elser was held for around five and a half years as a **special prisoner** in the concentration camps of **Sachsenhausen** and **Dachau**. The regime may have wanted to put him on show in a show trial after a victory. On **9 April 1945**, a few weeks before the end of the war, he was shot on orders from above. Only much later was he honoured in Germany as a resistance fighter.

gewusst: Elser acted almost five years before the better-known assassination attempt of 20 July 1944.
Hitler escaped the bomb only because he left the hall around 13 minutes too early.

teile.einleitung: Eritrea is a state in the Horn of Africa, on the Red Sea. The country became independent from Ethiopia in 1993. Since then the same president has ruled without elections, and many young people flee abroad.
wichtigste: Eritrea lies on the Red Sea.
The capital is called Asmara.
Until 1941 Italy was the colonial power.
In 1993 Eritrea became independent from Ethiopia.
Isaias Afwerki has been president since 1993 (as of 2026).
Many young people flee from the unlimited national service.

abschnitte.text: Eritrea lies in the **Horn of Africa**. Its long coastline borders the **Red Sea**. The capital, **Asmara**, lies high up in the highlands. It is known for its modern buildings from the Italian colonial period and has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 2017.

From 1890 Eritrea was an **Italian colony**. In 1941 the British drove out the Italians and administered the territory. Later Eritrea was annexed to **Ethiopia**. A liberation movement fought against this for about 30 years. In 1993 the population voted for **independence**.

**Isaias Afwerki** led the liberation movement and has been president since 1993 (as of 2026). Since independence there has been no national presidential election. Since 2001 all **independent media** have been banned, and many journalists are being held without trial. Eritrea has been at the very bottom of the press freedom ranking for years.

Young people have to do **national service**, in the army or in other work for the state. Officially it lasts 18 months, but in reality it often lasts many years. Experts and the UN describe it as a form of **forced labour** under strict control. This is a main reason why many young people leave the country.

Since about 2010 people from Eritrea have submitted a particularly large number of **asylum applications** in Switzerland. They are among the largest groups of asylum seekers. Today tens of thousands of Eritreans live in Switzerland. How Switzerland should deal with applications from Eritrea is debated politically again and again.

gewusst: Because of its many buildings from the 1930s, Asmara is sometimes called “Little Rome”.
Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a border war from 1998 to 2000 and only made peace in 2018.

teile.einleitung: Juan Carlos I was King of Spain from 1975 to 2014. The dictator Franco had chosen him as his successor, but Juan Carlos helped to turn Spain into a democracy.
wichtigste: Juan Carlos was born in exile in Rome in 1938.
He is the grandson of King Alfonso XIII.
In 1969 Franco named him as his successor.
During the coup attempt in February 1981 he backed the constitution on television.
In 2014 he abdicated, and his son became King Felipe VI.
In 2020 he moved to the United Arab Emirates.

abschnitte.text: His grandfather **Alfonso XIII** was King of Spain until 1931. He left the country when the republic was proclaimed. That is why Juan Carlos was born in **Rome** in 1938. His father **Juan de Borbón** was regarded as the rightful heir to the throne but never became king. Juan Carlos only came to Spain as a child.

The dictator **Francisco Franco** passed over Juan de Borbón. In 1969 he named Juan Carlos as his successor instead. Franco expected Juan Carlos to continue his regime. After Franco's death in 1975 Juan Carlos became king. But he supported the transition to democracy.

In **February 1981** armed plotters occupied the Spanish parliament. During the night the king appeared on **television** in uniform. He ordered the army to protect the constitution. After that the coup collapsed. Since then many Spaniards have seen him as the saviour of democracy.

In 1962 Juan Carlos married **Sofía**, a daughter of King Paul of Greece, in Athens. In June 2014 he abdicated. His son became the new king as **Felipe VI**. Because of allegations about his finances, Juan Carlos left Spain in 2020 and then lived in **Abu Dhabi**.

gewusst: King Juan Carlos I of Spain was born not in Spain but in Rome.
His father was regarded as heir to the throne, but Franco skipped him and chose the son.

teile.einleitung: The Enabling Act of 1933 was a law that gave Adolf Hitler almost unlimited power. With it his government was allowed to pass laws without asking parliament. It was a decisive step by which Germany turned from a democracy into a dictatorship.
wichtigste: The Enabling Act gave Hitler almost unlimited power.
The Reichstag passed it on 23 March 1933.
After that the government was allowed to issue laws without parliament.
Only the SPD voted against it in the Reichstag.
The KPD members of parliament had been arrested or were on the run.
The law practically abolished the separation of powers.
It is regarded as the legal basis of the Nazi dictatorship.

abschnitte.text: Its official name was the **“Law to Remedy the Distress of the People and the Reich”**. It allowed the government under Reich Chancellor **Adolf Hitler** to make laws itself. These laws were even allowed to depart from the constitution. As a result parliament, the **Reichstag**, lost its most important task. The separation of powers had practically been abolished.

Hitler had become Reich Chancellor on 30 January 1933. At the end of February 1933 the Reichstag building in Berlin burned. The Nazis used the **Reichstag fire** to suspend fundamental rights and arrest many communists. Hitler needed a two-thirds majority for the Enabling Act, because it changed the constitution.

On 23 March 1933 the Reichstag met in the **Kroll Opera House** in Berlin, because the Reichstag building had been damaged. Armed men of the SA and SS stood in the hall and outside, intimidating the members of parliament. The KPD members had been arrested or had fled. 444 members voted Yes, among them the Centre Party. Only the 94 **SPD** members present voted No.

The SPD chairman **Otto Wels** explained the No vote in a brave speech. He said that they could be robbed of their freedom and their lives, but not of their honour. It was the last free speech in the Reichstag. Shortly afterwards the SPD was banned, and Wels had to flee into exile.

The Enabling Act marked the start of the **Gleichschaltung**, the forcible bringing into line of the federal states, trade unions, parties and associations. By July 1933 all other parties had been dissolved or banned. At first the law was limited to four years, but it was extended several times. It remained in force until the end of the Second World War in 1945. Because of this experience, Germany’s Basic Law of 1949 protects democracy particularly strongly.

begriffe.erklaerung: The German parliament at that time.
When at least two out of every three people voting have to agree.
The head of government in the German Reich at that time.
A violent fighting force of the Nazi Party.

gewusst: The Enabling Act consisted of only five short articles.
Only after German reunification did the Reichstag building in Berlin, with its present-day glass dome, once again become the seat of parliament.

teile.einleitung: The Milgram experiment is a famous study in psychology that the American Stanley Milgram carried out from 1961. It was meant to show how far people will go when an authority gives them orders. The shocking result: many people follow orders even when they harm others by doing so.
wichtigste: The experiment was carried out by the psychologist Stanley Milgram at Yale University in the USA.
As “teachers”, participants were supposed to give a “learner” electric shocks for mistakes.
In truth there were no real electric shocks; the learner was an actor.
An experimenter in a grey lab coat repeatedly told the participants to carry on.
In the best-known run, about two thirds of the participants went up to the highest level of 450 volts.
The experiment shows that many people obey orders even when they harm others by doing so.
Today the study is considered ethically problematic because the participants were put under great strain.

abschnitte.text: In 1961, the psychologist **Stanley Milgram** began a series of experiments at Yale University in the USA. The participants believed it was a test about learning and punishment. In reality, Milgram wanted to find out how strongly people obey an **authority**. He published the results in 1963.

The participant played the “teacher” and sat in front of a machine with switches from 15 to 450 volts. A supposed “learner” in the next room had to learn pairs of words, and for every mistake the teacher was supposed to give a stronger **electric shock**. But the learner was an actor who was in on it and only pretended to be in pain. When the teacher hesitated, the experimenter calmly said things like “Please continue”.

Beforehand, experts had expected that only very few people would go to the end. In the best-known run, however, 26 out of 40 people, or about **65 per cent**, pressed up to the last switch. Many sweated, trembled or protested, but carried on all the same. In other versions, for example when the victim sat in the same room, far fewer people obeyed.

Milgram wanted to understand how crimes like those under National Socialism could happen. Shortly before, in 1961, the trial of the Nazi perpetrator **Adolf Eichmann** took place in Jerusalem; he had claimed he was following orders. The experiment shows that it is not only “evil” people who do terrible things, but also ordinary people under pressure. Dictatorships exploit exactly this **obedience**.

Many experts criticise the experiment because the participants were deceived and put under great stress. Today such studies have to be checked by an **ethics committee**. The most important lesson is this: you should question orders and listen to your own conscience. Anyone who says no also makes it easier for others to resist.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person whom you believe to have power or knowledge and whom you therefore obey, for example a boss or a police officer.
When you do what someone orders without resisting.
A planned test meant to find something out.
The question of what is right and wrong and how we should treat others.

gewusst: The participants had answered a newspaper advertisement and received a small payment of 4.50 dollars for taking part.
The experiment was later repeated in many countries, and the results were often similar.

teile.einleitung: On 26 April 1937, the Basque town of Guernica was bombed from the air. Thanks to Picasso's famous painting “Guernica”, the attack during the Spanish Civil War became a symbol against war.
wichtigste: Guernica, Gernika in Basque, is in the Basque Country in Spain.
The attack took place on 26 April 1937, on a market day.
The main attackers were the German Condor Legion.
In 1937, Pablo Picasso painted “Guernica” for the World Exhibition in Paris.
The painting is done only in black, white and grey.
Since 1992 it has hung in the Museo Reina Sofía in Madrid.

abschnitte.text: **Guernica**, **Gernika** in Basque, is in the **Basque Country** in the north of Spain. The town is especially important to the Basques. The **Tree of Gernika**, an oak, stands there. In the past, the representatives of the Basques met beneath it. It is an old symbol of Basque freedoms.

In the **Spanish Civil War**, General Franco fought against the Spanish Republic. On **26 April 1937**, Guernica was bombed. It was a market day, and many people were in the town. The main attackers were the **Condor Legion**, a unit of the German air force that supported Franco. Italian aircraft took part as well. The Tree of Gernika survived.

The Spanish Republic had asked **Pablo Picasso** for a painting for its pavilion at the **1937 World Exhibition in Paris**. After the attack, he chose Guernica as his subject. Picasso did without bright colours and painted only in **black, white and grey**. The shades of grey are reminiscent of newspaper photos and strengthen the gloomy effect. The painting is regarded as one of the best-known **anti-war paintings**.

Picasso decided that the painting could only go to a **democratic Spain**. For this reason, it hung in the **Museum of Modern Art** in New York until 1981. After that, it was exhibited for eleven years in the Casón del Buen Retiro, a building belonging to the Prado. Since **1992**, “Guernica” has hung in the **Museo Reina Sofía** in Madrid.

gewusst: “Guernica” only returned to Spain after the end of the Franco dictatorship.
The old Tree of Gernika survived the attack of 1937.

teile.einleitung: A state under the rule of law is a state in which everyone, including the government, is bound by the law. Independent courts, the separation of powers and fundamental rights protect people from arbitrary treatment. A working rule of law is the best protection against a country becoming a dictatorship.
wichtigste: Under the rule of law, everyone has to obey the law, including the government.
Power is shared among parliament, the government and the courts; this is called the separation of powers.
Independent courts check whether laws are applied correctly.
Fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and equality before the law protect everyone.
Separation of powers, free elections, free media and independent courts protect a country from dictatorship.
Regular free elections and independent courts are signs that power is kept in check.
Switzerland is a state under the rule of law; its highest court is the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne.

abschnitte.titel: What is the rule of law?
abschnitte.text: Under the **rule of law**, it is not the powerful who decide as they please, but the **law**. Laws are made in a set procedure and apply equally to everyone. Presidents, ministers and police officers may not simply do what they want either. Article 5 of the Swiss Federal Constitution says that the law is the basis and the limit of all state activity.

Power in the state is shared among three branches; this is called the **separation of powers**. Parliament makes the laws, the government carries them out and the courts administer justice. In Switzerland these are the **Federal Assembly**, the **Federal Council** and the Federal Supreme Court. The French thinker Montesquieu made the idea famous in the 18th century.

Under the rule of law, courts may not be influenced by the government. Everyone can defend themselves in court if they feel the state has treated them unfairly. Until a verdict is reached, the **presumption of innocence** applies, meaning that you are considered innocent until your guilt is proven. The Swiss Federal Supreme Court is based in Lausanne, with parts of it also in Lucerne.

Under the rule of law, every person has **fundamental rights**, for example freedom of expression, freedom of religion and protection from torture. All people are equal before the law, whether rich or poor. Anyone who is arrested is entitled to a lawyer and a fair trial. In 1974 Switzerland also joined the European Convention on Human Rights.

In a dictatorship these safeguards are missing: a ruler can control the courts and the media and lock up opponents. That is why the rule of law is seen as the best protection against abuse of power. Particularly important are the **separation of powers**, regular free elections, free media and independent courts. Many dictatorships began with these protections being dismantled step by step.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sharing of state power among parliament, the government and the courts.
Everyone is considered innocent until a court has proven their guilt.
When someone decides without rules, just as they please.
Important rights that every person has and that are protected by the state.

gewusst: The goddess of justice, Justitia, is often shown blindfolded, because the law should apply equally to everyone.
Anyone in Switzerland who has gone through all the courts can still turn to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.

teile.einleitung: Mobutu Sese Seko ruled the Congo, which he called Zaire, as a dictator from 1965 to 1997. He enriched himself from the state without limit, while the people stayed poor. For a long time he was supported by the West.
wichtigste: Mobutu came to power in a military coup in 1965.
In 1971 he renamed his country Zaire.
His trademark was a leopard-skin hat.
His rule is seen as an example of a kleptocracy.
Western countries saw him as an ally against communism.
In 1997 he was overthrown by Laurent-Désiré Kabila.

abschnitte.text: The Congo became independent from Belgium in 1960. Soon there were serious conflicts. The first prime minister was **Patrice Lumumba**. He was murdered in January 1961 with the involvement of Mobutu's people. At that time Mobutu was an officer. In 1965 he finally took power with a **military coup** and soon allowed only one party.

In 1971 Mobutu gave the country the name **Zaire**. With the campaign **Authenticité**, meaning “authenticity”, Western first names and clothing were to be replaced by African ones. He now called himself Mobutu Sese Seko. His trademark was a **leopard-skin hat**. For a time, suits with ties were banned.

Mobutu and his followers took huge sums from the state treasury. Such rule is called a **kleptocracy**, which means “rule by thieves”. The country is rich in mineral resources such as copper and diamonds, but most people stayed poor. Roads, schools and hospitals fell into ruin.

During the **Cold War**, the USA and other Western countries supported Mobutu for a long time. He was seen as an **ally against communism**. That is why his crimes were often overlooked. In 1974 the famous boxing match **Rumble in the Jungle** between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman took place in the capital **Kinshasa**.

After the end of the Cold War, Mobutu lost a lot of support. In 1996 an uprising began under **Laurent-Désiré Kabila**. In May 1997 Mobutu fled, and Kabila took power. Since then the country has again been called the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Mobutu died in exile in Morocco in September 1997.

gewusst: In 1997, Switzerland froze Mobutu's money in Swiss banks.
For the “Rumble in the Jungle” fight, each boxer received several million dollars, paid by Mobutu's government.

teile.einleitung: The March on Rome was a takeover of power by the Italian fascists in October 1922. Thousands of supporters of Benito Mussolini moved towards the capital. In the end, the king appointed Mussolini head of government, and Italy became a dictatorship step by step.
wichtigste: The March on Rome took place at the end of October 1922.
Benito Mussolini was at the head of the fascist movement.
The march was led by four leaders, the Quadrumvirate.
King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign the state of emergency.
After that, he appointed Mussolini head of government.
Mussolini had himself called “Duce”, which means “leader”.

abschnitte.titel: Italy after the First World War
abschnitte.text: After the First World War, Italy was in a bad way. There was unemployment, there were strikes and there was a lot of discontent. In 1919, **Benito Mussolini** founded a movement from which the **fascists** emerged. Their supporters wore black shirts and often used violence against political opponents. Before that, Mussolini had worked, among other things, as a **journalist**.

At the end of October 1922, thousands of **Blackshirts** gathered and moved towards Rome. The march was led by four leaders, the **Quadrumvirate**. The word means “group of four men”. The fascists wanted to put pressure on the government and come to power themselves.

Prime Minister **Luigi Facta** wanted to declare a **state of siege** so that the army could stop the fascists. But King **Victor Emmanuel III** refused to sign. Facta resigned. Instead, the king offered Mussolini the post of head of government. Mussolini had stayed in Milan and travelled to Rome on the **night train**, where he was appointed on 30 October 1922.

At first, Mussolini governed together with other parties. In the following years, however, he expanded his power more and more. Other parties were banned, and the press was controlled. Mussolini had himself called **Duce**, which means “leader”. Italy became a **fascist dictatorship**.

The March on Rome became a model for other movements. In Germany, Adolf Hitler tried to come to power in a similar way in 1923 with the **Beer Hall Putsch** in Munich. However, the putsch failed. Later, Mussolini and Hitler worked closely together.

gewusst: Mussolini himself did not march at all but travelled comfortably to Rome by train.
As a young man, Mussolini lived in Switzerland for a while.

teile.einleitung: Idi Amin was an officer who ruled the East African country of Uganda as a dictator from 1971 to 1979. A central feature of his rule was the brutal persecution of political opponents, with mass killings. He is seen as one of the cruellest dictators in Africa in the 20th century.
wichtigste: Idi Amin ruled Uganda as a dictator from 1971 to 1979.
He came to power through a military coup.
His rule was marked by brutal persecution of political opponents and mass killings.
Estimates speak of 100,000 to 500,000 deaths.
In 1972 he expelled the Asian minority from Uganda.
In 1979 he was overthrown by troops from Tanzania and Ugandan rebels.
He died in exile in Saudi Arabia in 2003.

abschnitte.text: **Idi Amin** was born around 1925 in north-western Uganda; his exact date of birth is not known. Uganda was a British colony at the time. Amin joined the British colonial army and gradually rose through the ranks. He was tall and strong and was Ugandan heavyweight boxing champion for several years. After Uganda became independent in 1962 he became a senior officer.

On 25 January 1971 Amin took power in a **military coup**. President Milton Obote was abroad at the time. At first many people cheered because Amin promised improvements. But soon he had soldiers and officers killed whom he considered unreliable. He ruled without a parliament and without elections.

Amin had political opponents, journalists, judges, clergy and entire ethnic groups persecuted. His secret services arrested, tortured and killed people without trial. Experts estimate the number of victims at 100,000 to 500,000 people. Amin gave himself grand titles and medals. This **personality cult** was meant to display his power.

In 1972 Amin ordered all people of Asian origin, mainly families with roots in India, to leave Uganda within 90 days. Tens of thousands lost their homes and businesses, and many went to Great Britain. After that the country's **economy** collapsed. In 1976 a hijacked passenger plane landed at **Entebbe** airport, and Amin supported the hijackers. An Israeli special forces unit freed the hostages.

In 1978 Amin sent troops into neighbouring **Tanzania**. Tanzania struck back, and together with Ugandan rebels, Tanzanian soldiers captured the capital Kampala in April 1979. Amin fled first to Libya and later to **Saudi Arabia**. He lived there until his death on 16 August 2003, without ever being put on trial. Uganda took many years to recover from his rule.

begriffe.erklaerung: When the military overthrows a government by force.
A territory that is ruled by a foreign state.
The exaggerated worship of a ruler.
A person who is held captive in order to force others to do something.

gewusst: Among other things, Idi Amin called himself “Field Marshal” and “Conqueror of the British Empire”.
Most of the Asians expelled from Uganda found a new home in Great Britain.

teile.einleitung: Write for Rights (in German “Briefmarathon”, letter marathon) is a worldwide campaign by Amnesty International. Every year people write letters for individuals whose human rights are being violated. Together they want to put pressure on governments.
wichtigste: Amnesty International organises Write for Rights every year.
It takes place around Human Rights Day on 10 December.
The letters go mainly to governments and authorities.
The campaign began in Poland in 2001.
In German it is called the “Briefmarathon”.

abschnitte.text: Every year Amnesty presents a few **individuals** or groups who are in danger. Some are in prison although they are innocent, others are being threatened. Participants write to **governments and authorities** and demand that prisoners be released or that injustice be ended. In addition there are **letters of solidarity** to the people affected, so that they know they have not been forgotten.

Write for Rights takes place around **Human Rights Day** on 10 December. On this day in 1948 the UN adopted the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights**. It says that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. Many schools, clubs and families take part, including in Switzerland.

The campaign began in **Poland in 2001**. After that it spread to many countries. In English it is called **“Write for Rights”**. Today people in a great many countries write about the same cases at the same time every year.

In 1961 the London lawyer **Peter Benenson** published a newspaper article about forgotten prisoners. With it he founded **Amnesty International**. The organisation campaigns against torture, against the death penalty and for political prisoners. In 1977 it was awarded the **Nobel Peace Prize**. Amnesty’s symbol is a candle wrapped in barbed wire.

gewusst: After a Write for Rights campaign, people for whom many letters were written are sometimes released.
Letters from many countries show a government that the world is watching closely.

teile.einleitung: The Kim dynasty is the family that has ruled North Korea since it was founded. Power passed from the grandfather Kim Il-sung to his son Kim Jong-il and then to his grandson Kim Jong-un.
wichtigste: North Korea was founded on 9 September 1948 under Kim Il-sung.
After his death in 1994 his son Kim Jong-il took over the leadership.
Since the constitution of 1998 Kim Il-sung has been regarded as “Eternal President”.
Kim Jong-il relied on the Songun policy, “military first”.
Since 2012 Kim Jong-un has been at the head of the Workers' Party of Korea.
Kim Il-sung and Kim Jong-il lie in the Kumsusan Palace of the Sun in Pyongyang.

abschnitte.text: On **9 September 1948** the **Democratic People's Republic of Korea** was proclaimed in the north of Korea, with **Kim Il-sung** at its head. Shortly before, the Republic of Korea had been founded in the south. Kim Il-sung died in 1994. The constitution of 1998 declared him **“Eternal President”**. The country is governed by the **Workers' Party of Korea**.

After his father's death, **Kim Jong-il** led North Korea from 1994 until December 2011. This is seen as the first hereditary transfer of power in a Communist state. His policy was called **Songun**, which means “military first”. Propaganda claims he was born on the sacred mountain of **Paektu**. However, historians believe he was born in 1941 in a Soviet military camp near Khabarovsk.

Since 2012 **Kim Jong-un** has been at the head of the party. According to media reports, he is said to have gone to school under a false name in the **Bern area** in the 1990s. Schools in Gümligen and Liebefeld are mentioned. This is not completely certain. However, the authorities confirmed that there was a North Korean pupil in Köniz.

The ruling family tolerates no rivals. In February 2017 **Kim Jong-nam**, a half-brother of Kim Jong-un, was attacked with the nerve agent **VX** at the airport in **Kuala Lumpur** in Malaysia and died. He was Kim Jong-il's eldest son and lived in exile. In the **Kumsusan Palace of the Sun** in Pyongyang, Kim Il-sung and Kim Jong-il lie embalmed on display.

gewusst: According to the constitution, a dead man is still North Korea's “Eternal President” today.
The Kumsusan Palace of the Sun used to be Kim Il-sung's official residence.

teile.einleitung: From 1976 to 1983, Argentina was ruled by a military dictatorship that was one of the cruellest in South America. Thousands of people were persecuted, tortured and murdered, and many disappeared without a trace. To this day these victims are called the “Desaparecidos”, the disappeared.
wichtigste: On 24 March 1976, the military overthrew President Isabel Perón.
A military junta under General Jorge Rafael Videla took power.
The persecution of opponents of the government is called the “Dirty War”.
“Desaparecidos” are people who disappeared without a trace because the government persecuted them.
Human rights groups estimate the number of the disappeared at up to 30,000.
The mothers of the disappeared protested every week in the Plaza de Mayo in Buenos Aires.
After defeat in the Falklands War in 1982, the dictatorship collapsed, and democracy returned in 1983.

abschnitte.text: Argentina is in the south of South America, and its capital is **Buenos Aires**. On **24 March 1976**, the military removed President Isabel Perón. At that time the country was marked by an economic crisis and political violence. The new junta under **Jorge Rafael Videla** called its rule the “Process of National Reorganisation”.

The dictatorship had people arrested whom it considered opponents: students, trade unionists, journalists, teachers and many others. They were taken to secret camps, tortured and often murdered. Because the government denied what it had done, the families did not know what had happened. These victims are called **Desaparecidos**, meaning “the disappeared”.

The term **“Dirty War”** refers to the state persecution and murder of supposed opponents of the government. Some prisoners were drugged and thrown out of aircraft over the sea; these are known as **death flights**. Babies of imprisoned women were taken away from their mothers and given to other families. Some of these children are still searching for their true origins today.

abschnitte.titel: The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo
abschnitte.text: From 1977, mothers of the disappeared met every Thursday in front of the presidential palace in the **Plaza de Mayo**. They wore white headscarves and asked publicly: where are our children? Later, the “Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo” searched for their stolen grandchildren. With the help of genetic tests, well over a hundred of these children were able to find their families again.

abschnitte.titel: End and coming to terms with the past
abschnitte.text: In 1982, Argentina lost the **Falklands War** against Great Britain, after which the junta lost its support. In October 1983, Raúl Alfonsín was elected president in free elections. A commission collected the crimes in the report **“Nunca más”**, which means “Never again”. Several generals, including Videla, were later put on trial and convicted.

begriffe.erklaerung: Spanish for “the disappeared”: victims who were secretly abducted by the dictatorship.
A group of military officers who govern together.
Rights that all people have, for example the right to life and freedom.

begriffe.wort: Coming to terms with the past
begriffe.erklaerung: Carefully investigating past crimes so that they are not forgotten.

gewusst: During the dictatorship, the 1978 Football World Cup took place in Argentina, and Argentina became world champions.
Today 24 March is a national day of remembrance for the victims of the dictatorship in Argentina.

teile.einleitung: The Führer principle was a basic rule of the National Socialists in Germany. It meant that it was not elections or majorities that decided, but a “leader” (Führer) whom everyone had to obey. At the top stood Adolf Hitler, who answered to nobody.
wichtigste: The short formula was “authority downwards, responsibility upwards”.
The Führer principle replaced elections and majority decisions with appointment from above.
It had applied in the Nazi party since 1921.
From 1934 employers were called “works leaders” and their employees “followers”.
Gauleiters ran the party districts and answered directly to Hitler.
Historians nevertheless speak of a polycracy, meaning many rival centres of power.

abschnitte.text: Under the **Führer principle**, every leader could give orders to those below him. He was only answerable to the next leader above. The short formula was “**authority downwards, responsibility upwards**”. At the very top stood Hitler, who did not have to answer to anyone. The slogan “Führer, command, we follow!” shows what was demanded: carrying out orders without objection.

abschnitte.titel: The end of having a say
abschnitte.text: As early as July 1921 Hitler made sure he became chairman of the **Nazi party** with dictatorial powers. After 1933 the National Socialists extended the principle to the state, local authorities and associations. Leaders were no longer elected but **appointed** from above. Votes and **majority decisions** were considered “un-German” and were abolished. This is the opposite of a democracy in which, as in Switzerland, the people have a say.

Within the party, the Reich was divided into **Gaue** (districts). Each was headed by a **Gauleiter**, who answered directly to Hitler and had great power in his region. The “Law for the Ordering of National Labour” of 1934 brought the principle into businesses too. The employer became the “**works leader**”, and the employees became the “**followers**”, who owed him loyalty.

From the outside the Nazi state looked strictly organised. In reality, the party, the state, the SS and special commissioners often had the same tasks and competed with one another. Historians call this a **polycracy**, rule by many centres of power. The British historian **Ian Kershaw** made the phrase famous that people had to “work towards the Führer”. Many officials tried, without precise orders, to anticipate what they thought Hitler wanted, and so drove the radicalisation forward.

gewusst: The phrase “working towards the Führer” comes from a speech by a Nazi official in 1934.
At universities, too, the rector was no longer elected but appointed as a “Führer rector”.
